#5294. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

#5293. Ripple's RLUSD Overtakes PayPal's PYUSD

Ripple's US dollar-backed stablecoin RLUSD has set a new record by surpassing PayPal USD (PYUSD) in market capitalization to cement its position as a top stablecoin globally.

Recent data from CoinGecko shows that RLUSD's market cap has grown to around $2.71 billion, enabling it to surpass its competitor, PayPal's stablecoin, with a market cap of around $2.69 billion.

This milestone was achieved less than two years after Ripple's formal introduction of RLUSD in December 2024, underscoring its rapid growth in the crypto market.

A prominent XRP Ledger validator, Vet, also commented on this development to underscore the increasing significance of RLUSD in the stablecoin industry.

"RLUSD is now a Top 5 USD backed stablecoin. On its way to be in Top 3," Vet commented.

Vet noted Ripple's long-standing contribution to building the XRP Ledger. He added that the increasing adoption of RLUSD could potentially lead to faster adoption of the blockchain by traditional financial institutions.

Vet stressed the increasing relevance of RLUSD's rising payment volume and increased use of the stablecoin on the XRP Ledger.

He also noted that RLUSD has opened the door to numerous integrations with banks and crypto exchanges.

The XRP Ledger validator further noted that these integrations could motivate financial institutions to not only run infrastructure to support the XRPL but also integrate other tokenized assets on it.

This new record for RLUSD comes on the back of several key institutional partnerships and exchange integrations for RLUSD that Ripple has been announcing recently.

On Oct. 28, Ripple announced a partnership with Coinbase to provide RLUSD for retail and institutional users across Coinbase Exchange, Coinbase Prime and its retail trading app.

As part of the partnership, Coinbase also announced support for RLUSD across different blockchain networks such as the XRP Ledger, Ethereum and Base.

On the other hand, Ripple's partnership with banking giant BNY, which is the custodian of reserves for RLUSD, is also deepening.

Besides this, Ripple has also managed to secure support from Standard Chartered, which launched institutional custody services for RLUSD on the XRP Ledger back in October.

#5292. XRP Price Prediction: Bears Are Paying to Short XRP, A Short Squeeze?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is struggling to reclaim $1, but its derivatives market is showing an increasingly unusual setup. Traders betting against the token are now paying funding fees to maintain their positions. This creates an interesting possibility for the XRP price prediction. If buying pressure returns, bearish traders could face mounting losses and forced liquidations.

However, the market is not quite ready for a bullish victory lap. Open interest is falling, long positions have already suffered heavy liquidations, and XRP still needs to reclaim important resistance levels.

XRP traded around $0.95, following another difficult session for the crypto market. Meanwhile, its futures market is flashing a rate that dropped in aggregated funding to -0.0068% every eight hours, equivalent to roughly -7.4% annually.

Negative funding means short sellers pay long traders to maintain their perpetual futures positions. In other words, bears are effectively paying a premium to maintain their bearish exposure.

Hyperliquid showed an even more pronounced imbalance, with XRP funding reaching approximately -10.2% annually. The figures suggest bearish positioning has become increasingly expensive across several derivatives markets.

However, there is another side to this trade. XRP open interest declined 5.74% over 24 hours to approximately $1.97 billion, so traders are reducing leverage rather than aggressively opening fresh positions.

While XRP traders debate whether another recovery is coming, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is approaching an important milestone of its own. The Bitcoin Layer 2 project has raised more than $33.2 million during its presale, with its token currently priced at just $0.0136.

The presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, leaving a narrowing window before its anticipated token launch. Buyers choosing the staking option are also being offered an advertised 35% APY during the presale period.

Bitcoin Hyper aims to bring faster Bitcoin transactions and decentralized applications to a new Layer 2 environment. Its architecture combines Solana Virtual Machine execution with zero-knowledge proofs and Bitcoin settlement.

The project has already introduced testnet components, including its explorer, wallet, faucet, and bridge. With the presale approaching its scheduled conclusion, the remaining allocation and upcoming launch milestone could attract additional attention from traders looking beyond established crypto networks.

The immediate question is whether bearish positioning has become sufficiently expensive to trigger an unexpected reversal. A negative funding rate alone cannot confirm a short squeeze. XRP needs to attract fresh spot buyers, recover momentum, and force short sellers to close their positions.

The first important hurdle remains $1.00. Reclaiming this psychological level could encourage sidelined buyers to return and create additional pressure on leveraged shorts.

A sustained move above $1.00 would put $1.10 within reach, followed by a potential test of $1.20 if short liquidations accelerate.

However, the bearish scenario remains firmly in play. Losing the recent $0.89 low could expose XRP to another decline toward $0.80, particularly if Bitcoin continues weakening.

For now, the XRP price prediction hinges on whether negative funding translates into actual buying pressure. Bears are paying longs, but bulls still need to deliver the rally. If they do, the same traders betting against XRP could become the fuel behind its next recovery.

#5291. XRP, Dogecoin, and Solana Doomed? Billionaire Tim Draper Predicts Altcoins Will Be Absorbed By Bitcoin — Here’s Why

Could Ripple’s XRP, Dogecoin, and Solana eventually lose their place in the crypto market as Bitcoin strengthens its dominance? Billionaire investor Tim Draper believes the future of cryptocurrencies could look very different, predicting that altcoins will eventually be absorbed by Bitcoin.

Draper’s bold forecast raises fresh questions about the long-term survival of major digital assets and whether BTC’s growing influence could ultimately leave even established altcoins struggling to remain relevant.

Tim Draper has drawn a striking comparison between Bitcoin’s potential dominance and Microsoft’s rise to power in the software industry, arguing that the OG crypto could eventually absorb innovations pioneered by competing digital assets.

In a recent post on X, Draper suggested that Bitcoin could follow a similar path to Microsoft, which built its dominance not necessarily by inventing popular software applications but by incorporating successful innovations into its broader ecosystem.

To illustrate his argument, Draper pointed to Microsoft’s handling of early software pioneers such as Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect. Although these companies helped establish demand for spreadsheet and word-processing applications, Microsoft eventually introduced Excel and Word and integrated both into its operating system. The company also acquired PowerPoint early on, turning the presentation software into another core part of its productivity suite.

According to Draper, this strategy allowed Microsoft to absorb successful ideas while the companies that initially popularized them gradually lost their competitive edge. He believes Bitcoin could follow the same playbook, with alternative cryptocurrencies serving as testing grounds for innovations that could eventually migrate to the Bitcoin network.

“Altcoins are the Lotus 1-2-3s and WordPerfects of this era,” Draper wrote, arguing that competing blockchain projects may demonstrate the value of new technologies before Bitcoin adopts them. In his view, Bitcoin’s powerful network effects and growing ecosystem could give it the gravitational pull needed to attract innovations from across the broader cryptocurrency industry.

Draper further supported his argument by highlighting Bitcoin’s expanding share of the overall cryptocurrency market. The billionaire recalled watching the flagship cryptocurrency’s market dominance climb from approximately 40% to 50% and eventually reach 61%. He views this steady increase as evidence of Bitcoin’s growing influence and its ability to strengthen its position despite the emergence of thousands of competing digital assets.

“Bitcoin is that platform,” Draper asserted.

If his prediction proves accurate, established altcoins such as Ripple-linked XRP, Dogecoin (DOGE), and Solana (SOL) could face an increasingly challenging competitive environment. Each has built its reputation around distinct use cases and communities, but Draper’s argument suggests that Bitcoin could eventually incorporate innovations that currently give these competing networks their appeal.

For instance, XRP is best known for its focus on cross-border payments and the expanding financial ecosystem built around the XRP Ledger. Dogecoin, meanwhile, has evolved from an internet meme into one of the cryptocurrency market’s most recognizable assets, backed by a dedicated community. Solana, on the other hand, has established itself as a major smart contract platform, attracting developers with its high transaction speeds and relatively low fees while supporting a diverse ecosystem of decentralized finance (DeFi), NFTs, meme coins, and tokenized real-world assets.

Ultimately, Draper’s thesis is that these innovations could be a boon for BTC rather than guarantee the long-term dominance of the altcoins that pioneered or popularized them.

#5290. XRP, ETH, DOGE: Tim Draper Predicts Bitcoin to Absorb Altcoins

Billionaire and longtime Bitcoin (BTC) supporter Tim Draper predicts a future where Bitcoin absorbs the innovations of other altcoins.

Draper's statement has major implications for big cryptocurrencies like XRP, Ethereum (ETH) and Dogecoin (DOGE), which have built their own ecosystems and now compete in the wider cryptocurrency market.

In a recent post on X, Draper compared Bitcoin's rising dominance to Microsoft's path to becoming the dominant software company, as the company absorbed successful innovations from other businesses.

"Microsoft never invented the spreadsheet, word processor, or slide deck. They absorbed them," stated Draper.

The billionaire investor brought up pioneering software like Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect, which eventually saw their dominance give way to Microsoft's Excel and Word.

Draper predicts that this could apply to the cryptocurrency industry, as Bitcoin could become the ultimate absorber of innovations from alternative blockchain networks.

"Altcoins are the Lotus 1-2-3s and WordPerfects of this time," wrote Draper.

Smaller cryptocurrencies are thus essentially incubators for technological innovations that could eventually become part of the bigger Bitcoin ecosystem, according to Draper.

"They show that it works, then the innovation that pulls the strongest gets ported to the Bitcoin platform," he added.

Draper also supported his statement by citing the rising market share of Bitcoin in the overall cryptocurrency market.

The billionaire investor recalled observing how Bitcoin dominance rose from about 40% to 50% and then even further to 61%.

"Bitcoin is that platform," said Draper, claiming that the biggest cryptocurrency could follow a path similar to Microsoft's.

This statement has implications for the future of big altcoins like Ethereum, XRP and Dogecoin.

Ethereum is the leading smart contract and dApp platform, while XRP is mainly known for its cross-border payments and the wider XRP Ledger ecosystem. Meanwhile, Dogecoin is one of the most iconic meme coins in the cryptocurrency market.

Still, the growing ecosystem around Bitcoin, which adds more scaling and programmability through solutions such as the Lightning Network and projects like Stacks, shows how Bitcoin is trying to expand beyond its basic use case as a cryptocurrency.

Binance said on Monday, November 16, that it will pass the next Microsoft and Applied Materials cash dividends to holders of its tokenized stocks, MSFTB and AMATB. It will snapshot balances on Thursday, November 19, the same day both stocks go ex-dividend.

Tokenized stocks are crypto tokens that track a real share, held by a custodian, and trade around the clock. Binance’s versions, called bStocks, do not pay the dividend in cash. Instead, the net amount is reinvested, and each holder’s token balance grows slightly.

We compared both tokens with the real shares since late August. During market hours, they tracked closely. Over weekends, their price called Monday’s opening move only half the time.

Here is what holders get, and what the token prices tell traders this week.

Both companies declared their payouts in September. Microsoft will pay $0.98 a share, up from $0.91. Applied Materials, a maker of chipmaking equipment, will pay $0.53 a share. Both go to shareholders of record on November 19 and are paid on December 10.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

Binance does not state the tax rate. The standard U.S. rate on dividends paid to foreign holders without a tax treaty is 30%. At that rate, we worked out what holders get:

A dividend only matters if the token tracks the stock. So we compared both tokens with the real shares, using Binance hourly candles and Nasdaq prices since late August.

During market hours, the match is close. At the Nasdaq close, the tokens sat at a median 0.06% from the official closing price across 58 sessions. The widest gap was 0.28%.

Weekends are different. The tokens keep trading while Wall Street is shut, so we checked whether their weekend price predicted Monday’s opening move.

Thin trading in tokenized stocks explains part of it. MSFTB traded about $183,000 in the past 24 hours on Binance, and AMATB about $114,000. This weekend, AMATB stood 1.8% below Friday’s $370.50 close on Sunday night, while MSFTB was down 0.2%. On our numbers, those weekend quotes said little about where the stocks would open.

On the 4-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, MSFTB trades at $527.61 on Binance. It sits just above its 50-period exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $526.02, and its 200-period EMA at $526.95. With both averages flat and close together, the trend is neutral.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

For holders of tokenized stocks, the dividend adds about a tenth of a percent to their balance this quarter. The bigger lesson is in timing: on weekdays, the tokens follow the stock, but weekend prices are a weak guide to Monday.

Meanwhile, Chainlink's struggles in the market continue. The price has already broken below the 200-period moving average, and it's now in something of a free fall. LINK is trading at around $9.89, with the asset losing the $10 level as the decline continues.

The next support area in this scenario is around $8.20; below this, another potential support sits near $7. There are earlier trading ranges between the current price and those levels, so the path down isn't necessarily clear. However, a drop towards the lower level would essentially invalidate all of the gains LINK has seen since June.

Overall, the situation isn't much different from that of other tokens. If we overlay the charts for Stellar, Chainlink, Ethereum and others, we'll get roughly the same picture: recovery attempts followed by renewed pressure.

The difference is that with LINK, we might see an additional spike in volatility that quickly weakens the possibility of a rapid rebound, as the moving averages are only just converging. Such a move would be especially damaging if sellers remain in control. When a downtrend is accelerating, the price drop can become critical.

Overall, positive factors for LINK are quite hard to find right now. Despite the fact that the RSI is already approaching the oversold zone, LINK could still find a way to drop even lower.

A recovery is unlikely until a catalyst emerges in the broader market, with higher highs and sustained buying needed to show that the asset is finally moving towards a proper recovery.

Although Cardano usually follows the rest of the cryptocurrency market, here we see a situation similar to the three other tokens we have already discussed. The asset has already broken a fairly strong support that formed around $0.20, and the next potential buying area is now under substantial pressure, being tested around $0.17.

Apart from that, Cardano has already dropped below the halfway point of the recovery from June to October. Despite the RSI already showing oversold conditions, we aren't seeing much room for a bounce here.

On the positive side, volume is clearly moving down and isn't adding strength to the downtrend, which is a substantial advantage. We should also keep in mind that without a bullish catalyst, we most likely won't see a quick recovery here.

There is even a slight increase in volume compared with the beginning of November, hinting at the possibility that bears still have enough strength to pull the price down. The moving averages could come together closer to the next support, which might become the basis for a faster price surge. However, this is not guaranteed at this point.

Overall, Cardano has been in a downtrend since 2025, so the local spikes we could see from July to October shouldn't be taken as a guaranteed sign that the asset is recovering. Even though the price previously broke above the 200-day moving average, that wasn't enough to keep the recovery going.

Cardano might eventually move above it again and go further, but that is not guaranteed either.

#5286. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

#5284. XRP Ledger Announces Major Fix to Come December 3

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) will be delivering a major update on Dec. 3, which will address the occasional sluggishness the blockchain network has been experiencing in recent weeks.

As stated in a recent XRP Ledger Operations announcement, the network will be rolling out its new version 3.5.0, which will exclusively include technical improvements and bug fixes, such as a lasting fix for the relatively slow ledger closing times.

"XRPL version 3.5.0 will be on Dec 3. Just improvements/fixes, including a long-lasting fix for the occasional slow ledger close times," XRP Ledger Operations said.

The developers have informed users that the interim fixes to help improve the situation have already been working effectively.

"Interim fixes already helped improve close times, and we are watching the network very closely," it added.

This is a critical advancement in improving the reliability of the XRP Ledger, a network widely used to process cryptocurrency payments, tokenization, and stablecoin transactions.

The latest improvement to the XRPL comes after the blockchain network suffered technical issues in October, when some ledgers were closing much slower than usual.

The XRP Ledger usually closes new ledgers once every three to five seconds. This ensures that transaction confirmations happen fairly quickly.

However, intermittent sluggishness was seen on the network, as XRP Ledger Operations admitted on Oct. 21. The team later confirmed that its developers were already working on the issue.

Afterward, XRP Ledger Operations started sharing a recommended configuration update for xrpld software with network operators such as validators and other infrastructure providers.

The temporary fixes were helpful. On Oct. 22, XRP Ledger Operations shared that the occasional slower ledger closures were no longer happening, thanks to the new recommended configuration.

That said, the developers remain hard at work to deliver a software fix that will correct the issue once and for all, a long-term solution that would not rely solely on temporary changes.

That is why the December release is expected to finally bring that permanent fix.

In the meantime, Vet, one of the notable XRP Ledger validators, has already assured the community that the blockchain network is always being monitored as developers work on more improvements.

In a recent post on X, he stressed that a great amount of work has been put into network monitoring, information security and engineering.

Vet said that their engineers are always on call to address any possible incidents.

Strategy said on Monday, November 16, that it bought 485 Bitcoin last week for $33.4 million, less than half of the 1,036 BTC it bought the week before. MSTR stock fell 6% at Monday’s open to about $105 as Michael Saylor’s company, which now holds 850,849 BTC, slowed its buying.

The same filing shows where most of the money went. Strategy spent $228.1 million buying back its own preferred stock, STRC, nearly seven times what it spent on Bitcoin.

Strategy has acquired 485 $BTC and repurchased $228M of $STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/9dZBx810Wi

We added up Strategy’s weekly filings since mid-October. Over five weeks, it spent about $1 billion on preferred buybacks and about $200 million on Bitcoin. MSTR stock, Strategy’s common shares, fell 6% at Monday’s open to about $105. Bitcoin itself trades near $65,000, down 21% since early October.

So why are Strategy’s Bitcoin buys slowing, and what is MSTR stock doing?

Explore: Binance Pays Microsoft and Applied Materials Dividends on Tokenized Stocks: How Much Holders Get

Strategy reports its purchases every Monday in a filing with the SEC called an 8-K. Its latest filing covers November 9 to 15. We lined it up with the four before it.

STRC, nicknamed “Stretch,” is a preferred share that pays a monthly dividend and is meant to trade near $100. It fell to about $85 in July and is back at $99.60, close to that target. Buying it back cuts Strategy’s dividend bill, which runs at about $1.43 billion a year across all its preferred shares.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

The second reason is the price of MSTR stock itself. Strategy pays for most purchases by selling new MSTR shares. That works best when the stock trades well above the value of the Bitcoin behind each share.

Strategy’s own dashboard puts that ratio, called mNAV, at 1.11. At that level, selling shares adds little Bitcoin per share, so each new share does less for existing holders. Last week, Strategy sold $244.7 million of MSTR, but only $33.4 million of it went into Bitcoin.

MSTR stock has fallen faster than Bitcoin:

There is also a limit on the buybacks. Strategy has $332.2 million left under its preferred repurchase program, less than two weeks at the current pace. Once it runs out, Strategy has to choose between raising the limit and moving that money back to Bitcoin.

On the daily chart of Hyperliquid’s 24/7 MSTR contract, the stock trades at $104.75. It sits below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $131.98, and its 200-day EMA at $133.37.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Strategy has not stopped buying Bitcoin, but it has changed its priorities. For MSTR stock, next Monday’s filing is the one to watch. A bigger Bitcoin buy would show the cash is moving back to Bitcoin. Another week dominated by STRC would point the other way.

#5282. Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Address From 2010 Suddenly Activates With $3.4 Million

A Bitcoin (BTC) address from 2010 has become active after being dormant for over 16 years. The address has transferred around $3.4 million in BTC.

According to blockchain tracking platform Whale Alert, the address held 50 BTC, which was roughly equivalent to $3,442,939 at the time of activation.

The dormant address had been inactive for 16.2 years. Back in BTC's early days, all 50 BTC were worth just $3.

Notably, this wasn’t the only old Bitcoin address that suddenly became active.

According to Whale Alert, another dormant Bitcoin address holding 50 BTC worth roughly $3,442,129 became active after 16.2 years.

The two transfers took place within minutes of each other on Nov. 13. Hence, the total value of the newly activated Bitcoin comes to around $6.89 million.

There’s no confirmation about who owned these wallets. Also, it’s not confirmed if the same individual or entity owns these addresses.

The reason these addresses are significant is that they date back to 2010, which is considered to be the Satoshi era.

In simple terms, the Satoshi era refers to the first few years of Bitcoin, mainly 2009 and 2010. During those years, the pseudonymous founder of Bitcoin, Satoshi Nakamoto, was pretty active in the network's development.

To be precise, Bitcoin came into existence in January 2009. It initially carried a block reward of 50 BTC. This block reward of 50 BTC continued until Bitcoin had its first halving in November 2012.

This is why these newly activated addresses’ holdings of 50 BTC match the rewards miners could receive during the early days of Bitcoin.

These old addresses always raise a lot of interest as Bitcoin had relatively few miners and users during those times.

However, this does not mean that these wallets are owned by the mysterious founder of Bitcoin.

This recent activation comes after a series of interesting activations in the crypto world. These are long-dormant crypto addresses that have become active over the past month.

On Oct. 22, a Bitcoin address with 170 BTC worth roughly $14.38 million became active after being dormant for 13 years, as reported by Whale Alert.

Prior to this, on Oct. 20, a dormant address with 500 BTC worth around $41.54 million became active after 10.7 years. In 2016, these holdings were worth just $194,955.

Later, crypto analytics platform Arkham linked the 500 BTC transaction to addresses belonging to convicted Irish drug dealer Clifton Collins. Previously, his crypto holdings were deemed inaccessible.

On Oct. 17, Whale Alert tracked activity involving old Bitcoin addresses holding 248 BTC and 167 BTC worth roughly $20.24 million and $13.65 million, respectively.

Binance has published the final results of an unscheduled Proof of Reserves (PoR) report, two weeks after the cryptocurrency exchange lost $6.34 billion in an October hack.

According to Binance, the snapshot was taken on Nov. 12 at 00:00 UTC, and it shows that the exchange fully backs the balances of its clients. Shiba Inu (SHIB) is backed at 100.04%, and the other major assets on the exchange are fully covered as well.

The latest report comes after the Oct. 29 attack, during which hackers stole funds from Binance across ten blockchains in 20 minutes. Among the stolen funds were nearly 500 billion SHIB. After the attack, the exchange took an additional reserve snapshot at Bitcoin block height 975493.

Binance data shows that the net account balances of users stand at 50.67 trillion SHIB, and the exchange holds 50.69 trillion SHIB in its wallets. Of that amount, 50.68 trillion SHIB is held at the addresses of Binance itself, and the remaining 7.46 billion SHIB is held by third-party custodians.

Besides SHIB, the report also shows that the other major cryptocurrencies are fully backed. Compared with the previous check on Nov. 4, the BTC balances of users went up by 0.35% to 687,912 BTC, and the coverage ratio for Bitcoin stands at 100.05%. The ETH balances went up by 1.04% to 3.48 million ETH, and the BNB balances increased by 1.03% to 42.95 million BNB.

Still, the USDT balances of users went down by 3.68% to 24.3 billion USDT. At the same time, the stablecoin has the highest coverage ratio in the report at 104.34%.

Arkham Intelligence data shows that the known wallets of Binance currently hold 58.82 trillion SHIB. That is 5.88% of the total supply of the meme coin, and these tokens are worth $251.16 million. In this context, Binance wallets hold 8.13 trillion SHIB (about $34.7 million) more than the amount shown in the PoR report.

According to Binance, the PoR report only covers the deposits of clients and the coins that the exchange keeps to back them, so the company's own funds are not included in the report. Based on the Arkham data, Binance holds about 16% more SHIB than it owes to its clients.

According to Arkham, Binance is still the third-largest exchange by SHIB holdings. Only the burn address with 410.44 trillion SHIB (or 41.04% of supply), the U.S.-based exchange Coinbase with 74.53 trillion SHIB, and South Korea's Upbit with 64.14 trillion SHIB hold more of the meme coin. Robinhood, Crypto.com and Bithumb come after Binance with 57.12 trillion, 34.95 trillion and 16.74 trillion SHIB, respectively.

Finally, Binance said that the PoR system is still computing the final Merkle Root Hash using zk-SNARKs. After that, users will be able to log into their profiles and check that their balances are included in the overall ledger.

At press time, the price of SHIB stands at $0.00000426.

#5278. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

#5277. Important Ethereum (ETH) Bug Might Be Finally Fixed

One of Ethereum's consensus clients has merged a fix for a validator pubkey cache poisoning attack, according to a pull request on GitHub. The patch addresses a vulnerability around the Gloas fork, which could result in some nodes rejecting valid signatures due to a bug in the global pubkey cache.

Gloas is the consensus layer part of the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade.

The issue lies in a mechanism where the client stores validator public keys and their indexes in a global cache.

Technically, deposits that are already finalized should give the same validators on every chain, though it is a different story at the fork boundary.

The attacker needs 3 pending deposits just before the fork. The first one is a large top-up for an existing validator. The other two are new keys: A with builder credentials and B with regular validator credentials.

On the canonical chain, the top-up consumes the balance churn, so A and B are processed after the fork. A becomes a builder, and B takes the next validator index.

On the attacker's side chain, the topped-up validator gets slashed before the fork, and its deposit is skipped. This leads to A being processed earlier, essentially taking B's index.

The buggy cache assumed both chains would produce the same validators and imported A's key globally.

At the fork, affected nodes would reject all valid signatures from B on the canonical chain and fork off.

Realistically, the attack is somewhat complicated, as it needs a slashing at the right moment and a side chain, so it's unlikely to happen by accident.

According to the PR, the fix is to only add keys to the global pubkey cache once their activation eligibility epoch is finalized.

A new HeadPubkeys structure also combines keys from the head state and the global cache, so nodes don't miss keys if the chain finalizes without new blocks.

Whether other consensus clients had a similar issue is yet to be confirmed. In other words, the closer Glamsterdam gets, the more edge cases around the fork boundary developers have to catch.

The first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011, by David Schwartz.

According to the official XRP account on X, the date 11/11/11 marked the beginning of Schwartz's work on what would later support one of the cryptocurrency industry's established payment-focused blockchain networks.

Schwartz, now Ripple CTO Emeritus, was one of three engineers, alongside Jed McCaleb and Arthur Britto, who began developing the XRP Ledger in 2011. The three were inspired by Bitcoin to build an alternative that would address some of its problems, especially in the areas of sustainability and payments.

In June 2012, the XRP Ledger went live. Shortly after Chris Larsen joined the group in September 2012, a company called NewCoin was formed; it soon changed its name to OpenCoin before becoming Ripple. The founders of the XRPL donated 80 billion XRP, the network’s native digital asset, to the company.

Ripple has locked up most of its XRP in escrow, about 55 billion XRP, and releases 1 billion XRP on the first day of every month.

The anniversary on November 11 marks the start of the XRP Ledger’s development, as what began with Schwartz's first code in 2011 eventually morphed into a blockchain network designed to enable value transfers.

November is also a big month for XRP as U.S. spot XRP ETFs celebrate the first anniversary of their landmark launch.Canary Capital’s XRP exchange-traded fund, listed under the ticker XRPC, began trading on November 13, 2025, and is the first spot XRP ETF on a U.S. exchange.

In upgrade news, XRPL version 3.5.0 is scheduled for December 3, 2026. This release includes only improvements and fixes, including a permanent fix for occasional slow ledger close times.

#5271. Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

The Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

The vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

#5265. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery plan has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

SlowMist's finding is precise: the withdrawal function released assets without independently verifying the actual event on the source chain. A signature confirmed that the signer approved a message. It did not confirm that the message matched a deposit that existed, that was still unused, and that involved the same recipient, token and amount.The replay angle deserves attention, even though SlowMist's summary only implies it. A bridge normally marks each source event as consumed, keyed to something fixed like the source chain, transaction hash and log index, so it can be paid out once. If replay protection keys on the contents of the receipt instead, changing the recipient, token or amount produces a receipt the contract has never seen. Five edited receipts against one deposit would then look like five fresh claims. That is one plausible way the pieces fit together, not a finding the researchers have published.Bridge history offers parallels. In 2022, Wormhole lost about $325 million when an attacker got a forged message past its signature verification, and Nomad lost about $190 million after a misconfiguration let nearly any message pass as valid. The Ankr case is smaller, but it shares the same root: the verification step accepted something it shouldn't have.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

The lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

Japanese tech and fintech conglomerate Rakuten Group is among the institutional holders of a U.S. spot XRP ETF, according to the company's latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Rakuten also holds funds tracking Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana, and these positions were worth roughly $6.42 million combined at the end of the quarter on Sept. 30, 2026.

The filing shows that Rakuten held 6,690 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF worth $111,255. At press time, the price of XRP stands at $1.03, and the shares of the Bitwise fund trade at $11.51, according to SoSoValue, so the XRP ETF stake of Rakuten is now worth about $77,000.

Rakuten is not the only institutional investor in the new XRP funds, and Raymond James Financial has also disclosed positions in spot XRP ETFs, according to SEC filings.

The largest position of Rakuten is in BlackRock's spot Bitcoin fund, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, and Rakuten held $5,893,593 worth of its shares at the end of the third quarter. Besides, Rakuten owns $263,632 of the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF and $150,728 of the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF.

U.S. rules require any institutional manager holding more than $100 million in U.S. exchange-listed securities to disclose its portfolio every quarter, no matter where it's based. Rakuten Group holds about $1.4 billion in U.S. equities, and most of that amount is in shares of satellite operator AST SpaceMobile. In this context, the crypto ETF positions account for less than 0.5% of the U.S. portfolio of Rakuten.

Rakuten is one of the largest tech companies in Japan. The market capitalization of Rakuten stands at about ¥1.4 trillion ($9 billion), and the annual revenue of the company is more than ¥2.5 trillion ($16 billion).

The Rakuten ecosystem spans more than 70 services, from the Rakuten Ichiba marketplace and carrier Rakuten Mobile to banks and brokerages. According to Rakuten, these services have more than 100 million users in Japan and more than 2.1 billion users worldwide.

The latest filing comes amid outflows from spot XRP ETFs. According to SoSoValue, the funds lost $10.42 million on Nov. 9 and another $7.62 million on Nov. 10, and there were no flows on Nov. 11 and Nov. 12. On Oct. 28, the total net assets of the funds stood at $1.51 billion.

Still, the cumulative net inflow of spot XRP ETFs stands at $1.79 billion, and the total net assets of the funds are $1.16 billion, or 1.77% of the market cap of XRP. Finally, the Bitwise XRP ETF is the largest of the five spot XRP funds, and its net assets stand at $420.29 million, according to SoSoValue.

Stellar (XLM), the blockchain co-founded by Jed McCaleb, has become the leader in daily market cap growth for tokenized real-world asset (RWA) funds, according to Token Terminal data published by the RWA Foundation. Over the 24 hours to Nov. 13, the market cap of tokenized funds on Stellar went up by $44.9 million, and the network surpassed both Ethereum and Solana.

Over the same period, the market cap of tokenized funds on Solana, Ethereum and zkSync Era increased by $29 million, $10.8 million and $3.5 million, respectively.

Stellar is currently the second-largest blockchain for tokenized funds after Ethereum, according to Token Terminal. Over the past year, the RWA market on Stellar has grown roughly sixfold and reached $4.67 billion, according to rwa.xyz. At press time, the price of XLM stands at $0.1476.

According to the Stellar Development Foundation, Stellar was designed with the requirements of banks and transfer agents in mind. In this context, the compliance tools are built into the base layer of the network, and an issuer can vet investors through trustlines, freeze accounts and claw back assets.

Transactions on Stellar settle in 3 to 5 seconds, and the fees on the network are measured in fractions of a cent. Besides, users can move funds to and from fiat currencies through local providers, which are called anchors on Stellar.

Franklin Templeton's BENJI money market fund has run on Stellar since 2021, and it was the first U.S. mutual fund on a public blockchain.

Today, Spiko, Ondo and WisdomTree are also building their own funds and tokenized U.S. Treasuries on Stellar. Spiko offers euro funds managed by Amundi, and Ondo has launched its USDY token on the network.

In May 2026, DTCC and the Stellar Development Foundation announced that the Depository Trust Company (DTC) will tokenize the assets it holds in custody on Stellar. According to DTCC, DTC-tokenized assets are expected to become available on the network in the first half of 2027.

On Nov. 12, DTCC also announced that it will connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027.

#5262. Hoskinson Credits Cardano’s Staking Model After Binance Hack Leaves Network Unaffected

Charles Hoskinson has credited the underlying architecture for keeping Cardano (ADA) and Midnight (NIGHT) unaffected by the recent Binance hack, arguing that years of deliberate design decisions are now paying off.

The Cardano founder acknowledged that the network’s early focus on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, liquid non-custodial staking, and the need for Layer-2 (L2) solutions built around its Extended UTXO (EUTXO) model, came in handy during the hacking incident.

Hoskinson went further, saying these were not accidental advantages but deliberate choices based on anticipating the blockchain industry’s evolving needs. Furthermore, he suggested that the recent hacking demonstrated the importance of building networks with security and resilience at their core.

Cardano’s staking model continues to grow, with the Cardano Foundation reporting that 57.6% of ADA’s circulating supply is staked.

Notably, every delegated coin backs a stake pool that helps produce blocks and secure the network.

Unlike traditional staking models that lock up assets, Cardano’s liquid staking allows holders to delegate their ADA while retaining full control. As a result, they can spend, transfer, or move their funds without first having to unstake them.

Therefore, this approach is unique because it combines network participation with financial flexibility while supporting a decentralized pool ecosystem. Additionally, it reduces reliance on centralized custodians, boosting the network’s broader resilience.

Meanwhile, Cardano is expanding its real-world utility since police in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, recently began using its blockchain technology to track forensic evidence in active criminal investigations.

More importantly, the Cardano Foundation said evidence scans and laboratory results will be recorded on-chain, creating a tamper-resistant audit trail designed to strengthen the integrity of investigations.

#5258. Strategy Sends Crucial Message on Bitcoin's Quantum Security

Strategy, the world's largest corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, has sent an important message regarding Bitcoin’s future resistance to quantum computing attacks.

The company, which was co-founded by renowned Bitcoin champion Michael Saylor, recently posted on X that the Bitcoin network can implement new security measures as and when they are needed.

“Quantum-resistant upgrades can be adopted if & when it's needed,” wrote Strategy.

These comments come at a time when the crypto industry is debating whether the rise of quantum computing could, in the long run, threaten Bitcoin’s cryptographic security.

Given that Bitcoin leverages elliptic curve cryptography for transaction security, quantum computing could pose a significant threat to Bitcoin.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer has the potential to reverse-engineer private keys from exposed public keys. This could give attackers access to the Bitcoin holdings associated with those keys.

At this point, there is no known publicly available quantum computer that can successfully break Bitcoin’s cryptography in this manner.

While speaking at the World Bank in Washington in October, Saylor said that the Bitcoin network would be able to defend itself against any realistic quantum computing threat by coming together and upgrading the software.

Saylor estimated that such an upgrade would take about 90 days once a worldwide consensus is reached on the need for quantum-resistant cryptography.

Saylor also warned against the hasty introduction of new cryptography. He reasoned that more complex security measures may themselves introduce weaknesses.

However, the 90-day estimate has come under scrutiny because such a network-wide shift would involve developers agreeing on technical changes and Bitcoin users moving their funds to new, secure addresses.

Interestingly, Strategy has also initiated efforts aimed at research and development for Bitcoin’s long-term security.

In July, Strategy was part of a group of seven major financial institutions and crypto companies, including BlackRock and Coinbase, that formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium.

The Bitcoin Security Consortium has committed $15 million over three years. One of the areas of focus of the consortium is post-quantum cryptography.

In fact, Bitcoin developers are already working on ways to address the quantum computing issue.

One of the most prominent proposals is Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360 (BIP-360). This BIP introduces a new type of transaction output, Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR).
