#5257. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is announced, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

#5256. Nakamoto Sells More Bitcoin (BTC)

As per its latest quarterly financials, David Bailey's Bitcoin treasury firm Nakamoto Inc. (NASDAQ: NAKA) has sold an additional 184 BTC from its Bitcoin stash.

Nakamoto Inc., a firm that built its corporate strategy around Bitcoin, held a total of 4,283 BTC as of Sept. 30. The figure is down from 4,467 BTC at the end of June.

Bitcoin Treasuries data shows that Nakamoto Inc. sold 184 BTC in the third quarter of 2026. The firm now has a total of 4,283 BTC in its Bitcoin stash. Nakamoto currently sits in 21st place on the Bitcoin 100 corporate treasury rankings.

The recent company filing indicates that Nakamoto Inc. generated around $13.2 million in proceeds from digital asset sales in the third quarter. However, the filing does not appear to specify whether the 184 BTC were sold in a single transaction.

Nakamoto currently holds approximately $357.9 million worth of Bitcoin despite selling more BTC in the latest period.

This is not the first time in 2026 that David Bailey's firm has reduced its Bitcoin stash.

In March, Nakamoto Inc. sold around 284 BTC worth $20 million to meet working capital needs and fund operations following its acquisitions of BTC Inc. and UTXO Management.

Nakamoto sold its BTC at an average price of around $70,422 per Bitcoin. That was far less than its original Bitcoin purchase price.

In the first quarter, Nakamoto Inc. also received a premium of around 43 BTC from its derivatives strategies before selling around 40 BTC.

Nakamoto Inc. also sold a large chunk of Bitcoin in June.

The company sold around 600 BTC for 35.6 million USDT, as per the company's second-quarter financials.

Combined with proceeds from certain Bitcoin derivative positions, the company generated around $48 million from those transactions.

Nakamoto Inc. used $45 million of that sum to partially repay its Bitcoin-backed loan from cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, reducing its principal amount from 210 million USDT to 165 million USDT.

The recent Bitcoin sell-off comes as Nakamoto continues working to meet its substantial debt obligations while expanding its business operations.

It had roughly 3,030 BTC pledged as collateral for debt as of Sept. 30. That left 1,253 BTC unpledged.

On Nov. 11, Nakamoto Inc. extended the maturity of a 60 million USDT loan from Kraken by one year. The company moved the loan maturity date from December 2026 to December 2027. Nakamoto currently has no remaining principal maturities in 2026.

#5255. Bitcoin May Never See a New ATH Again, Peter Brandt Floats Grim Scenario as Bearish Pattern Emerges

Bitcoin investors may have witnessed the cryptocurrency’s final record-breaking rally, at least according to veteran trader Peter Brandt. The legendary chartist has sounded the alarm over a potentially massive bearish pattern emerging on Bitcoin’s weekly chart, warning that if the formation holds, the apex crypto’s October 2025 all-time high above $126,000 may never be surpassed in his lifetime. His alarming assessment comes as BTC reels from a brutal market downturn, adding fresh uncertainty to an already battered crypto market.

Peter Brandt has raised the possibility that Bitcoin may have already reached its ultimate price peak after spotting a potentially significant bearish formation on its weekly chart. In a November 15 post on X, the renowned chartist questioned whether BTC was developing a legitimate head-and-shoulders (H&S) top, a technical pattern often associated with a major trend reversal.

Brandt suggested that if the formation proves valid, he could construct a technical case that Bitcoin’s previous record high was its last, potentially remaining unbeaten for the rest of his lifetime. His warning is particularly striking given that Bitcoin reached a record of $126,080 in October 2025 before suffering a sharp correction.

The H&S formation typically features three peaks, with the middle one (the head) rising above the two surrounding peaks (the shoulders). The pattern is considered bearish when the price breaks below the neckline, which connects the two troughs separating these peaks. Such a breakdown could signal weakening buying pressure and open the door to further losses. In Bitcoin’s case, the asset is approaching a crucial support zone between $60,000 and $65,000, which could serve as the neckline of the potential bearish formation.

However, Brandt has not confirmed that Bitcoin has completed this formation. His assessment remains conditional on whether the chart structure represents a legitimate bearish reversal, meaning traders will likely watch the potential neckline for signs of confirmation.

Bitcoin has extended its recent decline, with selling pressure intensifying on Nov. 13 as the flagship cryptocurrency dropped below the psychologically significant $70,000 threshold for the first time since August. The latest downturn has deepened its weekly losses to approximately 14.8%, highlighting the growing bearish sentiment weighing on the broader crypto market.

Meanwhile, crypto analyst James Check has pointed to another worrying development, suggesting Bitcoin is experiencing its fourth capitulation event since reaching its all-time high. According to Check, daily realized losses have surged, doubling from about $420 million to more than $850 million in just 24 hours.

Check also offered a more optimistic perspective, arguing that Bitcoin has entered what he describes as a “deep value” zone. He noted that the cryptocurrency last traded in similar territory in February and late June this year, with the previous comparable occurrence dating back to the 2022 crypto bear market.

However, the pundit cautioned that entering this zone does not necessarily mean Bitcoin has reached its market bottom. Instead, he suggested that investors who begin gradually accumulating BTC at these levels could eventually benefit if historical patterns repeat, potentially turning the current market weakness into a long-term buying opportunity.

The price of XRP fell below $1 on Friday for the first time since mid-August, according to TradingView. The cryptocurrency dropped to $0.9974, and it has now closed in the red for nine days in a row. At the start of November, XRP was trading at $1.30. On Saturday, the price of XRP stands at $1.025.

In the autumn, the price of XRP reached a peak near $1.60, and the cryptocurrency has lost almost 38% since then. Still, the drop has not pushed XRP out of its range on the weekly chart. The lower weekly Bollinger Band is at $0.90, and XRP is still trading above it, so the cryptocurrency is not in free fall, according to the indicator.

The latest decline comes amid a sell-off in U.S. tech stocks after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO. Traders are also betting on a December Fed rate hike after the October U.S. inflation data, according to CME FedWatch. Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday, and most altcoins went down as well.

Spot XRP ETFs in the U.S. have also seen outflows this week. According to SoSoValue, the funds lost $10.42 million on Nov. 9 and $7.62 million on Nov. 10, and they had no flows on Nov. 11 and Nov. 12. By Nov. 13, spot XRP ETFs recorded net outflows of $18.04 million.

The total net assets of spot XRP ETFs stood at $1.16 billion as of Nov. 12, down from $1.51 billion on Oct. 28. Since launch, the cumulative net inflow of the funds stands at $1.79 billion. The Bitwise XRP ETF remains the largest of the five funds, and its net assets stand at $420.29 million.

According to Santiment, the number of wallets holding at least 10,000 XRP went up by 2,260 over the past 30 days. The number of wallets with 1 million XRP or more stood at 2,147 as of Nov. 13, and Santiment data shows that it is the highest number of such wallets in 2026.

On Aug. 14, the price of XRP fell to $0.986, according to TradingView, and it was the last time XRP traded below $1 before this week.

#5249. XRP Scams Soar Across Social Media, Here’s What To Watch Out For

Scam attempts aimed at XRP holders have reached intense levels, according to recent alerts from a well-known figure in the XRP Ledger community. Vet, a pseudonymous X account who also works as a dUNL validator while contributing to the XRP Ledger

Foundation has used his platform several times to highlight the growing threat.

In a recent check using platform data tools, he found that around 11.5 million posts directed at the XRP community appeared within a single 30-day stretch.

The vast majority dangled fake airdrops or reward schemes designed to trick people into handing over funds or linking their wallets. He described the sheer number as eye-opening and pushed users to stay highly alert.

Vet has also pointed out how quickly fraudsters react to genuine positive news. When real companies announce partnerships or integrations involving the XRP Ledger, scammers often rush to set up lookalike addresses and launch tokens that borrow those brand names.

His advice is straightforward: treat every unexpected offer with suspicion, and trust only details that come directly from the company’s official channels. In many cases, the real institutions never publish public issuer addresses.

He has spoken about the constant stream of scam tags that can make notifications almost impossible to manage. Seeing community members engage with these posts frustrates him, and he keeps returning to the same clear message. No one is giving away free XRP. The safest move is usually to ignore the approach completely.

Even specific token launches have drawn his scrutiny. After a large Japanese firm introduced a yen-backed stablecoin, Vet warned that any version appearing on the XRP Ledger under a similar ticker was almost certainly fake without an official issuer confirmation.

His ongoing posts underline a simple reality. Rising interest in XRP attracts more bad actors who try to cash in on the attention. For everyday holders, staying skeptical and double-checking everything remains the best protection.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) is set to get more exposure in the U.S.-regulated financial market after the North American Derivatives Exchange (Nadex) self-certified a new strike event contract tied to the meme cryptocurrency's price.

On November 10, 2026, an official Nadex notice said the exchange certified a swap based on the price of SHIB at a specific time and date. The product, called the Shiba Inu Strike Event Contract, began trading on or after Nov. 13, 2026.

The filing is available through the official records of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). The regulator’s database shows that the SHIB Strike Event Contract is certified as a swap, with November 10 listed as the certification date.

The product allows traders to wager that a particular price of SHIB will be attained or surpassed at some point in the future. This opens another avenue for market players to take positions based on the price fluctuations of Shiba Inu without having to buy or hold the underlying token.

Nadex (North American Derivatives Exchange) is a CFTC-regulated U.S. financial exchange acquired by Foris DAX Markets (part of Crypto.com), bringing the Shiba Inu product to a regulated platform.

Shiba Inu Japan community member Kuro reacted to the development, saying SHIB is now the underlying asset for a new financial product in the U.S.-regulated market.

"Nadex, an exchange owned by Crypto.com, has officially filed a new trading product based on SHIB’s price, and it has also been listed in the official records of the U.S. CFTC. This product lets traders predict whether SHIB will exceed a certain price at a specified time, alongside assets such as BTC, ETH, and XRP," Kuro added, saying another opportunity for SHIB to be used in the U.S. financial market has just opened up.

At the time of writing, SHIB was down 3.33% over the last 24 hours to $0.00000414 amid broader crypto market weakness that coincided with strength in the U.S. dollar.

The dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025 on Friday, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pulling down both cryptocurrencies and gold.

Vitalik Buterin now favors leanPCS as a potentially faster route for EIP-8288.

leanPCS could enable STARK verification at an estimated 20,000–40,000 gas.

EIP-8288 remains a draft, with leanPCS integration and its reference implementation unfinished.

Ethereum’s quantum-safe upgrade may have found a faster route forward, but the technical work isn’t finished.

Vitalik Buterin has shifted his support toward leanPCS under EIP-8288, arguing it could deliver much of leanSTARK’s flexibility without forcing developers to standardize a new instruction-set architecture first.

That’s a significant change in direction. It isn’t a completed upgrade, though.

EIP-8288 aims to reduce the amount of cryptographic data Ethereum must carry on-chain. Instead of publishing every signature or proof, nodes aggregate verification results into STARK proofs, which can then be aggregated further.

The chain ultimately receives compact claims and a master proof, rather than every underlying cryptographic object.

The motivation is becoming harder to ignore. Current 65-byte ECDSA signatures could grow to 1–6 kilobytes under proposed quantum-safe schemes.

Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…

Meanwhile, zero-knowledge proofs could expand from roughly 200–1,000 bytes to around 128 kilobytes when using STARKs. Putting all that data on-chain isn’t a practical scaling strategy.

Buterin’s latest explanation separates three approaches. leanSPHINCS supports a specific hash-based signature scheme, offering quantum-safe accounts with a proposed cost of 4,096 gas for 64 bytes.

leanSTARK is more flexible. Users could prove almost any computation, but Ethereum would first need to agree on a programming language or instruction-set architecture. That’s a difficult standard to lock in.

leanPCS offers a middle path. A polynomial commitment scheme proves a statement about a polynomial, and Buterin estimates STARK verification through this mechanism could cost around 20,000–40,000 gas.

It may require more claims on-chain than leanSTARK. In exchange, developers retain greater flexibility over off-chain proof systems.

The published EIP-8288 draft currently specifies leanSPHINCS and reserves leanSTARK, while leanPCS isn’t yet included as a verification mode. Its reference implementation remains listed as TBD, and no activation date is confirmed.

That gap matters. An endorsement isn’t a specification, and a specification isn’t a working network upgrade.

For now, Ethereum’s quantum-safe upgrade has a potentially faster technical direction, but leanPCS still needs formal integration, implementation and approval before it can become part of the network.

Bitcoin's recent sell-off has raised questions about whether investors are selling liquid crypto holdings to secure allocations in Anthropic's massive IPO.

Anthropic's offering has attracted strong demand, with its order book reportedly reaching six times the shares available during the roadshow.

Fundstrat's Tom Lee and Xapo Bank's Seamus Rocca have pointed to the IPO as a potential source of capital rotation, although direct evidence of Bitcoin whale selling to fund the offering remains limited.

Bitcoin (BTC) is facing renewed selling pressure as Anthropic’s massive IPO draws billions of dollars in investor demand, raising a new question across crypto markets: are investors selling Bitcoin to get into artificial intelligence? BTC has fallen sharply from its October highs, while Anthropic’s upcoming Nasdaq debut is attracting significant interest from institutional and retail investors. Some market strategists believe the IPO could be pulling liquidity away from cryptocurrencies as investors prepare cash for the offering. Is Anthropic’s IPO becoming an unexpected competitor for Bitcoin investment capital?

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO is emerging as a major liquidity event at a time when Bitcoin is struggling to regain investor demand. The company’s offering has reportedly attracted orders worth six times the available shares by the end of its roadshow’s first week. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of approximately $1.3 trillion and could raise more than $61 billion, making it one of the largest public offerings in market history. Its shares are expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

$BTC looks like another source of funding for $ANT IPO based on its price action.

Investors seeking allocations in a high-profile IPO may need to free up cash from existing holdings. Bitcoin is among the most liquid assets that investors can sell quickly to raise capital. Seamus Rocca, CEO of Xapo Bank, has suggested that investors preparing for Anthropic’s offering may be selling Bitcoin and other liquid assets to secure IPO allocations. He described the offering as a potential source of liquidity pressure on crypto markets.

The possibility of capital moving from crypto into AI stocks has also attracted attention from Fundstrat’s Tom Lee. Lee suggested that retail investors could be selling cryptocurrencies to fund purchases of Anthropic shares ahead of its Nasdaq debut. He also warned that the IPO could create a supply shock across equities as investors liquidate existing positions to participate in the offering.

BREAKING: TOM LEE SAYS THE AI STOCK SELLOFF, THE ANTHROPIC IPO AND POST-HACK FUND RETURNS MAY BE FUELING CRYPTO SELLING pic.twitter.com/vCqoQZh0zg

His comments come as Bitcoin faces broader selling pressure despite continued interest in its long-term investment case. Lee also pointed to weakness in technology stocks and margin calls among retail traders as possible contributors to the recent market decline.

The argument is straightforward: when a major IPO attracts exceptional demand, investors may shift money from existing positions into the new opportunity. Bitcoin’s liquidity makes it a potential source of that capital.

Bitcoin’s decline has intensified as several sources of market pressure converge. BTC recently dropped toward $65,000, extending its correction by more than 20% from early October levels. Anthropic’s IPO is one possible explanation for the liquidity shift, but it is not the only factor. Technology-stock volatility, concerns surrounding Strategy’s market position, rising short positions and outflows from BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF have also weighed on market conditions.

Anthropic’s IPO could create short-term competition for investment capital, particularly if demand continues to exceed the available share supply. Once the offering is completed, some of that temporary pressure could ease. However, a recovery in Bitcoin is not guaranteed. Investors will continue to monitor ETF flows, derivatives positioning, macroeconomic conditions and demand for digital assets.

The larger question is whether Anthropic represents a temporary liquidity drain or a broader shift in investor preferences toward AI-related equities. If Bitcoin continues losing capital while Anthropic attracts record demand, the market may be witnessing more than a routine crypto correction. It could be an early sign of investors changing where they want their money invested.

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has doubled down on his comments about completing the blockchain's development. In an AMA, the Cardano founder was asked about finishing Cardano; he answered in the affirmative, saying yes, the roadmap was done.

In a recent livestream titled "Finishing Cardano," Hoskinson maintains that his job with Cardano was done. "My job is done with Cardano," he said, doubling down on his recent statements and on where things stand with Cardano.

Finishing Cardano https://t.co/LtFVLOHrxk

Hoskinson said he saw a barrage of criticism and negative comments after his remarks, with some speculating that he had failed, that Cardano was a failed project, or that he was leaving Cardano. He, however, maintains that there is no ambiguity in his statements.

Hoskinson revisited the launch of Cardano (ADA) in 2015 in response to critics who claimed that he or the Cardano project had failed.

"So, let's look at 2015. There was a crowd sale conducted to sell ADA into Japan. The price for this was less than 0.2 cents per ADA. And Bitcoin was actually used as the settlement system for this. They bought in yen and settled in Bitcoin. So there are even on-chain records of the sales tranche. The total amount of money raised was $72 million."

Highlighting the growth of the Cardano cryptocurrency, Hoskinson noted that the market valuation has increased immensely from an initial $72 million. "We built a network that went from a $72 million valuation to an all-time high of $100 billion," Hoskinson stated.

Cardano reached an all-time high price of $3.09 on September 2, 2021, which corresponded to an all-time-high market capitalization of nearly $100 billion at that peak.

Following ADA's drop from this ATH, Cardano's market valuation sits at $6.03 billion. Hoskinson maintains that this is still growth, up from an initial $72 million. "Even in its deflated state, everybody's saying it's destroyed and it's a dead coin and all these other things. It's $6 billion. It went from 72 to six," Hoskinson said.

Hoskinson specifically reiterated that the Cardano roadmap is not being abandoned and went on to reveal further growth credentials: "We delivered a fully decentralized, recursively self-improving ecosystem. We left behind a community-led and community-owned treasury that, at its all-time high, had $4 billion in value, and initiated a constitution."

"We built an entire on-chain governance system, wrote a constitution, got the entire community involved, and created a recursively self-improving system that's fully decentralized—the most decentralized cryptocurrency on the planet," Hoskinson added.

#5242. Binance Tightens Security With Zero-Knowledge Proof Upgrade

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by volume, has continued to deploy new measures to strengthen security on its exchange after it suffered the biggest cyberattack ever seen in the history of crypto late last month.

In a bid to foster transparency and regain its users' trust, Binance has just announced the completion of a major upgrade to further strengthen its security.

In an announcement shared on November 14, Binance said that it has generated a new zero-knowledge proof for its Proof of Reserves (PoR) system.

According to Binance, the upgrade allows users to independently verify that it holds sufficient assets to cover their account balances on a 1:1 basis.

The exchange further shared snapshots to prove that it maintains reserves above its users' net account balances across six major cryptocurrencies, boosting their confidence in its operating standards.

It also added that the update covers all assets affected by the recent attack, and the exchange showcased its reserves for the following crypto assets: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether, BNB, Solana, and USDC.

While withdrawals are being restored in batches, with the last phase scheduled for next week, Binance has continued to improve its operations to replenish all affected assets and tighten security to regain users' trust.

Following its latest move, Binance revealed that its Bitcoin reserves are currently at 100.05%, slightly above the 100% mark. This means that Binance's Bitcoin reserves amount to about 688,283 BTC, substantially above its net user balances of 687,912 BTC.

The case is similar for the rest of the tokens: Ethereum reserves are at 100.02%, while BNB and USDC recorded ratios of 100.39% and 100.07%, respectively.

While Binance also reported stronger reserve ratios for USDT and SOL, at about 104.34% and 105.86%, respectively, it is evident that Binance holds more of these assets than the total amount owed to users.

Binance has specified that the Proof of Reserves covers assets that are in its custody on behalf of users, rather than its entire corporate holdings, assuring users that their funds are fully backed.

#5241. Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

Enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the plan, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

The Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a new set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something big needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its new tracks.

The best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

The final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also shows raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

A 100% Aye result says little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

That is the real change. Under the new rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

Node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote showed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the new ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

#5240. From $2 to $60,000: The Eternal “Bitcoin Is a Scam” Timeline

As Bitcoin hurtles toward the $60k support level, critics are having a field day once again, calling it a scam and a pyramid scheme, among other things. However, one analyst noted that the digital currency has fallen every 4 years or so over the last 3 cycles, and the digital asset is simply following established trends.

The post documents that every major price drop has been met with triumphant celebrations over the digital currency’s demise. BTC has already dropped 50% from its all-time high (ATH) of $126.5k set roughly a year ago. While naysayers are having a field day right now, seasoned investors understand that the premier digital currency has a history of recovering well in the years that follow.

Bitcoin first experienced a major crash in 2011 when it dropped to $2. It was the first time it happened on such a noticeable scale, and many legacy analysts quickly declared it “dead” or a scam. However, Bitcoin recovered well and experienced a major bull run two years later that propelled it above $1,000 for a short while. This represented a 500x price increase.

Afterward, Bitcoin started to cool off again, and in 2015, the premier digital asset crashed to $250, sparking another episode of critics calling it a scam. However, the digital asset once again started to rise strongly two years after this occurrence and reached as high as $19,500 in late 2017, representing a 78x increase.

However, 2018 proved brutal for the cryptocurrency, and it dropped to sub-$3,000 levels near the end of the calendar year. Once again, the naysayers, led by Peter Schiff, were quick to declare it dead. The cryptocurrency remained on the defensive for about a year before beginning a major price recovery. By the end of 2021, Bitcoin had risen to $69k, representing a 23x price increase.

The 2022 bear market, like clockwork, soon followed, and the digital asset dropped to $15k, once again triggering critics. However, the bearish scenario eventually ended, and Bitcoin started to recover strongly in early 2024, resulting in a major price boom that pushed the cryptocurrency to $126.5k by October 2025, representing an 8.4x gain. Now, the digital currency is struggling above $60k and may likely fall even further below the key support. Critics are active, and in all practical purposes, this is peak FUD season.

Bitcoin’s recent troubles align with previous cycles, and it is important for long-term investors to stay patient and avoid panic selling.

Data from XRPL explorer Bithomp reveals that the Batch and Ticket features on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) are increasingly being adopted, with both setting new daily records in November.

The data indicates an increasing use of two XRPL features intended to enhance transaction flexibility and efficiency on the network.

Batch activity reached a new daily high for the month at 1.962 million on November 3, 2026. Ticket activity came next at 1.553 million on November 7, 2026, also setting a new November record. The increase indicates that these features are being embraced in the XRPL ecosystem. Batch functionality allows multiple transactions to be grouped and executed together and was activated on the XRPL mainnet on October 9, 2026.

The growth in batch activity, which neared 2 million on November 3, 2026, comes less than one month after its launch.

This is significant, as Batch is a prerequisite or accelerant for several high-value XRPL use cases already under contract or in the active pipeline, including atomic multi-party settlements. Institutional workflows (custody transfers, DvP settlement, cross-border payment finalization) require two or more accounts to act simultaneously.

On the other hand, tickets provide a way to reserve transaction sequence numbers, giving users more flexibility in managing transactions.

XRP Ledger metrics are in the green, with the transaction count up 75.9% to 4.3 million; active accounts jumped 128%, while XRP burned as fees rose 136%. Payments volume surged 137% in the last 24 hours to $1 billion, according to XRPScan data, while NFT mints rose 240% in the same timeframe.

Not only is the XRP Ledger seeing increased activity, but Ripple led stablecoin market cap growth by issuer over the past 24 hours, up $90.9 million, 4x the next issuer, multipli.fi, at $21.3 million.

Ripple's RLUSD market cap has grown 96% this year, across Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, to $2.7 billion from $1.4 billion in January. Most of that growth came in July, when Ripple launched Ripple Mint. RLUSD market cap stood just under $1.5 billion that month and rose to $2.3 billion by August.

In a milestone for the network, one year ago today, the first US ETF to hold only XRP began trading. Since then, US spot XRP ETFs have accumulated over 1.16 billion XRP.

#5238. Bitcoin Price Crashes to $72,700 as Leveraged Traders Buy the Dip: Is the Bottom In?

The crypto market crash deepens as $1B+ in longs get liquidated. Bitcoin sits mid-range at $72,969; fear at 28 isn’t a bottom yet.

Bitcoin fell below $73,000 on Thursday, November 12, extending a week-long crypto market crash in which traders who bet on a rebound were forced out of their positions again and again.

Bitcoin touched $72,735 on Binance, a hair above Tuesday’s $72,727 low and its weakest price since August 20. It trades at $72,969, down 9.4% from the November 4 close.

BREAKING: $BTC just fell to its lowest level since August.

Over $210 million worth of longs liquidated in the past 24 hours.

The dumping continues… pic.twitter.com/R7NVGivFnD

— Crypto Rover (@cryptorover) November 12, 2026

The altcoins are doing worse. Over seven days, Ethereum has lost 16.4%, Solana 14.7% and XRP 21.3%. CoinGecko values the whole crypto market at $2.42 trillion on Thursday, and Bitcoin makes up 60.5% of it.

Leverage made every drop bigger. More than $1 billion of bets were liquidated on Monday alone, almost all of them longs, the positions that profit only if prices rise. Liquidation means the exchange closes a trade by force once the trader’s collateral runs out, and those forced sales push the price down further.

So is this the flush that ends the crypto market slide, or is there more to come? The data has an answer, and it is not a comforting one.

The sell-off had no single cause. Four pieces of bad news landed one after another:

Each hit forced out more leveraged longs across the crypto market. Thursday’s slide continued the pattern on a smaller scale. We added up every forced closure in Bitcoin, Ether, Solana, XRP and Dogecoin futures on OKX, one of the largest exchanges, over the past 24 hours. Longs lost $27.6 million, against $12.3 million for shorts.

EXPLORE: Bitcoin Price Slides Toward $73K as Nvidia Plunges 9% and MSCI Drops Saylor’s Strategy

Big liquidations usually clear out the crowd. This time, the crowd came back.

In plain terms, traders keep buying every dip with borrowed money. That leaves fuel for another round of forced selling if Bitcoin drops through the next support. Bottoms tend to come when funding turns negative and open interest falls hard, a sign that leveraged buyers have given up.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Next Crypto to Hit 1 Dollar

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, which scores market mood from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed), reads 28 today. Fear is usually read as a buy signal. The history says it is not enough on its own.

We checked every day since February 2018 when the index sat at 28 or lower, 943 days in all, and where Bitcoin stood later.

This year’s two bottoms came with real panic. When Bitcoin hit $60,000 on February 6, the index read 9. When it bottomed at $57,800 on July 1, it read 11. Today’s 28 is fear, but it is not capitulation, the moment sellers give up all at once.

On the weekly chart, where each candle covers one week, Bitcoin has spent 2026 in a wide range. The low is $57,800 from July 1 and the high is $87,396 from late September. The midpoint is $72,598, almost exactly where Bitcoin trades now.

The price lost its 50-week exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $78,219. Its 200-week EMA sits at $69,597. Bitcoin closed below that line for 16 weeks this year, in February and March and again from June to mid-August, and both of the year’s bottoms formed during those stretches.

For the crypto market, three signs would say the bottom is close: the fear index dropping toward the teens, funding turning negative, and open interest falling as longs give up. None has shown up yet. Until they do, the 200-week EMA at $69,597 is the line that separates a pullback inside the 2026 range from a retest of the summer lows.

The Modern Wealth Survey is an online study conducted for Charles Schwab by Logica Research among a national sample of Americans from August 24 to September 17, 2026.

#5230. Bitcoin Price Crashes Below $69,000: Is the Worst Still to Come?

Bitcoin news: BTC hit $67,568 as longs were liquidated. Fear is Extreme, but BTC fell further after 15 of 16 past readings.

In Bitcoin news on Friday, November 13, the BTC USD price fell as low as $67,568 on Binance as a wave of forced selling wiped out leveraged bets on a rebound. It was the cryptocurrency’s lowest price since August 19.

Bitcoin trades at $68,772, down 6.7% in 24 hours and 9.1% in a week. Ether lost 5.5% and Solana 3.4% on the day.

BREAKING: Bitcoin falls below $69,000 and ETH nears $1,900 as selling pressure accelerates in crypto.

Crypto markets have now lost -$150 billion in 48 hours. pic.twitter.com/29QW0khxOh

— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) November 13, 2026

Most of the damage came from liquidations, when an exchange closes a leveraged trade by force once the trader’s collateral runs out. CoinGlass data cited by several outlets put the 24-hour total at about $1.4 billion, close to 90% of it from longs, the bets that prices would rise. Those forced sales pushed Bitcoin through $70,000 in about two hours overnight.

The mood has flipped with it. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index dropped from 28 to 20 on Friday, its first Extreme Fear reading since July.

In Bitcoin news this week, the question is no longer whether the market is scared. It is whether Extreme Fear means the bottom is close, and what the daily and weekly charts say.

The slide started on Thursday afternoon, when Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. It picked up speed after midnight UTC, when Bitcoin broke below the $72,727 low from Tuesday and kept falling.

We added up every forced closure in Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP and Dogecoin futures on OKX, one of the largest exchanges, over the past 24 hours.

Investors have also kept pulling money from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, funds that buy and hold the coin itself, adding to the selling.

EXPLORE: Bitcoin Price Crashes to $72,700 as Leveraged Traders Buy the Dip: Is the Bottom In?

On Thursday, we listed three signs that would point to a bottom: the fear index dropping toward the teens, the funding rate turning negative and open interest, the value of open futures bets, falling as longs give up. Overnight, two of them showed up.

One sign still points the other way. On OKX, 3.19 accounts are long for every one that is short, about the same as before the crash. Many traders are still buying the dip with leverage.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best New Crypto to Hodl

Extreme Fear sounds like a buy signal. History says it usually comes early. We found every time since 2018 that the index first dropped to 20 or lower after at least a month without such a reading. There were 16, and we followed Bitcoin for 90 days after each.

The most recent case fits the pattern. Extreme Fear first appeared on June 3 at $64,014, and Bitcoin still fell another 8.5% before it bottomed at $57,800 on July 1. Then it rallied to $87,396 in September.

For anyone reading this Bitcoin news as a buy signal, Extreme Fear says the bottom is getting closer. It has rarely said the bottom is here. A move to the 2026 lows would match the median path.

On the daily chart, where each candle covers one day, Bitcoin sits far below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 50-day EMA is at $78,226 and the 200-day EMA at $76,325.

On the weekly chart, where each candle covers one week, the key level is the 200-week EMA at $69,555. Bitcoin trades just below it, and the week closes on Sunday.

That line matters. Bitcoin closed below the 200-week EMA for 16 weeks this year, in February and March and again from June to mid-August, and both of 2026’s bottoms formed during those stretches.

The overnight flush did part of the work a bottom needs: leverage came out and funding turned negative.

For traders following Bitcoin news, the Sunday weekly close against $69,555 is the next test. History says the final low often comes weeks after the first Extreme Fear reading.

Nvidia earnings scheduled on November 17, with Wall Street expecting approximately $109 billion in quarterly revenue and $2.47 in adjusted EPS.

Data Center revenue is expected to approach $102 billion as demand for Blackwell GPUs and AI infrastructure remains strong.

Investors will focus on forward guidance, profit margins and leadership uncertainty to determine whether Nvidia can restore confidence across AI stocks.

Nvidia earnings could determine whether Wall Street’s AI trade stages a recovery or faces another wave of selling. The chipmaker is preparing to report its fiscal third-quarter 2027 results on November 17, with analysts expecting revenue of nearly $109 billion. However, strong financial results may not be enough to satisfy investors. Concerns surrounding AI spending, rising memory costs and leadership uncertainty have increased the pressure on the company. With Nvidia shares facing renewed volatility, can its latest earnings restore confidence in AI stocks, or is Wall Street preparing for another sell-off?

Nvidia faces exceptionally high expectations heading into its latest earnings report. Wall Street analysts expect the company to generate approximately $108.85 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share for fiscal Q3 2027. That would represent revenue growth of roughly 91% from $57.01 billion reported in the same quarter last year.

The company had previously guided for third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, putting its official forecast broadly in line with analyst expectations. The previous quarter provides a strong benchmark. Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in Q2 FY2027 revenue, up 106% year over year, while adjusted earnings reached $2.22 per share. Its Data Center business generated $89 billion, accounting for the overwhelming majority of quarterly revenue.

Nvidia’s Data Center business remains the biggest driver of its valuation, making this segment the most important part of the upcoming earnings report. Analyst estimates put fiscal Q3 Data Center revenue at approximately $101.8 billion. Demand for Blackwell GPUs and expanding AI infrastructure investments from cloud providers are expected to support the increase.

Investors will also examine the company’s Vera Rubin platform, which is expected to become an increasingly important contributor to future revenue. Nvidia has said that Vera Rubin is entering production, while its earlier guidance indicated that the platform could account for around 20% of Data Center revenue in Q3.

The bigger question is whether hyperscalers and AI companies will continue spending aggressively on computing capacity. Microsoft, Amazon, Google and other major technology companies remain important customers in the AI infrastructure cycle.

If Nvidia signals that demand remains strong into fiscal 2028, it could support sentiment across the semiconductor sector. Any indication of slower orders or delayed infrastructure spending, however, could pressure not only NVDA but also AMD, Broadcom and other AI-linked stocks.

Nvidia’s earnings call will face another important test: whether rising costs and business uncertainty are beginning to affect its growth outlook. The company previously guided for a non-GAAP gross margin of approximately 74% in fiscal Q3. However, management also warned that higher memory costs could push margins lower in the following quarter, with a projected range of 71%–72% for Q4 FY2027.

China exposure is another issue investors will monitor. Nvidia’s previous Q3 revenue outlook did not assume any Data Center compute revenue from China, leaving investors to assess how much additional growth could come from other markets.

Leadership uncertainty adds another layer to the earnings event. Recent reports surrounding Jensen Huang’s departure and the company’s leadership transition have increased investor concerns ahead of the results. Interim leadership will need to reassure investors about product execution, customer relationships and the company’s long-term strategy.

The earnings call could therefore matter as much as the financial numbers. Investors will be looking for clear answers on future demand, margins and management’s confidence in the AI growth cycle.

Nvidia stock is approaching a decisive earnings test after losing nearly one-third of its value from its October record high. #5224. Bitcoin Demand Dries Up as Miners Prepare to Dump 2,077 BTC: Is More Selling Pressure Coming for BTC?

Bitcoin demand weakens as miners transfer 2,077 BTC to exchanges; Antpool accounting for 97% ahead of an estimated 8% mining difficulty cut.

Bitcoin (BTC) demand is showing signs of weakness as miners move more coins to cryptocurrency exchanges. CryptoQuant recorded 2,077 BTC in miner-to-exchange transfers on November 10, approximately 16 times the 30-day daily average of 127 BTC. The move comes as Bitcoin struggles to regain momentum and the network approaches an estimated 8% reduction in mining difficulty.

The latest figures raise concerns about potential selling pressure, particularly as demand indicators weaken across spot and derivatives markets.

Meanwhile, miners could soon receive some relief from lower network difficulty.

Bitcoin's Rebound Fades as Spot Demand Weakens and Miner Flows Surge

“Leverage is being unwound, but spot demand has not recovered sustainably.” – By @xwinfinance pic.twitter.com/n03axjQKqt

— CryptoQuant.com (@cryptoquant_com) November 13, 2026

Explore: Bitcoin Price Crashes Below $69,000: Is the Worst Still to Come?

The 2,077 BTC transfer marked the largest daily miner-to-exchange movement since February 2026, according to CryptoQuant. Around 97% of the transferred Bitcoin came from Antpool, one of the network’s largest mining pools.

The movement represents a significant increase compared with the 30-day average of 127 BTC. Miners often transfer Bitcoin to exchanges when they need to liquidate holdings to cover electricity bills, equipment costs and other operating expenses.

However, CryptoQuant’s Miner to Exchange Flow indicator tracks transfers rather than completed sales. Miners can also move coins for treasury management or other operational reasons.

The latest activity therefore signals a potential increase in available selling supply, rather than confirmation that 2,077 BTC entered the market as sell orders.

Miner transfers are adding to concerns about an already fragile market. CryptoQuant’s 30-day demand-growth indicators showed negative readings across both spot and perpetual futures markets.

Spot demand stood at approximately -280,000 BTC, while perpetual futures demand reached around -82,000 BTC. Combined, the indicators produced a negative reading of approximately 362,000 BTC.

These figures point to deteriorating demand conditions. Spot demand is particularly important because it reflects activity in the underlying Bitcoin market, while perpetual futures activity provides insight into speculative positioning.

The negative readings suggest that buying activity has struggled to absorb available supply. If miners continue transferring Bitcoin to exchanges while spot demand remains weak, the market could face additional downward pressure.

However, these indicators measure changes in estimated demand, not a direct count of Bitcoin sold by investors.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best New Crypto to Hodl

Bitcoin’s next difficulty adjustment, expected around 14 November at block 975,744, may drop by roughly 8.4% after average block times rose to 655 seconds. The protocol reduces difficulty every 2,016 blocks (about two weeks) to maintain a 10-minute target; slower production eases mining and may boost BTC yield per unit of power.

This could aid miners amid weak prices and tight margins, but profitability still depends on electricity costs, hardware efficiency, fees and BTC value.

Bitcoin is trading near $69,200 after another sharp daily decline. The chart shows that BTC has broken below the $75,000–$76,000 support zone, which now represents an important resistance area. The immediate level to watch is around $69,000.

A sustained break below it could expose the $64,000–$65,000 support area, followed by $60,000. On the upside, Bitcoin would need to reclaim $75,000 to signal a potential recovery and improve its short-term outlook.

Bitcoin faces several challenges heading into the next difficulty adjustment. The increase in miner-to-exchange transfers, combined with negative demand indicators, suggests that the market is struggling to attract sufficient buying interest.

Still, the Antpool transfers should not be interpreted as proof of widespread miner capitulation. The data identifies a large movement from one mining pool, but does not establish that the coins were sold.

The upcoming difficulty reduction could improve mining conditions and help struggling operators manage their costs. However, it is unlikely to resolve the broader weakness in Bitcoin demand.

Investors will be watching whether exchange transfers translate into actual selling and whether spot-market buyers return. A recovery in demand would help absorb additional supply and provide a stronger foundation for Bitcoin’s next move.

#5223. SOL Eyes New Bullish Era as Solana Ditches ‘Beta’ Label After Six Years and Embraces Protocol Version 1.0

Solana has officially turned a major page in its history, dropping the long-standing ‘beta’ tag after more than six years and adopting protocol version 1.0. The milestone marks a significant step in the network’s evolution as it moves beyond its experimental phase, with ongoing efforts to improve transaction speed, finality, and overall performance. The development could also strengthen Solana’s appeal to developers and institutional players, raising fresh questions about whether SOL is poised for a new bullish chapter.

Solana has officially retired its six-year-old “mainnet beta” designation, with the network’s foundation saying the rebranding highlights the significant strides made since the blockchain first launched in March 2020.

“Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience,” the Solana foundation wrote in a Monday statement. “That progress continues with this simplification of nomenclature.”

The foundation emphasized that Solana has operated as a fully live network since its launch, arguing that retaining the beta designation had become outdated. It noted that the label, traditionally associated with technology still in its early testing stages, no longer accurately represented a blockchain already processing transactions and hosting active applications.

According to the Solana Foundation, the reclassification requires no action from users. Existing SOL holdings, account balances, and transaction histories will remain unchanged despite the protocol’s transition to version 1.0.

The foundation also advised developers and validator operators to stick to the specific instructions accompanying software releases, stressing that the new protocol designation does not mean all network upgrades or improvements become active automatically.

Solana’s move to protocol version 1.0 comes as the network continues pursuing major infrastructure improvements, with Alpenglow and Firedancer among its most closely watched developments. Both initiatives aim to strengthen Solana’s performance, reliability, and ability to support growing on-chain activity.

The first major milestone is Alpenglow, Solana’s new consensus protocol, which went live on mainnet on October 21. The upgrade targets transaction finality of approximately 150 milliseconds, a significant improvement from the previous 12.8-second timeframe. Transaction finality refers to the moment a blockchain permanently confirms a transaction, meaning it is considered settled and cannot be reversed under normal network conditions. Faster finality could make Solana more attractive for payments, decentralized finance, and institutional applications that require near-instant transaction settlement.

Meanwhile, Firedancer brings another important improvement through an independently developed validator client built by Jump Crypto. It provides an alternative to Solana’s existing Agave client, reducing the network’s dependence on a single software implementation. This client diversity could strengthen network resilience by limiting the risk that a bug affecting one implementation disrupts the entire blockchain.

The foundation added that the rebranding establishes a unified system for tracking Solana’s updates, allowing developers, validators, and infrastructure providers to identify protocol changes consistently, regardless of the software client they use.

#5222. New Monero Privacy Update Might Be Coming Soon: Key Improvement

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.

PR 11743 was opened on November 13 and is currently pending review. It is an updated version of a PR opened on November 8 by contributor vtnerd. After receiving feedback from another Monero developer, vtnerd, the PR was updated.

The issue lies in a mechanism where a node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P and then passes it to the regular Monero network.

Currently, when a Monero node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P, it relays that transaction to the rest of the Monero network.

While the transaction is technically private as it travels into the node, once it reaches Monero's public peers, the transaction is no longer private. This PR proposes that Monero nodes will only accept transactions from Tor and I2P peers over incoming connections. Transactions received over outgoing Tor and I2P connections would be ignored.

Once accepted, the transaction would be subject to a random delay before being relayed to the rest of the Monero network using Monero's existing transaction relay protocol, Dandelion++. Currently, a user can instruct their node to broadcast their transaction immediately.

Over Tor and I2P connections, this request would be ignored. No transaction would be exempt from the random delay.Being able to link a transaction's timing between the anonymity network and the Monero network is an easy way to deanonymize a user. If a transaction is broadcast to the Monero network immediately after being received from Tor, an observer watching both networks can link the two.

This is a similar concept to a previous PR from vtnerd that would have introduced a randomized delay when relaying transactions from Tor and I2P to the Monero network.

While the amount of code that would need to be modified is not particularly large, this does close a hole for users that rely on Tor and I2P to obscure their location.

When the patch lands in a release is yet to be confirmed. The PR is also labeled for a backport, so it might reach the current release branch as well.

The crypto industry’s run of friendly treatment in Washington looks set to end. Cody Carbone, chief executive of The Digital Chamber, warned that a Democrat-controlled Congress will be “very hostile” to digital assets. Broad market structure legislation such as the CLARITY Act is now unlikely to pass.

Lawmakers are instead expected to focus on investigating crypto companies with ties to President Donald Trump. The political shift comes as Bitcoin trades at its lowest level since July.

Carbone said in an interview that the industry is unlikely to get the broad legislation it had pushed for. The CLARITY Act, meant to set clear rules for how digital assets are regulated in the US, has been left in limbo.

Two longtime critics of the industry are set to gain influence over financial policy: Senator Elizabeth Warren in the Senate and Representative Maxine Waters in the House.

For crypto firms, the agenda in Washington is moving from passing rules to defending against scrutiny.

Trump’s Crypto Ties Move Into the Spotlight

The industry is preparing for sweeping inquiries into crypto businesses connected to the President. Carbone expects Warren and Waters to press hard on Trump’s links to digital assets.

The Digital Chamber’s plan is to counter those investigations by shifting the debate to the technology itself. Carbone wants supportive lawmakers to steer hearings toward topics such as tokenization, so the conversation is about substance rather than politics.

The strategy depends on finding allies inside the incoming majority. Carbone admitted that pro-crypto Democrats are “few and far between,” but said their numbers are growing.

Many of the newly elected Democrats are young and focused on technology. According to Carbone, several have told the industry they are “crypto curious.”

The Digital Chamber plans to target moderates and junior committee members. Carbone said no single Democrat can take on Warren alone, but a larger group could. The aim is to build enough support within the party to push back against the more hostile voices.

Opposition to data centers poses another major threat, Carbone said. Local resistance to energy-heavy facilities hits both crypto mining and artificial intelligence.

Carbone said voters made their concerns clear in the November election and have a right to be skeptical. Still, the industry argues that bans and moratoriums are the wrong response.

The Digital Chamber plans to show lawmakers how data centers can bring jobs and revenue to struggling districts. Carbone described blockchain, digital assets and AI as closely linked industries, and framed leadership in all three as a matter of national competitiveness.

The big warning was about America’s global position. Asked whether the US could lose its lead in the sector within the next two years, Carbone answered and said “100%.”

Developers in crypto and AI are already moving to friendlier places such as the UAE and Singapore. Carbone pointed to China, which holds the most blockchain patents worldwide, as the country most likely to take the lead if the US falls behind.

“If we don’t lead, other adversaries will,” Carbone said, arguing that the US must set the global rules before its rivals do.

Choosing a platform requires looking beyond advertised yields to understand token requirements, custody arrangements and withdrawal conditions.

Rates as of November 10, 2026. Stacks quotes a target annual yield, Babylon quotes APR, and other displayed rates may use different calculation conventions.

The main differences concern reward sources, custody arrangements, additional capital requirements and withdrawal flexibility.

Bitcoin staking rewards vary by source, denomination and additional capital requirements.

Stacks is a Bitcoin layer where BTC holders earn BTC.

Stacks miners commit BTC through Proof of Transfer (PoX) to compete for the right to produce Stacks blocks and earn STX rewards. The committed BTC is distributed to staking participants, providing the source of their BTC rewards. PoX has distributed over 4,200 BTC since January 2021.

Direct Bitcoin staking targets approximately 3% annualized yield, with weekly BTC rewards. Since September 2026, three staking bonds have sold out, bringing total BTC staked to 1,740 BTC.

Babylon distributes BABY rewards funded by newly issued tokens through the protocol’s inflation mechanism. Its displayed APR ranges from 0.04% to 0.52%, with the higher rate requiring participants to co-stake BABY alongside BTC.

Returns depend on reward distribution and BABY’s value relative to Bitcoin.

Core distributes CORE rewards to participants who delegate BTC to validators securing its blockchain. Rewards come from newly issued CORE block rewards and transaction fees.

Its displayed top-tier yield is 0.79%, with higher reward tiers requiring participants to stake CORE alongside BTC.

Starknet allows holders of supported tokenized Bitcoin assets to delegate them to validators securing the network.

Participants earn newly minted STRK tokens, with a displayed yield of 2.91%. Actual returns depend on network participation and STRK’s value relative to BTC.

Stacking DAO provides liquid Bitcoin staking through stBTC, a token representing an sBTC-based staking position. BTC rewards generated through Bitcoin staking on Stacks accumulate in the position, increasing the amount of sBTC backing each stBTC over time.

Its displayed yield is 2.31%, with rewards accruing automatically rather than requiring separate claims.

A 4% annual reward paid in a token that loses 50% of its value against BTC would be worth approximately 2% of the original BTC position, assuming other factors remain unchanged.

BTC rewards avoid this specific reward-token conversion risk, although staking still involves other costs and risks.

Stacks, Babylon and Core support native Bitcoin staking on Bitcoin L1, while Starknet and Stacking DAO use Bitcoin-backed assets on other layers.

In direct self-custodial staking, BTC remains timelocked on Bitcoin L1 under the participant’s custody. Institutions can also access this route through qualified custody infrastructure, including BitGo and Anchorage Digital.

BTC is locked on Bitcoin L1 and delegated to finality providers supporting the Babylon ecosystem. Bitcoin remains native, but the staking position is subject to protocol slashing conditions.

BTC holders timelock their Bitcoin on L1 and delegate staking weight to Core validators without transferring BTC to another chain.

Participants stake supported tokenized Bitcoin assets on Starknet, introducing dependencies on the underlying token’s backing and smart contracts.

Participants can deposit sBTC, a Bitcoin-backed asset on Stacks, or BTC, which is converted into sBTC. In return, they receive stBTC, representing their staking position and accruing BTC rewards. Part of Stacks’ Bitcoin staking capacity is allocated to this pooled staking route. Unlike direct staking on Stacks, this route is not self-custodial.

Native Bitcoin custody avoids certain bridge and wrapper dependencies but does not remove staking-specific risks.

Some protocols require additional token commitments, while others use them to increase rewards.

Stacks uses STX as staking capacity. Direct participants commit STX worth approximately 5% of their BTC position, locked for the staking term.

Babylon offers increased rewards through BABY co-staking, while Core uses CORE dual staking to determine reward tiers.

Starknet does not require participants to pair STRK with their BTC for standard delegation. Stacking DAO handles the underlying STX commitment without requiring participants to provide it separately.

These requirements affect capital efficiency because additional tokens introduce further price exposure.

Withdrawal conditions vary across staking models.

Stacks uses approximately six-month bonding periods for direct staking. Participants can exit early and recover BTC, but forfeit remaining rewards, while paired STX stays locked until the original term ends.

Babylon supports unbonding, subject to protocol-defined waiting periods and transaction requirements.

Core allows participants to choose how long to timelock their BTC on Bitcoin L1, with a minimum staking period of 24 hours. Once the term expires, BTC can be redeemed through a Bitcoin transaction.

Starknet allows participants to unstake tokenized BTC, subject to a seven-day withdrawal period during which rewards stop accruing. Liquid staking providers may offer alternative exit routes.

Stacking DAO supports instant stBTC-to-sBTC withdrawals when sufficient liquidity is available, subject to fees. Alternatively, participants can use a standard withdrawal with an approximately four-week cooldown. Converting sBTC into native BTC requires a separate withdrawal process.

Liquid staking provides flexibility, but instant redemption depends on available liquidity and protocol conditions.

Bitcoin staking risks depend on custody, reward assets and protocol conditions.

Token exposure: Stacks requires STX for direct staking, while Babylon and Core offer higher rewards through BABY and CORE commitments. Token price changes affect overall returns.

Slashing: Babylon can penalize staked BTC when delegated finality providers violate specified security conditions. Stacks’ self-custodial path does not apply BTC slashing.

Smart contracts: Starknet and Stacking DAO rely on tokenized Bitcoin infrastructure, introducing smart contract and asset-backing risks.

Liquidity and lockups: Native staking can restrict withdrawals, while liquid staking positions depend on redemption mechanisms and market liquidity.

Quoted yields should therefore be evaluated alongside custody arrangements, token requirements and withdrawal conditions.

Stacks is a strong option for eligible holders prioritizing BTC rewards and native custody. Babylon and Core offer alternative native staking models, while Starknet and Stacking DAO provide tokenized Bitcoin staking options.

Among the quoted figures, Stacks has the highest stated rate at approximately 3% target annual yield, followed by Starknet at 2.91%. Reward denominations and calculation methods differ, so these rates are not directly comparable.

Yes. Stacks distributes BTC rewards through direct Bitcoin staking, while Stacking DAO provides BTC-linked rewards through stBTC. Babylon, Core and Starknet distribute rewards in their respective native tokens.

Yes. Stacks, Babylon and Core support native BTC staking on Bitcoin L1. Their mechanisms differ in token requirements, withdrawal conditions and slashing exposure.

Risks include reward-token volatility, additional capital requirements, slashing, lockups, smart contract vulnerabilities and liquidity constraints. The relevant risks depend on the platform and staking method.
