#5213. Cardano's Hoskinson Says Everyone Will Be Happy Next Year

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson is sending out a hopeful message to the crypto space in the wake of a brutal market crash that is causing ADA to come very close to falling out of the top 20 crypto assets.

Recently, Hoskinson took to X to respond to a frustrated Cardano fan who posted a screenshot showing ADA falling almost 10% in the last 24 hours.

“It’s all going to be ok,” said Hoskinson. “Everyone will be happy next year after all this madness, hate and idiocy.”

The recent crypto market crash has proven to be extremely brutal for a lot of different assets, and Cardano is certainly one of the worst affected.

In recent trading, ADA has fallen all the way down to around $0.15.

At these levels, ADA is currently down around 95% from its all-time high of $3.09, which was reached in September 2021, based on data from CoinGecko.

This represents an almost complete loss of investment value for those who bought at the all-time high.

Overall, Cardano is also down around 35% in the last month and almost 60% since the start of 2026.

As a result, Cardano’s market cap has fallen all the way down to around $5.7 billion, with ADA dropping to 18th place in CoinGecko’s crypto rankings.

This is a very precarious position for the once-dominant altcoin Cardano, which is now extremely close to falling out of the top 20.

It seems as though there are a few different factors at play behind Cardano’s poor performance.

First of all, there has been a huge sell-off in the broader crypto market. Bitcoin has seen major drops, leading to more selling pressure on major altcoins.

This decline has coincided with a falling technology stock market, ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty, outflows from crypto investment products, and mass liquidations of leveraged positions.

That said, there are clearly some issues with Cardano beyond the wider market struggles.

For one, Cardano has faced a lot of criticism over the years for the blockchain’s relatively low adoption, even after years of development. This is especially evident when compared to other chains like Ethereum and Solana.

In fact, Cardano’s decentralized finance ecosystem has recently seen around $46 million in total value locked, as reported by DefiLlama.

Elsewhere, Hoskinson recently found himself embroiled in another controversy surrounding Cardano’s future.

In another recent X post, Hoskinson lashed out at certain commentators who keep bashing the blockchain for its apparent lack of adoption.

He noted that critics initially claimed Cardano suffered from poor on-chain metrics, few real-world use cases and technology that no one wanted to use.

Then, when Hoskinson decided to work on developing apps that would be able to attract millions of people and billions in assets, it seemed as though those same critics began claiming he was scamming everyone.

“You people are both stupid and scum. I can’t fix stupid,” said Hoskinson. “Grow up.”

As crypto adoption accelerates and blockchain infrastructure demand grows, investors are closely watching whether COIN stock can reclaim its previous highs. This Coinbase (COIN) stock price prediction explores the company’s fundamentals, technical outlook, and long-term price potential through 2030-2040.

Coinbase has transformed from a cryptocurrency exchange into a diversified digital asset infrastructure company. Its expanding ecosystem of institutional services, blockchain products, and recurring revenue businesses continues to reinforce the long-term outlook for COIN stock.

Coinbase has evolved into one of the crypto industry’s most strategically positioned companies, with its valuation increasingly linked to the expansion of the broader digital asset economy rather than trading activity alone. The company has built a diversified ecosystem spanning institutional brokerage, custody, staking, derivatives, stablecoin infrastructure, and Base, enabling it to participate across multiple segments of the blockchain value chain while generating a growing mix of recurring revenue.

The next phase of growth is likely to be driven by structural industry tailwinds rather than speculative retail demand. Increasing institutional adoption, the rise of tokenized securities and real-world assets, broader stablecoin usage, and continued expansion of on-chain finance could significantly expand Coinbase’s addressable market. Combined with its regulatory positioning and strong balance sheet, these factors strengthen the company’s competitive moat and reinforce a constructive long-term outlook for COIN stock.

Although Coinbase recorded $719 million in net income, approximately $715 million came from unrealized gains on crypto holdings.

Adding to the pressure, Morgan Stanley downgraded COIN to Underweight from Equal Weight and cut its price target from $258 to $120, citing weaker trading activity and a deteriorating earnings outlook. The price of Bitcoin has dropped by around 19% over the 50 days before the Nasdaq debut of Anthropic, and the decline is similar to the one that Bitcoin had ahead of the SpaceX listing in June. At press time, Bitcoin is trading at $65,450, according to TradingView. Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Nov. 13, and it dropped below $67,000 over the weekend.

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, is set to start trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Nov. 19. The AI company is offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each and aims to raise up to $64.4 billion in the IPO. At the top of the range, Anthropic would be valued at around $1.4 trillion, and the company has also arranged a $26 billion private placement.

SpaceX raised a record $75 billion in its IPO this summer, so the Anthropic listing is close to it in size. Before the SpaceX IPO, the price of Bitcoin also went down by around 19%.

Fundstrat managing partner Tom Lee called the current drawdown a temporary rotation of money into mega-IPOs, as investors sell liquid assets to buy shares in the largest offerings of the year.

Trump administration has nominated four candidates to fill key SEC and CFTC commissioner seats.

New SEC and CFTC commissioners could shape U.S. crypto rules without CLARITY Act.

Democrats will take control of Congress after lawmakers begin their terms in January.

The CLARITY Act remains stuck after failing to advance in the Senate. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is moving to fill key positions at the SEC and CFTC. Four nominees will face Senate review this week.

If approved, they could fill vacant positions and help the SEC and CFTC carry out their work as lawmakers struggle to agree on new crypto rules.

The White House sent four nominees to the Senate, including Democrat Kristin Johnson and a Republican Steven Levine for the SEC. Meanwhile, Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland for the CFTC.

🚨🗞️NEW: SEC, CFTC Nominees Head to the Hill; SCOTUS Rejects Custodia AppealFour nominees face Senate hearings this week for seats at crypto’s top regulators. Plus, Custodia’s fight for a Fed master account hits a dead end at SCOTUS, and more. ⬇️https://t.co/2VOGiML85o

The timing matters because both agencies are operating with limited staff. The SEC currently has only two commissioners, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the agency’s only serving commissioner.

If confirmed, the four nominees would give both agencies more members to debate and vote on policy.

For crypto companies, that could be important because the agencies are now expected to play a larger role after Congress failed to pass a market structure law.

The connection between the new nominees and the stalled bill is direct.

Nathan Anonick, a Republican, serves as legislative counsel to Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman. He also worked as a lead negotiator on the Agriculture Committee’s part of the CLARITY Act.

Matthew Rowland, a Democrat and CFTC attorney, has also worked on the CLARITY Act. He previously worked with Democratic senators Amy Klobuchar and Debbie Stabenow on the Senate Agriculture Committee.

That gives the two nominees direct experience with the same crypto legislation that is now stuck in the Senate.

The SEC nominees also bring different backgrounds.

Kristin Johnson, a Democrat, served as a CFTC commissioner from 2022 to 2025. She has focused on digital asset regulation, customer protection, risk management, and market integrity. She has also backed stricter rules around crypto custody and decentralized finance.

Steven Levine, a Republican, previously worked as counsel and deputy chief of staff to former SEC Commissioner Mark Uyeda. He later served as general counsel and senior adviser at the White House Council of Economic Advisers.

Levine would take the SEC seat previously held by Hester Peirce, who became a well-known supporter of clearer crypto rules while leading the SEC’s Crypto Task Force.

The timing of the nominations is also important. Democrats won control of both chambers in the November 3 midterm elections. However, Republicans still control the current Congress until the new lawmakers take office on January 3, 2027.

That gives Republicans a limited window to confirm Trump’s nominees before the change in power.

The Senate Banking Committee has scheduled Johnson and Levine for a November 19 hearing. The Agriculture Committee is handling the CFTC nominees, with the hearing schedule still developing.

If the nominees are confirmed, the SEC and CFTC could have a stronger role in shaping crypto policy while Congress remains divided over the CLARITY Act.

#5197. Why Binance’s ‘kill switch’ couldn’t stop hackers from draining $6.3B — Explained!

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

Binance encountered a rather expensive version of that problem on 29th October. Attackers compromised its wallet signing infrastructure and obtained authority to move cryptocurrency through mechanisms that did not depend on the exchange’s ordinary withdrawal process. Suspending withdrawals could interrupt that process. It could do considerably less about permissions already established on Ethereum.

By the time the attack was contained, approximately $6.3 billion had been stolen and Binance’s engineers had developed a specialised procedure to revoke malicious on-chain authority. The exchange could shut down affected services, but Ethereum would continue recognising the delegation until it was explicitly cleared.

Brian Cubellis, Chief Strategy Officer at Bitcoin custody platform Onramp, offered his two cents to AMBCrypto,

Pausing withdrawals turns off the exchange’s own software, but it does nothing about permissions the attacker has already written to the blockchain

The distinction is an uncomfortable one for an institution entrusted with billions in customer assets.

Binance subsequently coordinated freezes of stolen funds and began replenishing the affected holdings, reporting approximately 98% replenishment by 4th November. Its financial response was substantial.

However, it still is worth questioning what remained possible while its emergency controls were taking effect.

By the way, for those unaware, the attack began well before 29th October and nowhere near a blockchain.

According to Binance’s 3rd November incident report, an engineer downloaded a tampered installation package for an AI coding tool in June. The exchange detected the anomaly and replaced the device, but the attackers had already gathered intelligence about its employees and infrastructure. Well into September, another engineer was approached through a fictitious recruitment process involving interviews and a malicious coding assignment.

By 20th October, the attackers had used compromised employee systems and internal AI tooling to access additional machines. In doing so, they ultimately obtained credentials that opened the way to Binance’s wallet signing infrastructure.

It all paid off on the 29th. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, hot wallets transferred approximately 223.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker controlled addresses. Bitcoin and other assets followed. Chainalysis subsequently estimated the overall theft at approximately $6.4 billion.

What was the most consequential part of this intrusion though? The attackers gained access to Binance’s signing infrastructure, the very machinery responsible for authorizing transactions.

On Ethereum, the attackers exploited EIP-7702, a mechanism that allows an externally owned account to delegate execution to smart-contract code.

Ordinarily, that flexibility expands what a wallet can do. Here, according to Binance, the compromised signing infrastructure was used to grant malicious code execution rights over an Ethereum hot wallet. The exchange described 50 signed transactions involved in manipulating the account’s nonce and establishing the delegation.

The unsettling part comes next though. Those permissions remained valid on-chain even after Binance suspended withdrawals and shut down its hot-wallet services. The exchange could stop its own systems from processing transactions, but it could not simply switch off the authority the attackers had already established on Ethereum.

Then came another complication. Binance’s hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which distributes the production of cryptographic signatures across multiple participants or components rather than relying on a single conventional private key. That architecture can reduce certain risks, but it also meant there was no single private key available to revoke the malicious delegation immediately.

Binance’s engineers had to DEVELOP a specialised revocation procedure while the incident was UNFOLDING. Of course, this took additional time, prolonging the effort to contain unauthorized asset movements.

At 23:56 UTC, the final reported unauthorized Ethereum transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, was confirmed on-chain. Binance said it had been broadcast earlier and remained pending before confirmation. At 00:10 UTC on 30th October, the exchange cleared the malicious EIP-7702 delegation with a new authorization to the zero address.

The distinction between broadcast and confirmation matters. So does the absence of an established total for funds transferred after withdrawals were suspended.

Binance acknowledged that suspension alone could not stop every unauthorized movement, but its disclosures do not establish a reconciled post-suspension loss figure.

There is a comforting simplicity to the idea of a kill switch. Something goes wrong, someone pulls the plug and the damage stops. Unfortunately, the blockchain has no particular obligation to respect an exchange’s internal emergency procedures.

Consider a hotel discovering that someone has obtained an unauthorized key card. Closing reception prevents new cards from being issued. The existing card still opens the door. Cancelling it, securing the valuables, and recovering what has already disappeared are separate jobs.

Now, this comparison has its limits, but it captures the dilemma facing exchanges whose wallet permissions outlive their own systems.

The problem surfaced in a public exchange between Haseeb Qureshi, Managing Partner at Dragonfly, and  Tudor Anastasiu. Tudor Anastasiu is a blockchain infrastructure and security engineer and the founder of Anastasiu Labs.

The disagreement exposes a distinction that is easy to overlook in the middle of a breach.

A defensive sweep can move assets to safety, provided the exchange can authorize and execute it before the attacker does. However, moving funds does not necessarily invalidate permissions already granted on-chain and it certainly cannot retrieve assets that have already disappeared.

So, that leaves a rather awkward question: If the signing infrastructure itself has been compromised, how does an exchange authorize an emergency transaction without trusting the very system it suspects?

Carlos Vendrell, Founder of Zealynx Security, sees the answer in testing the procedure under exactly those conditions.

The drill should start from a list of every approval and delegation each hot wallet has given, then revoke one of them for real while assuming the normal signing service is the compromised part, and time it

Binance’s experience does not establish that MPC inherently prevents rapid revocation. Nor does its disclosure prove that no emergency procedure existed before the breach.

However, it does establish that engineers developed a specialised procedure during the incident and doing so took additional time.

There was another complication here, one that made the situation look almost absurd. The compromised wallet was reportedly STILL receiving money.

In an analysis dated 4th November, Four Pillars reported that Binance’s deposit-consolidation system continued collecting funds into a compromised Ethereum wallet identified as Binance 14. This allowed the attacker to sweep newly arriving assets.

Nexus Mutual’s reconstruction offers a particularly striking sequence.

At approximately 21:44 UTC, it says the attacker swept 200 million USDT that another Binance-labelled wallet had deposited roughly 72 seconds earlier. Seventy-two seconds! Barely enough time to make a cup of coffee, yet apparently sufficient for a fresh transfer to reach a compromised address and disappear.

The researchers’ findings raise a problem distinct from EIP-7702. An exchange can work to revoke an attacker’s authority while other operational systems continue directing funds towards a dangerous destination. Interrupting those internal asset flows is another containment task and requires its own controls and confirmation.

According to Brian Cubellis, emergency preparedness must account for the loss of the usual signing infrastructure.

An exchange should prove, before it is attacked, that it can cancel any permission on its wallets and move exposed funds to safety even if its own signing system has been taken over

That is easier prescribed than engineered though.

An independent emergency signing path may accelerate recovery, but it also introduces powerful authority that must be secured. Build too much dependence into the ordinary system and the emergency route may fail alongside it. Concentrate too much authority in the alternative and the supposed safeguard becomes another attractive target.

Once stolen assets leave the exchange’s immediate control, containment becomes a race involving investigators, stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks and the attacker.

Chainalysis’s investigation also described an attempt to move approximately $500 million in stablecoins through a swapping address. Within roughly 20 minutes, the attackers reportedly converted around $325 million into assets less susceptible to issuer freezes, including Ether. The remaining $175 million was frozen.

There was a reason for the rush. Stablecoin issuers such as Tether and Circle can freeze certain tokens at designated addresses. Bitcoin and Ether, by contrast, have no equivalent central issuer with that power. Converting the stolen stablecoins into other assets could therefore put them beyond the reach of an issuer-imposed freeze.

This whole episode illustrates the limits of intervention once funds have escaped. Investigators may be able to follow the money on-chain, but knowing where it has gone does not necessarily give them the power to retrieve it.

Binance nevertheless managed to secure a substantial portion of the stolen assets. In its 3rd November report, the exchange said that approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted through cooperation with issuers, law enforcement, and blockchain intelligence firms. By 4th November, it reported replenishing approximately 98% of the affected holdings through replacement purchases.

Of course, Binance had demonstrated considerable capacity to absorb the losses rather than pass them on to users. However, it tells us how much the exchange managed to secure or replace, not how effectively it prevented the attacker from continuing to move assets during the breach.

A year earlier, Bybit had encountered a different version of the problem with compromised transaction authority. In February 2025, attackers stole approximately $1.5 billion after compromising the environment associated with its Safe{Wallet} approval process.

According to Bybit’s forensic disclosure, malicious changes deceived signers into approving an unauthorized transaction. It also said that investigators found no indication that its own infrastructure had been compromised.

Both incidents exposed how much depends on the integrity of the authority behind a transaction. Multiple signatures offer limited protection when signers are misled about what they are approving. And as Binance discovered, shutting down a signing service does not necessarily invalidate authority already established on-chain.

An emergency kill switch sounds reassuring. Rather less reassuring is discovering, halfway through a breach, that the attacker has permissions your switch cannot revoke.

Binance’s experience raises an uncomfortable question for exchanges entrusted with billions in customer assets — Have they actually tested what happens when the systems responsible for protecting those assets become part of the attack?

An exchange should be able to demonstrate that it can revoke compromised permissions, move exposed assets to safety, and interrupt internal transfers without relying entirely on infrastructure it can no longer trust.

But what should customers make of an exchange’s public assurances when a breach is underway? AMBCrypto put that question to Vik Sharma, Founder and CEO of Cake Wallet,

A useful update names which approvals were revoked, which assets moved, and where, so customers can check it themselves

There are legitimate reasons to withhold sensitive operational details while an intrusion is underway. Once the immediate danger has passed, however, an exchange should be able to explain what its emergency controls actually stopped, when compromised authority was extinguished, and whether any assets remained exposed.

Binance deserves credit for publishing details of its response, coordinating substantial asset freezes, and committing its own resources to replenish affected holdings. Those measures helped absorb the financial damage. However, they also revealed why reimbursement and containment should never be confused.

A kill switch should buy defenders control, not merely time to figure out where control has gone.

#5191. Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC), chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, has asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, widening a congressional inquiry that has moved from Huang's private life to U.S. controls on chip exports to China. "The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote in a tweet announcing the requests on Thursday evening.

In a letter dated November 12, Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily at a public hearing on December 3 over public reports that "raise significant national security concerns." The committee has jurisdiction over export controls, "including their application to NVIDIA's exports of advanced semiconductors," he wrote. If Huang does not appear, the committee "is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas."

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Scott asked Lutnick to testify on December 10, noting Commerce's "central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations." A Lutnick spokesperson told NBC News that he had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily," while the White House said President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence" in Lutnick.

Separately on Thursday, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees, Reps. Brian Mast (R-FL), John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Rick Crawford (R-AR), wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department's under secretary for industry and security.

Huang was asked to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1 and Teter on December 2, with each given until 8 p.m. on Friday to agree or face a subpoena. Kessler, whose bureau administers export controls, was invited to a hearing on December 3.

"As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and MegaSpeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three chairs said in a statement. They called on Congress to add four chip security bills to the annual defense authorization bill.

It is their second request. A letter dated November 4 had asked Huang to brief the committees on November 18. Mast told reporters on Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, NBC News reported.

At the center of the inquiries is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials suspected the company of helping Chinese firms get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, The New York Times reported in October. Its sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times.

Megaspeed told the Times it had hired outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws, according to NBC News.

The Times reported that U.S. officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has rejected that as a smear, and Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether she was a spy, according to BBC News.

Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife and resigned on Thursday. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Moolenaar told reporters that Huang had "been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls," Roll Call reported. On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the Banking Committee's ranking member, and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) asked Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records on Nvidia chip exports to China.

China's foreign ministry warned on Friday that tighter U.S. export controls on semiconductors would threaten the stability of global supply chains, Al Jazeera reported.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% at $166.19 on Thursday and were up 2.7% at $170.63 in premarket trading early on Friday, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company has lost almost $500 billion in market value since the close on Friday, November 6. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.

#5189. XRP Ledger Passes 11.7 Million Sub-Dollar AI Agent Microtransactions

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Chandler Fang, founder of AI payments startup t54.ai, has said that the company's x402 Facilitator on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has processed more than 10 million AI agent transactions. Fang made the comments in an interview that the XRPL Foundation published on X on November 15, and the interviewer put the number of these payments at 11.7 million.

According to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very quickly in the three months," he said.

The x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang said that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

According to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang said.

Fang said that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower users to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

According to Fang, trust is the main issue for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang said.

t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang said that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

"The ten million transactions are just a starting point. I think next year you should expect a lot more transactions. Maybe even more transactions settled on XRPL will be done by AI agents than by humans," Fang said.

#5188. Why the ‘Blue Wave’ coming for Trump’s $1.5B crypto empire may be mostly good news

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Alaska is yet to be called, but the writing is on the wall for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. The Democrats have seized control of both the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives.

For all intents and purposes, this means that Trump is now a lame duck president.

That’s the least of his worries, though, as Democrats could now set their sights on investigating Trump’s crypto ventures. After all, this is a man who amassed a fortune of close to $1.5 billion from cryptocurrency ventures in the first year of his second term in office.

Donald Trump became the first sitting president to launch a memecoin, with OFFICIAL TRUMP [TRUMP] generating over $600M in licensing fees and royalties alone. All while a majority of the memecoin’s retail investors saw red.

He is also the “Co-Founder Emeritus” of World Liberty Financial [WLFI], a DeFi and cryptocurrency platform. According to public filings, the project, co-founded by Eric Trump, Barron Trump, and Donald Trump Jr., brought in $799M in 2025 alone.

Then there’s the matter of an Abu Dhabi-based fund buying $2 billion in USD1, WLF’s own stablecoin, to invest in Binance after the crypto exchange was fined over $4 billion for money laundering violations. Its founder, Changpeng Zhao, pled guilty and served a 4-month jail term before being pardoned by Trump.

Simply put, it can be argued that the president has used his position (and crypto) to monetize the presidency and enrich his personal fortune. Hence, the investigations.

Moving ahead, what should the industry expect now that the Democrats are in control of the U.S Congress?

Well, it wouldn’t be unreasonable to expect a gridlock. After all, many in the crypto industry have historically backed Republican candidates because they championed free market de-regulation and digital asset frameworks.

On the contrary, several prominent Democrats like Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is also expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, have often been vocal critics of the sector.

However, expecting the worst outcome possible here would allude to a very superficial reading of the situation. This is why it’s important to differentiate between what will happen, what can happen, and what won’t happen.

Yes, the likes of Warren haven’t been the most receptive towards the sector, but party-wide support has been growing over the years.

Consider this – following the latest midterm elections, there are a total of 50 pro-crypto senators against just 33 anti-crypto ones. Similarly, in the House, 241 are currently pro-crypto as opposed to 104 who are against crypto.

Those are significant numbers. More importantly, they also suggest that despite some historical bias, the sector enjoys some degree of bipartisan support.

The example of Fairshake is a case in point. The Crypto Super PAC spent millions backing 33 House candidates during the midterms. 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats. At the time of writing, 29 of them had already won.

Legislative evidence from before the midterms is worth looking at too. As Andrew Nalichaev, CEO of HAIA Finance, pointed out,

… support for rules concerning stablecoins has received bipartisan backing: the GENIUS Act passed the Senate 68 to 30 and the House 308 to 122. An important issue that led to the failure of the CLARITY Act in September was the ethics issue regarding officials involved in issuing or supporting tokens.

Likewise, Luke Jacobi, Founder and Editor at OptimistFi, told AMBCrypto,

Our small comparison of two House final-passage votes on July 17, 2025 found that 102 of 212 voting Democrats backed GENIUS, compared with 78 of 212 for CLARITY: 48.1% versus 36.8%. Both attracted cross-party support, but the 24-vote difference shows why a single ‘pro-crypto’ label misses policy-specific disagreement.

According to a recent report, over 30% of the population, or 70M people, now hold digital assets. It is evidence that despite some skepticism and vocal criticism, the industry has reached a level of financial integration that will be difficult to reverse right now.

It is also evidence that crypto is no longer a single-party issue. Both red and blue states have their own share of crypto holders. In time, their numbers will grow, and so will the degree of bipartisan support the industry enjoys from lawmakers.

However, the concerns about a possible legislative gridlock and its potential impact on the regulatory clarity the industry desperately seeks aren’t totally unwarranted. In the current landscape, Democrats control the U.S. Congress, while Republicans control the White House.

And while he did suggest that he looks forward to working with Democrats, President Trump has also asserted that he will wield his veto power if need be, especially since Democrats don’t enjoy a veto-proof or filibuster-proof majority.

This means that realistically, we can expect a certain level of gridlock across the board ranging from budgets, appropriations, and defense spending. Even crypto, if the new U.S. Congress is intent on investigating President Trump’s ventures.

Hence, the question: How big a concern could this be? According to Dmitri Mihhailov, General Partner at Prifinance,

Investigations do not change laws already on the books, and the most important one for the industry is already there – The GENIUS Act.

Mihhailov also told AMBCrypto that in his view,

… gridlock hurts what is still missing: a federal framework for crypto trading markets. Until Congress passes one, firms rely on agency guidance and court rulings, and a future SEC or CFTC can change guidance much more easily than a statute.

In fact, it can be argued that it’s not the investigation itself that could be concerning for the crypto-sector. Instead, it’s the calendar that could be the problem. Especially since congressional investigations consume time, staff, resources, and political capital, all of which can be used to pass necessary crypto legislation.

The “Wild West.” That’s the reputation the cryptocurrency industry had once upon a time.

Gone are those days, though, as the sector became more mainstream and was embraced by institutions and people world over. Banks, lawmakers, and even nation-states. Heck, even Trump did that within years of calling Bitcoin “a scam.”

Politics is a fickle game, though. It’s not unreasonable to contemplate that some legislators could turn on the industry if the congressional investigations into Trump’s crypto ventures go underway.

The thing is, as an industry, crypto has well and truly arrived on the world stage over the last few years. Despite perceptions, it is too big to be defined by a singular person’s business interests. In fact, more than political scrutiny, THAT would be the biggest threat to the sector.

The danger is that crypto as a whole becomes politically coded through its association with high-profile ventures like memecoins and politically connected stablecoins. If every crypto vote starts to look like a vote on a specific politician, moderates on both sides will find it easier to abstain or delay.

Then what could these investigations yield? Well, at the very least, clear-cut ethics, disclosures, and conflict of interest rules for public officials – proposals that were at the core of the CLARITY Act’s failure. And, at the end of the day, won’t that be a win for the industry as a whole?

So, no. While there might be some distancing, lawmakers won’t turn on crypto.

2026 hasn’t been a great year for the crypto sector so far. The markets aren’t exactly booming, billions have been lost to hacks, and the CLARITY Act failed to go through. Plus, the current President of the United States could soon find himself at the center of an investigation into his crypto dealings.

It is simply a matter of getting used to the new balance of power in Washington D.C.

#5187. Binance Warns About AI Scams

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.

The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its users that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.

"AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange said in a post.

The cryptocurrency exchange has assured its users that no one from Binance will ever reach out to them asking for money or offering unsolicited investment advice.

Binance says scammers are making realistic deepfake videos featuring executives and employees of the company.

Fraudsters are using these deepfakes, some of which are very realistic, to trick potential targets through fraudulent video calls.

That way, people who fall victim to the scam might think they are interacting with real Binance personnel.

Binance warned that scammers often try to reach potential targets through messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram. They impersonate Binance employees by using their names, photos, and job titles to appear credible.

After making contact with a potential victim, the scammer may try to convince them to send crypto, take part in an exclusive investment opportunity, or take other financial actions.

Binance has called on crypto users to be cautious about any unexpected messages they receive, even if they seem to be from someone at the company they know.

A realistic appearance no longer guarantees a person's identity, given that AI can now easily mimic voices and facial expressions.

Users should double-check any suspicious messages through official Binance support channels before taking any action.

#5186. Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Leading cryptocurrency Bitcoin has dropped 5.6% on the day, and is currently trading at just over $69,300, per Decrypt data. It comes after the latest consumer price index, or CPI, results came in "hotter than expected," experts said, with the drop was triggered by a "concentrated liquidation."

Bitcoin's plunge took it to a 24-hour low of $67,922, its lowest level since mid-August, when it boosted from $63,000.

"Bitcoin’s drop below $69,000 was directly triggered by a concentrated liquidation of leveraged long positions," Tim Sun, senior analyst at Hashkey, told Decrypt. "Though the deeper issue lies in steadily weakening market demand."

Sun highlighted U.S. Bitcoin spot ETFs recording six consecutive days of net outflows, according to CoinGlass. He also pointed to stablecoin supply shrinking and MSCI removing digital asset treasury firm Strategy from its funds.

"ETFs, stablecoin liquidity, and corporate treasuries have served as the primary capital pillars supporting this Bitcoin rally," Sun said. "With all three coming under simultaneous pressure, the market is losing the marginal buying power that previously propelled prices higher."

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies have also taken a hit. Ethereum has dropped 4.6% on the day to $1,953, BNB has slipped 4.7% to $639.46, and Solana is down 3.1% to $80.47, according to Decrypt data. The global crypto market cap has dropped 4.6% over the past 24 hours to $2.39 trillion.

It follows U.S. CPI rising 0.4% in October, which is "hotter than expected, even if the headline monthly rate eased to 0.4% from September’s 0.6%," according to CoinShares head of research James Butterfill. "More troubling was the composition," he added. "Food rose 0.5%, services remained firm, and core CPI increased 0.3%, with services excluding rent, a gauge of domestic price pressure the Fed watches closely, rising 0.5%. The inflation problem is therefore no longer easily dismissed as an oil story."

The consumer price index, or CPI, is a way of measuring inflation that tracks the average price changes of everyday goods and services over time. Central banks tend to use CPI to inform whether they'll cut or hike interest rates, meaning higher-than-expected CPI signals a potential Federal Reserve hike.

Polymarket predictors put a 97% chance on the Fed raising interest rates this year, up from 75% at the start of the week. The CME FedWatch tool, meanwhile, sees an 88% chance of a 25 basis point hike, with 12% anticipating a 50 basis point rise.

On top of the CPI, Bitcoin's downward move comes following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company, after reports of multiple affairs including with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive spread.

Huang's departure has sparked "severe volatility across tech stocks, further dampening market risk appetite," Sun told Decrypt. "This has prompted broader portfolio de-risking, amplifying the downward pressure on Bitcoin," he added.

For a crypto rebound to happen, Sun said that Bitcoin needs "long-term allocation capital" to flow back into crypto after ETFs, stablecoins, and digital asset treasury companies have taken a hit in recent weeks.

#5184. Will Aave’s $21M bet on Bitcoin’s lending potential restore DeFi liquidity or create new risk?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

One of the main metrics to look at is liquidity.

With over 4% of USDT supply being removed in Q4, worth around $10 billion, there is still not enough dry powder to confirm that the market has hit bottom. In this context, Aave’s decision to allow Bitcoin to be used within DeFi lending becomes a lot more impactful. Naturally, the question becomes — Can the move increase capital inflows by allowing users to use Bitcoin as collateral and therefore increase stablecoin volumes?

In essence, could this be the much needed catalyst for a DeFi resurgence?

In a recent development, Aave [AAVE] has gained DAO approval to add support for using Bitcoin as collateral.

The proposal will allow holders to lock up their BTC to borrow stablecoins. Notably, the proposal was unanimously approved on 9th November. This means Bitcoin holders can gain new liquidity through Aave’s $21 million credit market by borrowing stablecoins using their BTC as collateral.

As the chart below shows, Aave will be allocating $21 million to their credit products to five different stablecoins. The two largest stablecoins will be USDT and USDC which have been allocated $8 million each. These account for almost 76% of the total capacity.

Meanwhile, AAVE’s native stablecoin GHO will be allocated $1 million. The last $4 million will be split evenly between USDG and RLUSD with $2 million allocated to each.

Why does this matter? Well, this allocation shows that Aave is looking to blend both traditional stablecoins and newer assets to provide more options for borrowing. Consequently, this will allow Bitcoin holders to borrow against several stablecoin markets using their BTC as collateral.

As Aave Founder and CEO Stani Kulechov explained,

The Babylon-built Bitcoin-backed market on Aave V4 shows how easily new markets can be launched using the Hub and Spoke model. Native BTC collateral, without wrappers or custodians, unlocks a major new source of liquidity for on-chain borrowing and lending.

Crypto lending is slowing down as borrowers reduce their exposure amid market uncertainty.

According to Galaxy Research, the overall crypto-backed loan market fell by 16.78% during Q2, hitting a total value of $56.16 billion. This is the first time that all major lending sectors have fallen since 2022. DeFi lending also saw a sharp fall, with total active loans decreasing from $47.13 billion to $21.94 billion between April and July. In short, traders have lost interest in borrowing against their assets.

However, Aave has seen an opposite trend, with the platform noting all-time highs in active loans on the Aave V4 platform, increasing by almost 100% in Q2 to $500 million. Against this backdrop, the addition of Bitcoin to the lending market could lend further growth potential.

In essence, by allowing BTC holders to use their asset as collateral, the market could see more capital flowing into DeFi, more collateral on Aave, and more demand for on-chain borrowing.

Aave V4’s Hub-and-Spoke architecture provides an isolated environment in which integrations can deploy both standard and custom Spokes without affecting other assets on the Hub.

The crypto market is facing its worst liquidity crunch since the 2022 bear market.

The overall stablecoin market cap has fallen by about $14 billion over the past month. By 10th November, the total stablecoin market cap was around $290 billion, according to DeFiLlama. In fact, the last two weeks alone saw the most net stablecoin outflows ever in over four years. Over half of this drop came from USDT and a further 20% from USDC.

This pressure can be seen across the DeFi space. In fact, the total DeFi TVL fell to around $76.6 billion on 12th November, with stablecoin market cap sitting at $286.9 billion at press time. However, DeFi TVL also fell by 9.7% week-on-week.

Against this backdrop, Aave’s move could offer a new source of liquidity.

There is one technical distinction worth keeping though. This integration doesn’t automatically mean any new stablecoins will flow into DeFi. Instead, borrowers will have access to liquidity that is already sitting in Aave. For liquidity to grow, the protocol will also need to attract more lenders and fresh deposits.

As per the attached chart, there is still a long way to go before the lending market on Bitcoin hits significant levels.

BTC-backed loans reached $3.58 billion in 2025, representing just 0.24% of Bitcoin’s market cap. So, by supporting Bitcoin as collateral, Aave could help unlock this largely untapped lending demand.

Aave’s move could also expose its lending market to greater risks.

According to AMBCrypto, although this new borrowing opportunity on Aave will create new demand, it can also lead to greater speculation. Users can borrow stablecoins using BTC as collateral and then re-lend them into leveraged crypto positions.

Consider this — Bitcoin Futures Open Interest increased by 12.1% in 19 days up to late-October, despite a 5.3% price decrease in BTC. This indicated that traders were increasing their leveraged exposure.

This continued into November, with Bitfinex reporting that this was the fifth time traders added leverage to their positions while BTC fell. The previous 4 times this occurred, traders executed liquidations of long positions worth over $800 million.

For Aave, the concern is that easier access to Bitcoin credit could add another source of speculation.

Ultimately, the move by Aave to integrate Bitcoin comes at a time where DeFi needs liquidity. However, its impact remains to be seen still. While the integration could entice early lenders and stablecoin deposits, there is a risk that high levels of demand could come from speculation and cause further volatility in the market.

Thus, Aave may unlock a new source of liquidity. However, turning that liquidity into DeFi growth will be the test.

#5183. Nvidia Employees Push Board to Bring Back Jensen Huang: Report

Nvidia Employees Push Board to Bring Back Jensen Huang: Report

Some Nvidia employees are calling on the company's board to bring back Jensen Huang, days after he resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital relationships, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired.

An internal "suggestion box" post, submitted by a longtime engineer prior to Huang's resignation, urged the board to take employee sentiment into account before acting, Wired reported. It has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, several of which asked the board to find a way to reinstate Huang. "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," one anonymous commenter wrote.

The post also called on the board to share the findings of its investigation with staff and to formally seek their views on Huang continuing as CEO. One employee went further, sending a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit and declaring: "I stand by Jensen."

In the hours following Huang's departure, some two dozen Nvidia employees posted supportive messages on LinkedIn, while Wired said it could not find any employee posts backing his departure. The engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment, and Nvidia and its new board chair, Harvey Jones, did not immediately respond to the outlet.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and a board member on Thursday, ending a 33-year tenure at the company he co-founded. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, and Jones, a former CEO of Synopsys, became the board's first chair. Nvidia did not give a reason for the resignation.

Huang told staff on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, without naming anyone.

The New York Times had reported in October that surveillance of Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, indicated that she had developed a "close relationship" with the Nvidia CEO. Per the Times, U.S. officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, while the Financial Times reported that a U.S. memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied that she is a spy.

Alice Huang was CEO and chair of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, and was investigated by Singapore police over possible false declarations relating to the company's server purchases, the country's Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday. She was not investigated for espionage, it said.

Police found insufficient evidence that she had committed any offenses, but concluded she had knowingly given them inaccurate information to downplay her role at Megaspeed, according to the ministry. She was issued a stern warning, left Singapore in February and was barred from returning. Investigations into Megaspeed and six other people are ongoing.

Alice Huang is now living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not yet concluded whether Huang was a spy, and that the FBI was investigating the reports, according to Reuters, which was unable to reach her for comment.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Jensen Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reported directly to him. Powell has not commented.

On Thursday, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, whom it did not name. Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters, and Huang and a representative for the board did not respond. Huang has not commented on the reports since his Sunday email, according to Wired.

The calls inside Nvidia echo criticism of the board's decision from tech and crypto figures. Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao called it a mistake for Nvidia to let Huang resign, while Elon Musk said hiring him would be "an honor."

Huang still faces scrutiny in Washington. Congressional committees have asked him to sit for a closed-door interview on December 1 and to testify at a Senate hearing on December 3, as lawmakers examine Nvidia's chip exports to China.

He and Nvidia also face a proposed shareholder class action over his alleged ties to Alice Huang.

Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under Kress.

#5181. Brazil Takes Aim at Stablecoins With Shocking Money Laundering Claim

The head of the foreign exchange department at the Central Bank of Brazil has claimed that legitimately obtained money could be considered laundered if it’s used to purchase stablecoins.

The senior Brazilian official claimed that converting money into stablecoins could link it to money laundering, even when it was initially obtained legally.

According to a recent report, Gerson Romantini, who is the director of the foreign exchange department at the Central Bank of Brazil, allegedly made the controversial statements at a private event attended by representatives of financial companies.

Romantini claimed that funds acquired legally could be transformed once they enter the stablecoin ecosystem.

In his view, even legally obtained money could effectively be "dirtied" if used in certain stablecoin schemes, and thus be considered part of a money laundering operation.

It’s important to note that the comments attributed to Romantini do not represent an official statement that all conversions into stablecoins could be considered money laundering.

This statement comes as Brazil has already moved to tighten restrictions on how cryptocurrencies are used for international payments.

On April 30, the Central Bank of Brazil published Resolution No. 561, which took effect on Oct. 1.

The resolution limits the use of virtual assets for the settlement of international payment and transfer services, also known as eFX.

In practice, this means that payments between an eFX provider and its foreign partner must be settled through traditional foreign exchange operations or a Brazilian real account opened by nonresidents.

Crypto payments for these particular settlements are off-limits.

A practice called the "stablecoin sandwich" is particularly concerning.

The way it works is that a Brazilian fintech accepts a certain amount of reais from a customer, then uses this money to purchase stablecoins like USDT or USDC and sends the funds in crypto to an offshore company.

This company, in turn, can convert these stablecoins into fiat currency to make payments or send money to families.

This allows users to make international money transfers for a lower fee and circumvent some of the infrastructure banks use.

The controversial statements have already received a response from Brazil’s crypto industry.

In a statement on Nov. 14, the Brazilian Association of Tokenization and Digital Assets (ABToken) questioned the alleged classification of stablecoin transactions as money laundering.

ABToken maintains that the use of stablecoins is not necessarily illegal.

Furthermore, the association also cautioned that sweeping bans may create legal confusion and hinder legitimate business activities that use stablecoins for international payments.

#5180. Paraguay’s Cheap Hydropower Is Drawing a New Rival for Bitcoin Miners: AI

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Paraguay has become an important location for Bitcoin mining because of the cheap hydropower available near the Itaipu dam. Now a different kind of energy-hungry business is bidding for the same electricity: artificial-intelligence data centres. The country is approaching a turning point as special electricity contracts for crypto miners are due to expire at the end of 2027, potentially forcing operators to renegotiate at higher rates or move their equipment.

The question is no longer whether Bitcoin mining can use abundant renewable power. It is which businesses deserve access when that power becomes more valuable to the wider economy.

CoinDesk reported that Paraguay's state utility ANDE expects to collect about $350 million from crypto miners in 2026. Mining firms have benefited from electricity pricing around $44 per megawatt-hour, a level that helped turn the country into a major global mining location. The revenue is significant, but it does not establish that the arrangement will remain the best option once national demand and competing industrial uses rise.

The contracts matter because mining profitability is highly sensitive to electricity costs. A site can possess efficient machines and substantial computing power yet struggle if its price per unit of energy rises while Bitcoin mining rewards and transaction fees fail to keep pace. Operators make investment decisions years ahead, so uncertainty over access after 2027 can affect capital spending today.

ANDE plans to allow its special crypto electricity arrangements to expire on December 31, 2027, according to the report. A group of utility engineers has separately proposed limiting the combined allocation for crypto mining, AI and data centres to 700 megawatts, with electricity allocated through an auction at higher rates. That engineering proposal has not automatically become binding government policy.

One prominent operator, HIVE Digital Technologies, has a substantial portion of its mining capacity in Paraguay. Its disclosures indicate that continued operations at affected facilities depend on renegotiating power arrangements. That is a business risk rather than evidence that every mining machine is already shutting down. The timetable still leaves room for discussions, alternative contracts and changes in project plans.

The growing competition is more than an abstract forecast. A company connected to the proposed Iguazú AI City project has secured a long-term power arrangement, according to the same reporting. AI data centres generally need stable, predictable electricity supply to support hardware, cooling and customer service commitments. Their economics are different from Bitcoin mining, where machines can sometimes be switched off when prices rise.

That difference can be both a disadvantage and an opportunity for miners. AI projects may justify higher tariffs through long-term contracts and investment promises, but miners can potentially provide flexible demand when the grid has surplus power. The outcome will depend on how regulators value reliable revenue, employment, infrastructure investment and system flexibility.

The energy-versus-computing trade-off is unfolding worldwide. NewsBTC recently examined MARA's Bitcoin sales amid an AI data-centre strategy, and Hyperscale Data's evolving approach offers another example of companies reassessing where computing infrastructure generates the best returns.

For Paraguay, the next meaningful developments will be power-tariff decisions, contract renewals and evidence of actual investment by both mining and AI businesses. The state utility must also meet growing domestic electricity demand. Cheap hydropower created the mining boom; competition for the same resource may now determine how much of that industry stays.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has published a lengthy post on EIP-8037, a change planned for the Glamsterdam upgrade. In his latest post, Buterin wrote that something like EIP-8037 is, unfortunately, the only way for Ethereum to scale safely.

With the update, Ethereum will collect an additional gas fee for the creation of new accounts. Creating a new account would cost more than five times as much gas as it does now, with new storage slots and contracts getting more expensive too.

According to Buterin, execution is easy to scale, but Ethereum's state already grows by around 110 GiB per year, and every node has to keep it.

Unfortunately, it will bring more pressure on existing contracts, for example, the OP Stack bridge. The bridge has a hardcoded gas limit of 40,000, and even a small increase in state gas costs would push its operation above it. Mainnet has at least 13 contracts like that, according to the security firm ChainSecurity.

It's a double-edged sword: from one standpoint, it limits the ability of spammers and scammers to fill the network with junk accounts used by illicit actors; from the other, it creates additional financial pressure.

Glamsterdam being postponed is another pain factor here: considering the poor state of the market and Ethereum's struggle, it's clear that any delays in major updates negatively affect the network outlook. The new date is yet to be confirmed.

Vitalik Buterin has been hinting at the change in gas consumption for ages now. Back in 2024, he called multidimensional gas the hardest problem in his own post on the topic.

Setting strict limits was never a farsighted option, and developers have been told that for years. However, it's yet another question: who's actually to blame? Buterin himself admitted that this rule hasn't been written down or repeated since 2021, so newer developers simply didn't know about it.

He now suggests writing down a list of features that are likely to change, from gas mechanics to slot time.

#5177. Clearpool’s CPOOL-to-CLEAR Swap Approaches as Exchanges Begin Transfer Restrictions

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Clearpool’s move from CPOOL to CLEAR is reaching the point where a project timetable becomes an exchange-access issue. Its self-custody migration opens on November 17, while some trading venues have scheduled restrictions before that date.

The distinction matters because holders do not all follow the same process. A token in a personal wallet and a balance on an exchange may represent similar market exposure, but the organizations responsible for converting them are different.

Clearpool’s November 12 migration guide sets a one-for-one conversion and a February 17, 2027 deadline. It identifies CLEAR as an ERC-20 token on Ethereum. The guide separates holders using their own wallets from those whose exchanges will handle the migration.

That separation is more useful than treating the announcement as a universal instruction to transfer tokens. Exchange support, snapshot rules and the blockchain on which a balance is held can affect the appropriate process.

The guide is the informational starting point for verifying those arrangements. The existence of a public migration should not make unsolicited messages or lookalike websites credible. A legitimate project announcement can be copied by an impersonator without changing its appearance very much.

KuCoin’s notice schedules CPOOL deposits and withdrawals to close at 04:00 UTC on November 16, followed by trading bots at 07:00 and the CPOOL/USDT market at 08:00. The exchange says it will convert eligible balances automatically.

Its notice includes specific eligibility conditions: a minimum of 0.1 CPOOL and covered spot-account balances. Pending deposits or withdrawals at the snapshot are excluded. It also warns that later deposits of the old token will not be supported.

These details show why the project deadline alone is insufficient. An exchange can stop accepting an asset months before the broader self-custody window ends. Its reopening schedule for the replacement asset is another separate milestone, which KuCoin says will be announced after the swap.

A holder exchanging 1,000 old tokens for 1,000 new tokens preserves the number of units in that transaction. The conversion does not establish the new market price, total supply or the holder’s percentage interest in the network’s token economy.

Clearpool’s September expansion proposal paired the migration with treasury recapitalization and additional allocations. That document is background to the economic design; the November migration guide supplies the operational dates. The two should be read for their different purposes.

NewsBTC’s examination of Aave’s proposed division of lending revenue illustrates a related analytical point: an administrative parameter or token count is only one part of the underlying economics. Funding, incentives and realized activity still determine how a protocol develops.

Clearpool has linked its broader plans to institutional credit and expansion toward the XRP Ledger. Completing a token conversion would be an operational milestone, while launching products and attracting borrowers would require separate evidence.

That distinction also appears in NewsBTC’s reporting on financing tokenized collateral. A working token or interface is one component; enforceable claims, usable liquidity and dependable servicing make the financial product useful.

For this week’s transition, the immediate questions are concrete: whether exchanges apply their published rules, when replacement balances appear and when the new markets reopen. Those answers will reveal the quality of the migration more clearly than a change of ticker alone.

📉 Crypto Sells Off as Jensen Huang Exits Nvidia

Two weeks ago, The New York Times reported that Nvidia’s CEO had a close relationship with an executive at a Singapore chip buyer under US export-control investigation. Things escalated quickly from there.

On Sunday, Jensen Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years, and Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. On Wednesday, The Times reported a second relationship, this one with an executive who reports directly to him. Three Republican committee chairs were preparing a subpoena.

Thursday morning he resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The company gave no reason.

CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping the CFO job. She has been Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, through the entire AI buildout, and spent 13 years at Microsoft before that. The board also named Harvey Jones, formerly of Synopsys, as its first-ever chair, and started a search that will consider internal and external candidates with no timeline attached.

The stock fell as much as 14% before recovering to close down about 4%. Nvidia has now shed more than a trillion dollars in market value this month.

Bitcoin fell roughly 4% to a twelve-week low near $68,000, down from above $76,000 earlier in the week. ETH lost about 3% and is now below $2,000. Solana, BNB and XRP all fell between 3% and 5%. The broad market index was off about 4% on the day and 7% on the week.

It’s a bleak picture. But there are some local reasons for hope.

First, this is the exact price action that we mapped out in Wednesday’s newsletter, after analyzing the SPCX impact on Bitcoin and what similar price action for the Anthropic IPO would mean. TLDR - it mapped to a bottom on Nov 12 around the 200-week moving average (which hit last night).

Second, Binance reported Thursday afternoon that it has completed coverage of the assets affected by its $6.34 billion hack and published an expanded Proof of Reserves snapshot covering all 44 cryptocurrencies impacted. Many believe that the Binance post-hack aftermath has been weighing on crypto prices, and now perhaps this coverage will help alleviate some pain.

And then Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 results on Tuesday. Any positive news about Jensen succession planning, the Q3 results and/or future growth will likely stop the bleeding on one of the biggest assets across markets (also helping crypto most likely).

We will find out soon if it’s enough to stop the bleeding…

#5174. Major Wealth Advisor With $24 Billion in Assets Discloses XRP ETF Stake

Major U.S. wealth management company EP Wealth Advisors has revealed that it holds an investment in an XRP exchange-traded fund (ETF). This was disclosed in the company's latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

EP Wealth Advisors, a California-based investment advisory firm with about $24.4 billion in securities holdings, has revealed that it held 18,400 shares in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This was disclosed in the official SEC filing that the company submitted to the commission on Nov. 13. The filing showed that the investment was valued at $147,936 at the end of the third quarter.

Furthermore, the filing showed that the total portfolio value reported by EP Wealth Advisors stood at $24,380,879,896. This value comprises 1,603 items in the company's 13F information table.

It's worth noting, however, that this isn't the company's total assets under management. It's the value of its reportable securities holdings. There are also assets that are not included in Form 13F.

Interestingly, this isn't the first time EP Wealth Advisors has held an investment in XRPI. Data from its historical 13F filings shows that in the second quarter of 2026, the wealth management company held 13,425 shares in XRPI.

The recent filing shows that the company has now increased the number of shares it holds in the XRP ETF by 4,975 shares. This represents about a 37% increase in the company's XRPI holdings during the third quarter.

Nevertheless, this amount is very small relative to the company's multibillion-dollar securities portfolio. It represents less than 0.01% of the total value of its reported securities holdings.

It's also worth reiterating that Form 13F is simply a filing that shows institutional holdings at the end of a quarter. It doesn't necessarily represent the investment manager's current holdings.

The Volatility Shares XRP ETF was launched in May 2025. Its ticker symbol is XRPI, and it is currently trading on Nasdaq.

XRPI isn't a spot XRP ETF. This means it doesn't directly hold the cryptocurrency XRP. Rather, it primarily derives its exposure to XRP's price movements through XRP futures contracts.

This ETF essentially provides investors with a way to invest in XRP without actually having to hold or custody the cryptocurrency. The ETF aims to deliver investment returns that correlate with the performance of XRP.

As of Nov. 13, the most recent available data from the fund issuer shows that XRPI's net assets stood at about $77.9 million.

Canadian gamblers have spent the past two years quietly rerouting their deposits from Interac transfers and prepaid vouchers to Bitcoin wallets. The shift is practical, driven primarily by settlement speed. A bank e-transfer can sit in processing over a long weekend, while a BTC confirmation clears in roughly ten minutes regardless of province or statutory holiday. Searches for btc casinos and btc casino online have climbed accordingly, though the operators behind those results vary wildly in licensing, game fairness, and how seriously they treat withdrawal limits.

Roobet has built its reputation as the category’s reference point. Its BTC casino model skips fiat rails entirely, crediting deposits as soon as a transaction confirms on-chain rather than waiting for a payment processor to batch it overnight. That design choice is a big reason it keeps surfacing at the top of Canadian comparison lists, even against operators with longer track records.

Deposits move at network speed, which also means there is no chargeback mechanism once a transaction confirms. Players carry the volatility themselves between deposit and cashout, and a platform that converts to stablecoins at deposit removes that exposure in a way a straight BTC balance does not. The sector’s shift toward stablecoin settlement largely reflects players being burned by holding BTC through a losing session during a price drop. Withdrawal limits tell a similar story: a casino that caps daily cashouts low enough to slow a winning streak is usually managing its own liquidity risk. So users should be looking at the fine print on payout ceilings, which deserve more attention than the headline bonus.

Ranked side by side, the gap is less about game count and more about withdrawal friction and Canadian access.

Provably fair systems let a player verify, after the fact, that a game’s outcome wasn’t altered after they placed their bet, using a published seed and hash. It is a meaningful trust layer, but it only confirms a round wasn’t tampered with, not that the house edge is favorable. Canadian players comparing operators against real-money alternatives still need to check return-to-player rates game by game, since a verifiable algorithm and a generous payout rate are separate questions that marketing copy tends to blur.

Most offshore crypto casinos serving Canadians are licensed through the Kahnawake Gaming Commission, based in Mohawk Territory in Quebec, which has issued gambling licenses since 1999. Ontario is the exception: since April 2022 it has run its own regulated online market through iGaming Ontario, meaning operators without an Ontario registration are technically off-limits to residents there, even if the rest of the country can reach them freely. That patchwork is why “player protection” means something different depending on which province a deposit originates in.

None of that structure fixes the harder problem: crypto deposits remove the natural friction that used to slow a losing streak. A platform worth using still publishes deposit limits and self-exclusion tools on the same page as its game lobby, not buried three clicks deep. That detail tells a player more about the platform’s integrity than any welcome offer does.

#5172. Retail Sales and Fed Minutes Put Bitcoin’s Rate Outlook Back in Focus

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Bitcoin’s next macro test will come from a familiar combination: what Americans are spending and how Federal Reserve officials are thinking about interest rates. The week of November 16 brings October retail sales and the minutes of the Fed’s latest policy meeting, both relevant to a market already digesting persistent inflation.

The dates are confirmed on the agencies’ calendars. Their significance is more conditional. A release moves markets through the information it adds relative to expectations, and through how investors change their outlook for borrowing costs and risk.

The Census Bureau’s schedule places October’s advance retail and food-services sales report on November 17 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time, or 13:30 GMT. That gives investors a new reading on a substantial part of household spending.

Strong sales can support the view that demand remains resilient. Depending on the inflation backdrop, that may also reduce the pressure on policymakers to loosen financial conditions. Weaker sales can suggest cooling demand, but a sufficiently poor reading could bring concerns about growth rather than an uncomplicated boost to risk assets.

The survey’s definitions add a useful caution: dollar values are expressed in current prices. A rise in spending is not automatically an equivalent increase in the quantity of goods purchased. The categories and revisions matter alongside the headline monthly change.

The Federal Reserve calendar schedules minutes from the October 27–28 meeting for November 18 at 2 p.m. ET, or 19:00 GMT. They should provide more detail about the discussion behind that decision.

The October 28 statement held the federal-funds target range at 3.75%–4% by a 10–2 vote. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase. That disagreement makes the breadth of concerns about inflation and the conditions for another move especially relevant.

Minutes are a retrospective account, however. They describe deliberations before the latest inflation release and before this week’s retail figures. A forceful passage may explain October’s debate without settling what officials will decide after receiving newer information.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a 0.4% monthly rise in consumer prices for October, with prices excluding food and energy up 0.3%. NewsBTC’s coverage of the October inflation report and Bitcoin’s rate outlook explains why that release renewed attention on monetary policy.

There is also a data limitation worth preserving. BLS could not publish most October year-on-year changes because the corresponding 2025 survey data were unavailable following a lapse in government funding. The monthly numbers remain usable, but an invented annual comparison would give a false sense of precision.

For the coming releases, the more useful question is whether the new evidence reinforces persistent demand and inflation, or points toward a meaningful slowdown. Those interpretations can produce different reactions even when a headline number looks superficially positive.

Changes in expected interest rates affect the appeal of cash and bonds, financing costs and the willingness to hold volatile assets. Those channels offer a framework for interpreting Bitcoin’s response; they are not a mechanical rule that every stronger economic report must send its price lower.

NewsBTC’s account of the recent weekend sell-off also highlights conditions within crypto itself. Liquidity and positioning can amplify a macro surprise or overwhelm the first reaction.

The clearest reading will compare the actual data, Treasury-market response and sustained trading after the initial move. This week’s calendar creates two well-defined information points. It does not predetermine the next Bitcoin trend.
