#5171. Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

Home » Interviews » Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

An interview with Banxa’s Chief Product & Growth Officer on hidden scaling traps and the future of stablecoin payments.

Rapid growth is often seen as a sign of success in fintech. But as transaction volumes increase, weaknesses in payment infrastructure, fraud prevention and risk management can become harder to spot – and more costly to fix.

Shaun Heng, Chief Product & Growth Officer at Banxa, a global crypto payments infrastructure provider, knows these challenges firsthand. Before joining Banxa, Heng held product and growth leadership roles at MoonPay and CoinMarketCap, gaining experience across two major players in the digital asset space.

In this interview with DailyCoin, he discusses why rapid growth can expose hidden vulnerabilities in fintech, what it takes to build payment infrastructure that works at scale, and how stablecoins could reshape the future of global payments.

– When does rapid growth become a risk for fintech companies?

Our total transaction volume (TTV) grew 76% from January to August. Stablecoins increased by 117%. Great numbers. The first thing I asked was where they came from?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it. That happens more often than people admit.

When volume doubles, every weakness doubles with it. That could mean fraud attempts, chargeback exposure, reconciliation breaks. Just to name a few. So you’re always looking at a great number next to problems that may not have appeared yet.

The second challenge is that fast growth is almost never evenly distributed. It could be one particular partner, region, digital asset, or payment method. That concentration is invisible on a topline chart, so we always look deeper to understand the drivers and future success.

And team culture is real. In a quarter everyone has worked so hard and exceeded targets, nobody wants to be the one asking hard questions.

The discipline I would push for is simple: break down the growth before you celebrate it. Where is it coming from? Which rails is it riding on? And what happens if one of those rails is withdrawn next week?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it.

– What does a payment infrastructure provider need to deliver to make the crypto on-ramp experience seamless?

For a long time the industry shipped widgets, and a widget is a visible admission that someone else is handling this.

Banxa Native is headless by design. The partner owns the interface, the brand, the pricing presentation, the whole journey. We simply sit behind their stack. Users never

Returning users never verify twice, because existing KYC can be reused through token sharing. So, everything the user shouldn’t have to think about. That’s the definition of invisible.

In practice, it means the provider owns licensing, or a licensed local partner, in every market where money actually moves,  local payment methods, not just cards, because users pay the way their country pays.

Vietnam is the example I keep reaching for. We launched VietQR there in Q3, and it is already our top payment method in that region at roughly 42% of all transactions — driving a conversion rate close to eight times higher than cards. Same users, same product, same pricing. The only variable was letting people pay the way they already pay.

Then provider also need identity and KYC, including the ability to accept verification the partner has already done.  Settlement, in and out, with money arriving where it is supposed to on the day it is supposed to.

And it has to run in both directions, not just the buy flow. On-ramp, where a user pays with a local method and receives crypto. Off-ramp, where they sell and cashout to their own bank account.

A lot of products ship the first and treat off-ramp as a secondary problem, and that is precisely the moment a user discovers the money only moves one way.

For a European fintech, Banxa collects the local payment, exchanges and settles the fiat leg where the partner needs it. We carry the MiCA licence that passports across the EU — so they don’t have to build a crypto licensing and payments stack country by country.

One partner, one compliance review, one integration, both directions. That speed to market is usually why partners choose us.

– Banxa’s infrastructure supports stablecoin payments across B2B settlement, consumer payments, and cross-border transactions. What is the most overlooked challenge in making stablecoin payments work at scale?

Nobody has ever been excited about reconciliation, and it is the thing that decides whether you have a business.

A stablecoin transfer settles in seconds. That part is genuinely solved.

What is not solved is everything around it. The fiat leg still moves on banking hours and local scheme rules. You have a bank partner on one side, a chain on the other, and a treasury position sitting between them that has to be funded, hedged and accounted for.

Every transaction has to be matched across those systems, in the right currency, on the right day, with the right fee breakdown, in a form an auditor and a regulator will accept.

The second unglamorous thing is failure handling.

At scale, the interesting work is not the happy path. It is the payment that half-completes.

The most common example is card decline and for many reasons – bank limit, 3D Secure step that timed out etc. In most checkouts that ends the order and the buyer needs to start again, or more often leaves.

Then there are bank transfers that arrive three days late with a truncated reference. The refund that has to go back to a card when the crypto has already left.

Users judge you almost entirely on how those cases are handled, and those cases are where most providers quietly fall over.

We recently shipped Payment Method Switch, which lets the buyer change how they pay without losing the order. It separates the order from the payment, so a buyer can move from card to Google Pay without losing the order or redoing verification, and so they see the new method before confirming.

The third challenge is payment method coverage, which sounds like a commercial checklist and is actually an engineering and licensing dependency.

Supporting the way people pay in the US, Nigeria, Australia and Germany means four different integrations, four different fraud profiles and four different regulatory conversations. A switch only works if the alternative payment method is already connected and live for that buyer.

It matters because this is the layer the user is trusting without knowing it. When the plumbing is right, the experience feels effortless. When it is wrong, it does not feel like a backend issue. It feels like the product lied to them.

– Can KYC be more than compliance — can it actually become a growth advantage in crypto payments?

Yes, and I would go further. KYC is one of the highest-leverage product surfaces in payments. Most teams just never treat it as one.

Look at where users actually drop. It is rarely pricing. It is the verification step.

Someone has decided they want to transact, they have intent, and then they are asked to photograph a document on a screen that does not match the app they were just in. A meaningful share of them never come back.

That is not a compliance cost. That is a conversion problem.

So the advantage comes from three things.

First, verify once. If a partner has already verified a user to a standard we can rely on, that user should not be asked again. Banxa Native supports exactly this through token sharing, so returning users go straight to payment.

Second, verify proportionately. Not every transaction carries the same risk, so it shouldn’t carry the same friction.

Third, verify natively. No redirect, no third-party screen, no moment where the user wonders who they just handed their passport details to.

There is a trust argument too. In most of the world, people are more willing to move money with a platform that looks regulated, not less. Verification done well signals that this is a real financial product. Done badly, suggests the opposite.

My advice is to instrument it. Measure drop-off by step. Iterate. Most teams hand it to engineering once and never look again.

– Crypto payments come with a lot of risk, from payment disputes to fraud. Do you the industry underestimates the value of having someone else take on that risk?

Badly, yes. And the reason is that the cost of carrying it yourself does not show up as a line item until it is already a problem.

The fiat leg is reversible. The crypto leg is not. A card payment can be disputed months after the asset has left. That gap is where fraud lives.

So when a platform decides to run its own ramp, they’re usually pricing the integration work. What they are not pricing is the loss rate, the rules engine that has to keep up with it, the team watching it at three in the morning, the bank relationships that get withdrawn when your chargeback ratio crosses a threshold, and the capital you have to hold against all of it.

Those costs are lumpy and they arrive late.

The real value of transferring that risk is not just the losses avoided. It is focus.

With Banxa Native, the partner owns the experience end to end. We carry the regulated rails and the settlement behind it. They get to spend their engineering time on the things their users actually chose them for.

Risk you have not priced is still risk. Someone is carrying it.

– What’s one thing Web3 companies still see as “just compliance” that should really be treated as a product or growth issue?

Market access. Which licences you hold, and therefore which countries you can actually serve, is usually filed under legal. It is the single biggest determinant of your addressable market.

Teams spend enormous effort on acquisition and then discover the funnel is geographically capped. Users arrive, get to the payment step, and find out their country is not supported or their local payment method is not available.

From the user’s point of view, the product simply does not work. From the growth team’s point of view, the conversion rate is mysteriously bad in half the world. Nobody connects that back to a licensing decision made two years earlier.

The same is true of regulatory readiness ahead of a regime change. MiCA is the clearest recent example.

The companies that treated it as a legal deadline scrambled. The ones that treated it as a product decision kept serving European users without interruption while others paused service. Continuity of access is a growth outcome.

This is also why we think about our licence footprint as product surface area rather than paperwork. Banxa services users across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America and Asia-Pacific, and is MiCA-authorised as a CASP in the Netherlands. For a partner building on Banxa, that footprint is not a compliance appendix in the contract. It is the list of countries where their product works.

My general rule: if a compliance decision changes who can use your product or how easily, it was never only a compliance decision.

– What development in crypto payments could have the biggest impact on the industry over the next few years?

Stablecoins becoming the default settlement layer for ordinary businesses that have no interest in crypto.

That is the shift. It isn’t necessarily about more people buying digital assets. It’s about companies moving money across borders faster and cheaper, with the stablecoin being an implementation detail they never discuss.

The future isn’t crypto payments. It’s better payments.

Stablecoin supply has actually contracted since May, from around $310 billion to roughly $286 billion. But payment volume went the other way. Allium reported it at $482 billion in the first nine months of this year, up 45% year on year.

Banks, card networks and large fintechs are integrating this into their products right now.

What makes it transformative is the disappearance, not the technology.

Consumers will keep using the apps and currencies they already trust. The rails underneath will change. Identity handled once, not repeatedly. Settlement in minutes instead of days. Fees people can actually see.

In many emerging markets, this will go further and faster than people in Washington or London expect, because the alternative is genuinely slow.

Digital dollars become the practical choice for savings and cross-border flows, not a theoretical one.

Most users will never know a stablecoin was involved. That’s the point.

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has replied to XRP holders who criticized him for selling most of his XRP with a Saturday Night Live GIF of Natalie Portman saying, "I never said I was a role model."

According to Schwartz, his XRP holdings are down 88%, from a peak of roughly 26 million tokens to 3 million. His Bitcoin went from about 1,500 coins to one, and his Ether went from about 40,000 to six.

Schwartz wrote that he "really doesn't like risk." According to Schwartz, he and his wife agreed years ago to sell some of their coins every time crypto reached a new all-time high. Schwartz also said that he was a skeptic from the start and did not believe in the early price records of crypto. "When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous," he wrote.

#5168. DBS and JPMorgan Launch 24/7 Tokenized Dollar Transfers Across Borders

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

DBS and JPMorgan’s Kinexys have launched a service connecting tokenized dollar deposits in Singapore and the United States. The November 16 announcement moves a cross-bank project into commercial use, with Ant International as its first customer. The practical question is how much flexibility a treasury team gains when money can move between its banks outside the usual working day.

The DBS announcement describes a connection between permissioned blockchain accounts, using Partior for settlement orchestration. That creates a route between two banking environments rather than requiring a company to keep every participating account with the same provider.

For a business with separate regional operations, that distinction can be useful. Cash held for one subsidiary may be unavailable to another at the moment it needs to pay a supplier. A dependable interbank connection could reduce the need to position money in several places long before it is needed. The benefit would depend on the company’s access, account structure and funding arrangements.

The banks’ November 2025 framework announcement discussed interoperability across public and permissioned blockchains. It included the possibility of exchanging a JPMorgan deposit token on Base for equivalent value through DBS. Monday’s launch concerns the specified permissioned account networks; the broader examples in the earlier plan should not be treated as features all delivered at once.

Readers following JPM Coin’s separate expansion to Ethereum will recognise the distinction. A bank can support several digital-money products, with different eligible users and transfer rules. Connecting one pair of services does not automatically connect every token carrying a related brand.

DBS’ Token Services documentation places programmable payments and liquidity management within the same product family. Its Treasury Tokens service is designed to move value between group entities across markets. The new interbank link adds another possible route for those kinds of treasury workflows.

Consider a company that receives customer payments in one location while its operating expenses fall due elsewhere. It may otherwise keep a buffer in both places, even when its total cash position is comfortable. If transfers become reliable outside local banking hours, it could adjust those buffers more frequently. That is an operational possibility, not a savings figure established by the launch.

The same timing issue appears in Hong Kong’s work on continuous tokenized settlement. Extending a trading or business window is useful only if usable money can reach it. Treasury teams would still need to compare the full journey, including conversion, approvals, reconciliation and access to their ordinary bank accounts.

DBS identifies one limitation: moving funds between legacy demand-deposit accounts and Kinexys blockchain accounts has a Saturday downtime from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern time. Transfers inside the blockchain account network remain available around the clock.

That qualification is especially relevant for a customer planning weekend funding. Money already positioned in the appropriate account can have a different availability profile from money that first needs to enter it. An internal payment policy would have to reflect both routes rather than rely on a single headline about continuous service.

A named customer and a live connection give this project a firmer footing than an exploratory agreement. The commercial assessment now turns on repeated transfers: whether treasury teams can access the balances they need, account for them correctly and complete a payment at a predictable total cost.

#5167. ‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

Charles Hoskinson said that the Cardano "roadmap is complete" and that everything he said would be built has finished. It came during a YouTube livestream Saturday where Hoskinson sparred with disgruntled investors as ADA sits down 94% from its 2021 high, per Decrypt data.

One viewer, named shevilkid1738, pushed Hoskinson's buttons by claiming he'd promised Cardano would overtake Bitcoin. The Cardano founder clapped back, saying there was no evidence he ever said that.

"I never promised that. I said I'd love for it to happen, and I believe that Cardano is a better store of value than Bitcoin is for a variety of reasons," Hoskinson said. "I don't promise price appreciation, or people overturning things. I say it's absolutely possible."

Shevilkid1738 responded over an hour later with a quote where Hoskinson said he "thinks" Cardano is "probably" going to become the biggest cryptocurrency in the world. Hoskinson highlighted the word think and said that he has "taken it as far as I can," explaining that the network is now decentralized and doesn't rely on him as a founder.

The viewer wasn't happy and called it "insane" for a founder to no longer have a responsibility to those who invested in their project.

"Under what conditions does that obligation end?" Hoskinson said, "The roadmap is complete. Everything I said is going to be built has been built. It reached four times the value of Honda. There's millions of people that have used it, and millions of people continue to use it. It is self-determining and self-governing, with its ability to pick and choose its own leaders without my consent."

Cardano’s roadmap was split into five eras: Byron, Shelly, Goguen, Basho, and Voltaire.

Byron launched the network in September 2017, Shelley added staking in July 2020, and Goguen brought smart contracts via the Alonzo hard fork in September 2021. Basho, the scaling era, came via the Vasil upgrade in September 2022, before the Chang hard fork kicked off Voltaire, the governance era, in September 2024.

The final piece to the puzzle occurred in January 2025, when the Plomin hard fork gave ADA holders "real voting power" over the blockchain’s future. This marked the transition to "full decentralized governance," and apparently the end of the final roadmap era.

"The goal was simple. There's a roadmap. Byron, Basho, Shelley, et cetera, et cetera, and it's done," Hoskinson said. "I have no power over this ecosystem."

Ultimately, though, Hoskinson says the issue that investors have is financial.

"You want me to pump your bags. That's what you're really saying. The job's not done till it's pumped," he said. "But guess what? It's never done then, because somebody comes in at $3 ADA, and then expects it to be five. And then somebody comes in at $5 ADA and expects it to be seven. If you retire at five, you've defrauded the person at five. If you retire at three, you've defrauded the person at three. There's no winning."

#5166. Project Helix Xbox Console Will Run PC Games: What It Means for Web3

Home » Esports » Project Helix Xbox Console Will Run PC Games: What It Means for Web3

Microsoft VP Jason Ronald details how the next-gen console merges Xbox libraries with PC gaming.

Microsoft has officially clarified its vision for the upcoming Project Helix Xbox console, confirming in the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine that the next-generation system is built to run both traditional Xbox libraries and PC games. A hybrid shift could also open new doors for Web3 gaming.

As Microsoft celebrates Xbox’s 25th anniversary, the company has shared fresh architectural details about the Project Helix Xbox console, its upcoming next-generation console. When Microsoft first introduced the project earlier this year, it confirmed that the new system would bring Xbox and PC gaming closer together. This led many to assume that Helix would essentially be a Windows gaming PC packaged in a console design.

In a four-page Q&A inside the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, Vice President of Next Generation Jason Ronald pushed back directly against that framing.

“Project Helix is designed to be a console capable of playing games from your PC,” Ronald stated. “It is not a PC that can also play console games.”

For Microsoft, the distinction comes down to removing the friction traditionally associated with PC gaming, such as driver management, multiple launchers, and complex configuration menus, while keeping deeper controls accessible for enthusiasts.

“The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games,” Ronald explained. “But if you’re a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it.”

According to Ronald and the anniversary feature, Project Helix is being built around several core pillars:

Project Helix, which Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has previously described as a broader “family of devices” rather than a single box, is taking shape during a turbulent stretch for Microsoft’s gaming division.

After taking the helm earlier in 2026, Sharma oversaw major restructuring, studio closures, and layoffs, candidly remarking in July that the Xbox brand was “not healthy.” Simultaneously, ongoing global memory and storage component shortages have pushed up manufacturing costs across the hardware industry, prompting some players to urge both Microsoft and Sony to delay next-gen launches until prices stabilize.

Ronald acknowledged those supply-chain headwinds, calling the current hardware environment “brutal,” though he argued that the constraints are forcing Xbox engineers to innovate rather than simply throw costlier components at the machine.

Microsoft has not announced a price or consumer launch window for Project Helix, though alpha developer hardware is slated to begin shipping in 2027, with retail speculation pointing toward late 2027 or 2028.

For the Web3 gaming sector, Microsoft’s hybrid console-PC strategy could solve a long-standing distribution bottleneck.

Historically, console manufacturers have enforced strict platform policies against blockchain integrations, external crypto wallets, and NFTs, forcing Web3 studios to build almost exclusively for PC, web browsers, and mobile devices.

Still, Ronald noted that the ROG Xbox Ally served as a testing ground for unifying game libraries across multiple stores.

If Project Helix eventually supports third-party PC storefronts such as Steam and the Epic Games Store, it could create new opportunities for blockchain-enabled games to reach console audiences.

However, important questions remain unanswered. Microsoft has not confirmed third-party storefront support on Project Helix, nor has it announced native support for external crypto wallets, NFT functionality, or blockchain transactions.

Nevertheless, the direction is worth watching. If Project Helix successfully bridges the console and PC gaming ecosystems, it could create new distribution opportunities for Web3 games and help bring blockchain-powered gaming experiences closer to mainstream players.

#5165. From sportsbook to slots: Why Canadian crypto players want one wallet for everything

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Digital assets have changed more than the way money moves. They have also changed what users expect from digital products. A crypto holder can move between exchanges, wallets, and decentralized applications without treating every activity as a completely separate financial relationship. That expectation is increasingly influencing online gaming.

For many players, the traditional model of maintaining one account for sports betting, another for slots, and a third for live casino games feels unnecessarily fragmented. A unified platform offers a simpler alternative: one account, one balance, and a consistent payment experience across several forms of entertainment.

The appeal is particularly relevant to crypto-aware audiences in Canada. These users are already familiar with digital wallets, network confirmations, and assets that can move across borders and applications. When they enter an online gaming environment, they often expect the same degree of continuity.

The strongest argument for a unified platform is practical rather than promotional. Separate gaming accounts create separate balances, deposit histories, and withdrawal processes. Players may need to move funds repeatedly, learn different interfaces, and review different sets of account information.

A shared account reduces those steps. Funds deposited for a weekend sporting event may remain available for a slot session or a live-dealer table without requiring another external transfer. The player still decides how and when the balance is used, but the platform does not force a new payment journey for every product category.

This model can be especially useful when crypto is involved. Blockchain transfers are not the same as moving credits between sections of a website. Every external transaction may involve a network selection, a destination address, a fee, and a confirmation period. Keeping more activity within one verified account can reduce the number of blockchain transactions a player needs to initiate.

A large game or market catalogue has value, but variety alone does not create a coherent experience. A genuinely unified platform also needs consistent navigation, account controls and transaction information.

Players should be able to identify their available balance, review deposits and withdrawals, and reach account settings without relearning the interface each time they move from sportsbook to casino. Mobile behaviour matters as well. A platform that works smoothly on desktop but becomes difficult to navigate on a phone does not deliver a truly unified experience.

The same principle applies to support and identity checks. A single account can allow the platform to maintain one verified customer profile instead of asking the user to repeat the same process for each product. It can also provide one place for limits, security settings and support history.

The growth of combined platforms does not mean that sports betting, slots and live casino are becoming identical. Each product has a different rhythm.

Sports betting is event-driven. Activity often rises around major matches, tournaments and seasonal calendars. Slots and live casino games are generally available continuously. A unified platform allows those patterns to coexist without forcing players to maintain separate accounts.

That flexibility can also make the account more useful between major sporting events. A player who primarily follows football, hockey, or basketball may still prefer access to other entertainment from the same balance. Conversely, a casino-focused user may value the option to follow a major match without opening a new account elsewhere.

The commercial trend is therefore less about persuading every player to use every product and more about removing barriers when interests overlap.

Crypto payments can support a unified experience, but the presence of a digital asset logo does not guarantee a good payment journey. Players still need clear information about supported assets and networks, minimum amounts, processing steps, and withdrawal requirements.

Network compatibility is particularly important. The same asset may exist on several blockchains, and sending it through an unsupported network can lead to a failed or difficult recovery process. A well-designed deposit page should make the correct network and address clear before funds are sent.

Transaction visibility also matters. Blockchain explorers can show whether a transfer has been broadcast and confirmed, while the gaming account should show when the deposit has been credited. These are related but distinct stages. Clear status information reduces uncertainty.

Betplay illustrates the unified-platform model by bringing sportsbook, slots, and live casino products under one brand and account experience. Its relevance to a crypto publication comes from that combination: the payment layer is connected to several entertainment categories rather than a single-purpose casino product.

The practical value is continuity. A player can explore different parts of the platform without creating a new account or starting a separate balance for every vertical. The brand therefore fits a broader shift in digital entertainment toward consolidated accounts and fewer payment handoffs.

That does not remove the need for normal due diligence. Players should review the assets and networks currently supported, transaction instructions, terms, account limits, and withdrawal requirements before depositing. Product availability can also vary by location.

Any discussion of online gaming in Canada requires a regulatory qualification. Gambling is regulated at the provincial level, and the framework is not identical across the country. Ontario launched a competitive regulated internet gaming market in April 2022, overseen by the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario and iGaming Ontario. Other provinces use different models and rules.

As a result, Canadian users should confirm that a platform is available where they live and that its use complies with applicable provincial requirements. They should also meet the legal gambling age in their province.

Unified crypto gaming platforms reflect a wider digital trend. Users increasingly expect one identity, one payment layer and a consistent interface across related services. In online gaming, that can mean moving between sportsbook, slots and live casino without repeating the same financial and account-management steps.

The model is not valuable simply because it places several products on one website. Its real value comes from reducing friction while keeping balances, transaction information and account controls understandable.

For crypto-aware audiences, that combination is likely to remain compelling: choice across products, continuity across sessions and fewer unnecessary transfers between platforms.

#5163. Singapore and Germany Test CBDC Settlement Without Joining Their Ledgers

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Singapore and Germany have tested a way to settle foreign-exchange transactions using digital central-bank money while keeping their underlying systems separate. Project Simbolon, announced on November 16, uses cryptographic proofs to coordinate the two payment legs. Its interest lies in a practical design choice: institutions may be able to exchange value without first agreeing to run everything on one shared ledger.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s release says DBS and Deutsche Bank participated, with technology from Partior. The experiment covered euro–Singapore dollar payments in the central banks’ test environments. Zero-knowledge proofs verified settlement conditions without direct technical integration between the ledgers.

The intended payment-versus-payment arrangement makes each final transfer dependent on the other. Imagine a bank paying euros to receive Singapore dollars: it wants assurance that its counterparty’s payment will complete before its own funds become irretrievable. Making both legs conditional addresses that exposure at settlement. It does not make an unfunded account suddenly able to pay.

The central banks’ November 2025 cooperation agreement set out an ambition to improve cross-border transfers and develop common standards for payments, FX and tokenized securities. Simbolon is a milestone within that work, rather than the launch of a generally available international payment service.

Keeping ledgers independent can make collaboration more manageable. Each operator may retain its own infrastructure, access rules and upgrade process. The connecting arrangement then needs precise answers about which evidence is accepted, how long an instruction remains valid and what happens when one environment stops responding.

Those questions are related to the Meridian FX APAC trial covered by NewsBTC, although the two projects should not be conflated. Both address coordination across settlement systems; Simbolon’s announcement specifically centres on the euro–Singapore dollar test and its use of cryptographic proofs.

A treasury desk usually wants to know when it must commit funds and when it can use the proceeds. An arrangement that reduces uncertainty could allow it to fund a transaction closer to completion. The economic advantage would come from the timing of usable balances, not simply a faster message between computers.

MAS’ broader Project Guardian framework treats interoperability, custody, legal finality and operational resilience as connected requirements for tokenized markets. It spans several kinds of assets and money. That breadth matters because a securities transaction may involve more than a currency exchange: ownership records and collateral obligations must also remain consistent.

The challenge resembles the one behind delivery-versus-payment tools for tokenized securities. Coordinating asset and cash movements can reduce exposure between them, but the contractual rights associated with both sides still require a clear legal basis.

The central banks identify performance, legal, regulatory, operational and governance work as areas for further exploration. They also say a fuller technical report will follow. No commercial launch date or measured cost reduction is established by the announcement.

That leaves useful questions for the next stage. A production arrangement would need to explain recovery after an interrupted transfer, the treatment of expired instructions and which institution resolves a disagreement about completion. Testing those situations would show whether the connection is dependable when conditions become awkward.

Simbolon provides evidence that independent digital infrastructures can coordinate an FX settlement in a controlled setting. Turning that result into a financial service will require the institutions to make the same coordination reliable, legally effective and understandable to the people managing real balances.

#5162. 64K Bitcoin Miners Hijacked: Why the Attack Failed to Shake BTC

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » 64K Bitcoin Miners Hijacked: Why the Attack Failed to Shake BTC

An AI-assisted exploit of Luxor’s software briefly diverted 1.4% of Bitcoin’s global computing power.

An AI-assisted exploit of Luxor’s fleet-management software briefly diverted 1.4% of Bitcoin’s global computing power, netting the attacker over $10,500 while leaving the blockchain itself untouched.

A coordinated weekend cyberattack hijacked approximately 64,000 Bitcoin mining machines, temporarily redirecting up to 13 exahashes per second (EH/s) of computing power to an unauthorized address on the OCEAN mining pool.

While the incident exposed a major vulnerability in third-party mining management tools, the Bitcoin protocol itself was never compromised, and the diverted hashrate fell far short of the threshold needed to disrupt the blockchain.

Bitcoin mining hosting provider CoreX Hosting was the first to flag the suspicious activity on November 14, warning on X that thousands of machines were suddenly connecting to the OCEAN mining pool under a single external payout address.

Just a heads up, there is a big miner hack going on as we speak. Miners are being pointed at @ocean_mining with BTC address bc1qphukp9rjfc4rcej7erpm9ae20xmtspw8pcddrr .

Less than an hour later, approximately 13 EH/s of computing power, equivalent to about 1.4% of the entire Bitcoin network’s global hashrate, was pointing toward the attacker’s wallet. CoreX said it was working to restore the affected machines’ original mining configurations.

By 1:40 a.m. ET on November 15, CoreX confirmed the attack had been contained. The hashrate tied to the rogue address plunged from 13 EH/s down to roughly 100 petahashes per second (PH/s), signaling that nearly all compromised rigs had been recovered or disconnected.

Initially, blockchain trackers noted that the attacker had failed to mine a single block during the brief hijack window, suggesting the heist had yielded zero profit. However, because of how OCEAN’s payout model works, the attacker still managed to walk away with a modest payday.

Under OCEAN’s reward distribution rules, valid mining shares submitted during an active window remain eligible for payouts when the pool subsequently finds blocks.

On-chain tracking later confirmed that the attacker’s address received payouts totaling between 0.162 BTC (roughly $10,500) and 0.243 BTC across two to three block rewards before the eligible work window expired.

While the attacker’s haul was relatively small compared to the massive computing power hijacked, affected mining operators lost real-time revenue during the outage while continuing to pay electricity costs.

The incident took another turn on November 15, when mining services company Luxor confirmed that its Commander mining equipment management software had been exploited to redirect hashrate.

In a post on X, Luxor said its internal monitoring detected unauthorized pool reassignments affecting “just over a dozen” client accounts. Engineers patched the vulnerability within two hours and began reverting customer rigs to their original pools. Luxor emphasized that no user data was leaked and that its core mining pool and LuxOS firmware remained unaffected.

Last night our internal monitoring alerted us to an unauthorized redirect of hashrate through Commander. Our on-call engineering team jumped on it right away.Impact: just over a dozen client accounts. Affected machines were pointed to a different pool for a limited window. No…

In a follow-up statement, Luxor CEO Nick Hansen apologized to affected clients and said the attack involved a “sophisticated AI-enabled vector.”

He warned that AI-powered cyberattacks are becoming an increasing threat to crypto infrastructure, with automated systems probing for vulnerabilities around the clock.

Luxor promised to fully reimburse affected clients for lost mining revenue, paying them as if their machines had continued mining normally.

The incident exposes a vulnerability in Bitcoin’s mining infrastructure that exists outside the blockchain itself. Still, it never posed a systemic threat to Bitcoin: controlling the network requires over 50% of global computing power.

At its peak, the hijacked hashrate accounted for just ~1.4% of the network and lasted only a few hours—nowhere near enough to alter transactions or double-spend coins.

Because no user wallets were drained and Bitcoin’s consensus rules operated normally, the breach had no direct impact on Bitcoin’s market price, which hovered near the $64,500–$65,000 range amid broader macro-driven market volatility.

On the 15th of November, Luxor Technology confirmed that its Bitcoin [BTC] mining power was hijacked via Commander software, exposing vulnerabilities in its infrastructure.

The attacker failed to mine a BTC block; hence, they did not receive any reward. However, the attacked miners lost the opportunity to earn rewards, as the hashing time cannot be recovered.

Notably, the frightening aspect was that there was nothing wrong with the miners themselves. The management program perched above them was the weak point.

After realizing the compromise, Luxor Technology’s on-call engineering team jumped into the matter immediately.

#5160. CoinShares Enters Russell Index Review as Crypto Stocks Seek Broader Investor Access

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

CoinShares has moved a step closer to joining widely followed US stock benchmarks, opening a possible new route to investors who buy shares through index funds. The digital-asset manager said on November 16 that it had satisfied eligibility requirements for consideration in the Russell US index family.

For a crypto business, that is a meaningful change in distribution. Investors can gain exposure to the company through an ordinary equity portfolio without making a separate decision to buy a cryptocurrency. The size of any eventual benefit, however, will depend on the final index decision and the weight assigned to its shares.

CoinShares appears as CSHR in LSEG’s preliminary Russell 3000 additions, published for the December review. Its company announcement identifies several Russell benchmarks for which it may qualify, including the 2000, 2500 and 3000 families and associated styles.

The release describes about $789.9 billion of passive assets tracking potentially relevant indexes, using the company’s own mid-October compilation. That figure measures the pool attached to those benchmarks. It does not represent money committed to CoinShares, and treating it as a prospective inflow would greatly overstate the announcement.

Even after inclusion, a tracker’s allocation would reflect the company’s index weight and the fund’s mandate. The whole benchmark’s assets cannot be assigned to one constituent. A projected flow calculation would need the eventual weight, assets in the funds that actually track the relevant index and how closely each fund replicates it.

FTSE Russell’s published calendar says the December changes take effect after US market close on December 11. It schedules further preliminary-list updates through November and early December. CoinShares’ release gives a different date, so investors should use the index provider’s final notices to establish implementation.

Russell moved to twice-yearly reconstitutions in 2026. Eligible securities are ranked and screened under its rules, and the review refreshes how the indexes represent the equity market. A preliminary addition is therefore part of a defined process, with several remaining checkpoints.

This matters for anyone interpreting a press release as a completed trading catalyst. Eligibility, a preliminary listing and implemented membership describe different stages. Only the last establishes the actual benchmark change.

Buying an asset manager’s stock gives investors a claim on its business, including its costs, earnings and capital-allocation decisions. It is not equivalent to holding the coins in one of that manager’s investment products. A growing customer base can support fee income, while falling asset values or withdrawals can put that income under pressure.

NewsBTC’s coverage of the closure of CoinShares’ BTF fund illustrates that product-level decisions have their own mechanics. A fund can be wound down while the management company continues to operate and pursue other opportunities.

Potential Russell membership concerns that company’s equity. It does not reopen a closed fund, endorse a particular token or require the company to add Bitcoin to its treasury.

The announcement arrives as index treatment is attracting attention across crypto-linked stocks. NewsBTC recently reported on MSCI’s removal decision affecting Strategy and Metaplanet. Those cases involve another provider and different rules, but they show why the classification of a listed business can matter independently of cryptocurrency prices.

For CoinShares, the next evidence will come from updated constituent lists and final weights. A broader shareholder base could improve the company’s visibility and trading participation. Whether that translates into a more durable valuation will still depend on what the business earns and how effectively it uses its capital.

XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) shared a tidbit of XRPL's early history in a recent X post.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) still carries traces of Satoshi Nakamoto’s original Bitcoin design, highlighting two features.

In 2011, three engineers—David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto—began developing the XRP Ledger (XRPL). Fascinated by Bitcoin, they set out to create a better version that improved upon its limitations—with the goal of creating a digital asset that was more sustainable and built specifically for payments.

As reported, the first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written by David Schwartz, who is Ripple CTO emeritus, about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011.

Vet delves into the earliest part of XRP Ledger history, noting that 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, wrote. Vet added that Jed McCaleb also copied Satoshi’s timekeeping code into the XRPL, even including one of the Bitcoin creator’s comments shared as a screenshot.

Did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily? 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote. Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including one of Satoshi's comments. By the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone. In December 2014, Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment. Two design choices of Satoshi still remain on the XRPL and all of us use at least one of it. Signature curve secp256k1 (we also support Ed25519 thus not everyone uses this) and how XRPL addresses are generated from the public key with SHA-256 followed by RIPEMD-160, that's what all of us use.

The quote "Never go to sea with two chronometers; take one or three" is a classic maritime adage famously included by Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin) within the Bitcoin source code.

Vet explained that by the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone from the XRP Ledger. In December 2014, former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment.

However, two of Satoshi's design choices still remain on the XRP Ledger: the first is the secp256k1 signature curve, which Bitcoin uses and which the XRP Ledger continues to support. However, the ledger also supports Ed25519, meaning not every XRPL user relies on secp256k1.

"I remember David saying they used secp256k1 so no one would doubt the security because it's the same as Bitcoin's, etc.," Vet stated, citing the insight of the Ripple CTO emeritus on secp256k1, adding, "Lots of interesting things to dig into from the early days."

The second is the method used to generate XRP Ledger addresses from public keys. The process applies SHA-256 hashing followed by RIPEMD-160, a design inherited from Bitcoin that remains common to all XRPL addresses.

Asked why the timekeeping code and Satoshi's comment were removed, Vet explained that this became leftover code as new code was introduced, so it was cleaned up.

#5158. Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Britain's new crypto rules will still be in transition when global anti-money laundering assessors arrive next year, and the country will be judged on whether it can enforce against crypto laundering, a taskforce convened by the Royal United Services Institute has warned.

The report, published on Friday, sets out the issues the London-based defense and security think tank's taskforce expects to dominate the UK's 2027 evaluation by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The Paris-based body sets global standards against money laundering and terrorist financing, and its peer reviews, known as mutual evaluations, grade countries on whether their rules work in practice.

The UK's report is due to be agreed at FATF's February 2028 plenary. The taskforce, made up of experts from the private sector, law enforcement and civil society, met in September; its discussions are not attributed to individual members.

This will be the first UK evaluation in which FATF considers crypto, and the taskforce was clear that crypto is a "material risk" for the UK. The City of London Police assesses that 66% of investment fraud in the UK involves crypto, according to the report, while the UK's 2025 National Risk Assessment rated crypto money laundering high risk, up from medium in 2020.

The UK brought crypto firms under its money laundering rules in 2020, and legislation passed in February created a statutory crypto regime. The Financial Conduct Authority set out which crypto activities it will regulate in April and finalized its rulebook in June, but the mandatory regime does not take effect until October 25, 2027.

The taskforce doubted the UK would be able to show adequate implementation by the time FATF visits in June, and said the UK had moved more conservatively than Hong Kong, the EU and Singapore.

Members were unanimous that assessors would examine this, and pointed to over-the-counter brokers, which the National Crime Agency estimated in the 2025 risk assessment are likely to launder hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

The taskforce cited the Metropolitan Police's £5.5 billion (about $7.3 billion) crypto seizure, linked to a Chinese professional money launderer sentenced in 2025, as an encouraging sign of what the UK criminal justice system can do when it has the capacity. But one member said the success had not been repeated in enough cases, and that the UK had barely scratched the surface of crypto laundering. FATF is expected to test whether results match the risk rather than rest on one headline case, the report said.

It also warned that because the UK's regime, which resembles the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, focuses on identifiable crypto firms, it risks pushing the highest-risk crypto outside the FCA's perimeter. That would leave law enforcement to trace assets the regulator cannot reach, such as Tether's USDT, with the taskforce pointing to a July 2025 Treasury report that flagged the stablecoin as having been "extensively exploited" by Russian-speaking laundering networks. Members doubted law enforcement had been given the capability and resources to keep pace.

The taskforce did praise UK international cooperation, including Operation Destabilise, which targeted Russian-speaking networks converting street cash into crypto. But it flagged resourcing of the UK Financial Intelligence Unit and law enforcement's economic crime capacity as likely vulnerabilities.

FATF has been pressing countries on crypto enforcement more broadly. In July, it said nearly 93% of jurisdictions it surveyed had yet to apply its standards to qualifying DeFiplatforms.

WhiteBIT has relaunched its over-the-counter (OTC) platform and enhanced its institutional offering with a large-volume trading section for digital assets and fiat currencies. It is tailored for institutional and corporate clients, investment funds, family offices, and other participants in the market that seek a special approach when having high-value deals.

Unlike normal exchange trading, where big orders may impact market prices and execution expenses, OTC trades are transactions carried out outside the public order book, straight between a client and the trading desk. This can reduce the impact on the market, give more flexibility in terms of the execution period, and give more customization for institutional trading.

“The institutional engagement with cryptocurrencies is growing at the level of more than just access to cryptocurrencies. Equipped with a reliable compliance framework, a dedicated team of support, and processes that are predictable in their operations, funds, corporate treasuries, and professional investors require execution models that allow them to operate in the same way they do in traditional financial markets. By relaunching our OTC desk, we’re strengthening the infrastructure that enables these participants to execute large transactions more efficiently and with greater flexibility,” said Volodymyr Nosov, Founder and President of W Group, of which WhiteBIT is a part.

The relaunched desk supports crypto-to-fiat and fiat-to-crypto transactions in major fiat currencies, including the US dollar (USD), euro (EUR), British pound (GBP), and Swiss franc (CHF), as well as the stablecoins USDT and USDC. Also, the top 10 crypto assets by market capitalization are now available for trading on the OTC desk against USDT and USDC. Other crypto assets outside the top 10 and additional fiat currencies are available upon individual request.

WhiteBIT does not impose a fixed upper limit on OTC transaction sizes. Instead, the maximum amount is determined by the source of funds and the results of the required compliance checks, so capacity is set around each client’s actual activity.

Each client is assigned to a dedicated OTC manager, who provides them with support in negotiating the transaction parameters, agreeing the terms of execution, and support throughout the transaction. The service protects client data and transactional information and follows Know Your Customer (KYC), Know Your Business (KYB), and all applicable compliance regulations.

WhiteBIT is introducing a zero-fee offer for new OTC clients, covering their first transaction of up to $2 million. It is a one-time offer, valid for three months from release, after which it can be extended; transactions with the top 10 crypto assets are not covered by the offer. Deals with a value of more than 2 million are processed as a single tranche with an indicative price derived from the OTC pricing strategy established in advance with the client’s dedicated OTC manager, allowing institutional and corporate clients to plan bigger deals from the beginning.

The relaunch is a part of WhiteBIT’s institutional and professional market business growth strategy. With the addition of a dedicated OTC execution channel, WhiteBIT will aim to provide crypto liquidity and allow more flexibility in handling large-scale digital asset transactions for businesses and investors.

WhiteBIT is a leading global crypto exchange by user traffic, offering over 1020 trading pairs, 370+ assets, and supporting 8 fiat currencies. With a strong focus on regulatory compliance, WhiteBIT serves 10 million users across six continents and more than 150 countries. Founded in 2018, the platform is part of W Group, which has more than 40 million customers globally. WhiteBIT collaborates with Visa, FACEIT, FC Barcelona, Juventus FC, and the Ukrainian national football team. The company is dedicated to driving the widespread adoption of blockchain technology worldwide.

#5156. Unocoin Estimates $200,000 Loss as Backup-Key Finding Explains Wallet Transfers

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Unocoin has revised its account of a security incident that disrupted the Indian exchange, putting estimated cryptocurrency losses at about $200,000. The more significant technical finding is how transactions could proceed after the exchange asked its wallet providers to freeze activity.

Unocoin’s November 14 update identifies compromised backup keys as part of the explanation. The incident illustrates a distinction that can be easy to miss: suspending access to a service and removing the ability to authorize a blockchain transaction are separate things.

Unocoin said three operational hot wallets were compromised and promised to fund the identified loss from its own resources. Its earlier assessment had not identified missing cryptocurrency. The company also disclosed possible exposure of customer information, while saying it had found no evidence that KYC documents were accessed.

Those findings remain subject to investigation. An initial loss estimate is useful for assessing scale, but it is not the same as a final reconciliation of every asset and transaction. Potential information exposure also needs to be assessed separately from the amount of cryptocurrency taken.

That distinction matters for customers. Replacing coins can restore an account balance; it cannot make exposed contact or account information private again. A financial remedy and a data-security response address different consequences.

BitGo’s November 13 account says the affected Ethereum wallet used a two-of-three multisignature arrangement. Unocoin controlled the user and backup keys, while BitGo controlled the third. BitGo says the reviewed transfers used the two Unocoin keys and were broadcast outside its platform.

The design permits an owner to recover assets without depending on the service provider. That is valuable when a provider is unavailable, but the same independence means that the provider’s refusal to sign cannot prevent two other valid keys from acting together.

BitGo’s wallet documentation distinguishes self-custody arrangements from its custody products, including differences in who controls keys. A provider’s name therefore does not, by itself, tell a reader who had final authority over a particular wallet.

The broader control question is whether emergency credentials are separated effectively from everyday systems. A recovery mechanism has to remain available to its legitimate owner while being difficult for an intruder to assemble with other signing material.

NewsBTC’s coverage of business Bitcoin accounts with team approvals examined another part of that problem: permission to request or approve a transfer is not necessarily identical to possession of the cryptographic keys.

Combining several safeguards can help, but their independence matters. Two approvals provide less protection if one compromised system can obtain both. This is an architectural lesson from the reported signing arrangement, not a determination of the still-unknown route into Unocoin’s backup storage.

Unocoin says it is rebuilding infrastructure and investigating how the backup material was compromised. A convincing follow-up would connect that forensic explanation with a complete accounting of losses, restored services and the handling of potentially exposed information.

BitGo’s wider commercial growth, covered in NewsBTC’s report on its quarterly results, shows how large the custody and infrastructure business has become. Scale makes clear descriptions of individual service arrangements more valuable, particularly when several companies participate in one transaction process.

The available disclosures narrow the explanation considerably. They identify which keys authorized the reviewed Ethereum transfers. They do not yet provide a complete account of how those keys were obtained or establish that every part of the incident has been resolved.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve."

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

MacPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he said the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees."

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”

#5153. Bitcoin Hits 12-Week Low as Fed Rate Fears Undo Most of Summer Rally

Bitcoin Hits 12-Week Low as Fed Rate Fears Undo Most of Summer Rally

Bitcoin fell to roughly $68,500 on Friday, hitting its lowest price in 12 weeks as renewed U.S. inflation worries and investor withdrawals pushed the cryptocurrency further into the red.

BTC was down about 4.5% over 24 hours and 9.5% for the week, according to Friday market data. Ethereum traded near $1,925, while Solana slipped below $80 as selling spread across major cryptocurrencies.

The latest slide has erased most of Bitcoin's late-summer recovery. But not all of it: BTC remains approximately 16% above its late-June low near $59,000, even after retreating roughly 21% from its autumn peak around $86,000.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee warned Friday that inflation had spread beyond energy and tariffs, with rising services and medical costs and demand from AI data centers adding to price pressures.

“Are we on a path back to 2%? My feeling right now is we are not and we've got to deal with that,” Goolsbee said according to Reuters.

Goolsbee did not explicitly endorse a December rate hike. But other Fed officials have been more direct.

On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he supported raising interest rates by at least 25 basis points, or 0.25 percentage points, at the December 8-9 meeting.

He also established a threshold for considering something more aggressive.

“If the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed,” Waller said in his official remarks.

The report subsequently showed core CPI rising exactly 0.3%, exceeding the 0.2% forecast and meeting Waller's condition for considering a 50-basis-point increase.

Markets have responded accordingly. Futures-based rate probabilities as of November 13 showed a 91.9% probability of a quarter-point increase and an 8.1% probability of a half-point increase.

Those figures reflect trader expectations, not a decision by the Fed. The central bank's current target range is 3.75% to 4.00%.

Friday's producer-price report added to the concerns. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, less than forecast, but increased 6.5% year over year, the largest annual jump since 2022.

For Bitcoin, higher rates make traditional interest-bearing investments relatively more attractive, reducing the appeal of speculative assets.

Meanwhile, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have registered six consecutive sessions of net outflows, totaling approximately $1.49 billion between November 5 and November 12.

Thursday's $47.7 million withdrawal extended the five-day outflow streak, bringing another source of pressure to an already struggling market.

That does not mean institutional investors have abandoned Bitcoin. The funds still hold approximately $55.5 billion in cumulative net inflows, but it does show the state of nervousness that investors are feeling.

Weakening ETF demand, combined with forced liquidations of leveraged traders, can accelerate a decline when buyers are scarce.

Bitcoin's daily chart now shows a clear sequence of lower highs and lower lows, confirming a bearish short-term trajectory.

Its relative strength index, or RSI, has dropped to 25.4. Readings below 30 are generally considered oversold, suggesting the selling may be stretched.The average directional index, or ADX, stands at 25.3, indicating an established trend. Combined with declining prices, that suggests bearish momentum remains meaningful.

There is still one longer-term positive signal: the 50-day exponential moving average remains above the 200-day EMA, preserving a bullish moving-average configuration. But Bitcoin's price has fallen below the shorter-term average, indicating that recent momentum has turned against buyers.

Immediate support sits around $67,650, Friday's intraday low. Losing that level could expose a deeper support area near $64,000.

On the upside, Bitcoin needs to recover $70,815 and $72,775 before challenging the stronger resistance zone between $74,355 and $75,937.

The combination of extreme oversold readings and strong downward momentum leaves room for a temporary bounce, but not enough evidence to declare a bottom.

For now, traders face two major macroeconomic checkpoints: the Fed's November 18 meeting minutes and the November 25 PCE inflation report, both of which could influence expectations ahead of December's interest-rate decision.

#5151. Backpack Wins US Clearing Registration as Separate Exchange Bid Remains Pending

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Backpack has secured a US derivatives-clearing registration, adding a regulated institution for handling the obligations behind trades. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission registered TLD Clearing, doing business as Backpack Clearing, on November 13. The approval is a meaningful part of the group’s market-infrastructure plans, while a separate application to operate an exchange remains pending.

The CFTC’s public register permits Backpack Clearing to clear margined futures, along with fully collateralized futures, options on futures and swaps. This identifies the clearinghouse’s authorised scope; it does not show that every potential contract has launched.

A clearinghouse becomes the central counterparty to accepted trades and manages the resulting obligations. Its job differs from matching buyers and sellers on an exchange. A trading screen can display an executed order quickly, but the market also needs arrangements for collecting collateral, settling gains and losses and dealing with a participant that cannot pay.

The distinction is relevant to the broader industry push toward integrated derivatives operations. Coinbase’s earlier clearing registration showed another crypto group building this part of its infrastructure, under its own approved scope.

Backpack’s clearing-activities submission describes an intended central-counterparty model for contracts listed on registered markets. It includes initial and variation margin, risk-based requirements and default-management procedures. The filing also describes legally separate exchange, clearing and brokerage entities working within a coordinated framework.

That separation matters when a group offers several services under one familiar brand. A customer needs to know which entity holds its account, which one accepts a trade for clearing and which rules apply if something goes wrong. Shared ownership does not make those roles interchangeable.

The application contemplated a phased product rollout. Its list of possible future products should therefore be read as a plan subject to the relevant approvals and operating capacity, rather than a current trading menu. Clearing registration alone does not establish availability, customer eligibility or the amount of market liquidity.

The registration order records commitments to enforce clearing-member standards and maintain member funds separately from the clearinghouse’s own funds. It also says changes to material facts or circumstances may require a new or amended order.

These are operating obligations that continue after the approval date. For a clearing business, reliable performance depends on how it handles changing exposures and exceptional events, not only on passing an initial regulatory assessment.

Imagine a sharp market move that leaves one member owing more collateral. The clearinghouse needs timely prices, dependable calls for funds and a credible process if that member fails. The practical strength of the model would become visible through those controls and its ability to complete settlements under stress.

The CFTC’s record for TLD Markets lists its designated-contract-market application as pending, dated April 22, 2026. That is the status shown in the public record reviewed for this report. The clearing decision should not be described as approval of that separate exchange application.

Nor should the US registration be blended with other Backpack-branded activity, such as tokenized-equity collateral used in Kamino’s Solana lending market. Different products can sit within different legal entities and regulatory arrangements even when their branding overlaps.

For Backpack, the immediate achievement is a registered clearing operation with an identified scope. The next commercial milestones are the remaining relevant permissions and clearly documented products, participants and launch arrangements. Those details will determine what traders can actually access through the US structure.

Cryptocurrency exchange KuCoin has rolled out its largest Black Friday promotional event to date, putting more than 1.1 million USDT in rewards on the table as exchanges compete for retail trading volume ahead of the holiday season.

Running from November 16 to December 1, the campaign triples the size of KuCoin’s previous November promotions, which historically ranged from 15,000 USDT to 360,000 USDT.

Unlike past years that focused on single-product giveaways, the 2026 edition spans five trading and payment verticals—and adds VIP hospitality packages for the Tomorrowland Winter 2027 music festival.

The event marks the opening stage of KuCoin’s two-part PROOF series, titled ‘Tis The Season, with a separate Holiday Edition scheduled to follow from December 11 to December 30.

Futures traders stand to receive the largest share of the rewards, with up to 550,000 USDT available through trading-volume competitions, TraderPro return-on-investment (ROI) contests and a lucky draw.

The remaining rewards are spread across other KuCoin services. Spot and margin traders can each compete for up to 100,000 USDT by completing trading tasks and reaching volume targets. VIP users have up to 150,000 USDT available through trading challenges and volume-based leaderboards, while KuMining is offering up to 100,000 USDT to users who purchase cloud mining hashrate.

Another 100,000 USDT is allocated to crypto payments, with users able to receive fee cashback when buying or selling cryptocurrencies through bank cards or peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions.

Beyond the trading and payment rewards, the campaign also features a Grand Lucky Draw with additional prizes, including USDT, KuCoin merchandise gift boxes and a Tomorrowland Winter 2027 festival package with accommodation.

The advertised 1.1 million USDT in prizes covers several types of rewards, rather than direct cash payouts alone. These include fee cashback, trading-related rewards and prizes tied to competition results and trading volumes.

KuCoin has not yet provided details of the second phase, the Holiday Edition, scheduled to run from December 11 to 30. The exchange said information about its activities and rewards would be announced separately.

#5148. After 7 Years and 99% Speed Leap, Solana (SOL) Finally Drops Its 'Beta' Label

Solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was announced on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation said.

Solana launched on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status."

The Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

"For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

According to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation said.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

"A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once."

Earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

#5147. Hong Kong Reaffirms Year-End Crypto Licensing Bill as Tokenized Funds Expand

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Hong Kong’s Financial Secretary Paul Chan has reaffirmed plans to introduce a bill before the end of 2026 expanding the city’s digital-asset licensing framework. Speaking on November 16, he linked that regulatory work with a market moving toward regular use of tokenized investment products. The message was that more activity on blockchains still needs identifiable institutions responsible for the services around it.

Chan’s Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum speech names dealing, advice, management and custody as activities to be brought within the perimeter. He also highlighted the two licensed stablecoin issuers and the emergence of around-the-clock trading in tokenized money-market funds.

The timetable is a reiteration, not a newly enacted rule. In a November 4 Legislative Council reply, the government said it planned to amend the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance and extend the existing trading-platform regime. That earlier explanation helps locate the proposal: the focus is the businesses handling digital assets and the functions they perform.

For a customer, the same investment can involve several such functions. One company might recommend it, another execute the purchase and another safeguard the resulting holding. A useful regulatory structure has to make responsibility visible at each handoff.

The November 4 government reply reported 17 authorised retail investment products with tokenized classes at the end of September, representing about HK$10.3 billion in those classes. These included money-market funds and gold-related products. The figure concerns a defined set of investment products; it should not be presented as the size of Hong Kong’s entire digital-asset market.

The Securities and Futures Commission’s October 26 approval allowed secondary trading of ChinaAMC’s Hong Kong-dollar and US-dollar digital money-market funds on a licensed virtual-asset platform. Secondary trading lets investors exchange existing interests rather than relying solely on subscriptions and redemptions with a fund.

That creates a different set of questions from simply recording ownership on a blockchain. Investors need meaningful prices, sufficient counterparties and a clear understanding of how traded units relate to their rights in the underlying product.

If a platform offers trading through a weekend, its customer support, security and controls have to account for that window. Yet the assets held by a fund may trade on a different schedule. A round-the-clock token does not ensure that its underlying market has become equally liquid at every hour.

The cash side is another dependency. Hong Kong’s EnsembleTX settlement work addresses how tokenized money and investment transactions can fit together. The trading venue, fund, custodian and payment service each need a consistent view of what has completed and what remains outstanding.

Stablecoin distribution raises similar questions about access and redemption. Anchorpoint’s planned native HKDAP expansion shows why a network integration and the conditions under which customers can use a product are separate milestones. A new route for transferring an asset does not by itself explain every holder’s rights.

Chan’s speech does not itself set final licence conditions or establish a commencement date for the expanded regime. Those details matter to firms deciding whether to add a service, change a custody arrangement or work through another authorised provider.

The most useful next evidence will be the legislative text and its treatment of different business models. Clear definitions can help firms determine where their obligations begin, while practical transition arrangements affect how existing customers are served.

Hong Kong’s challenge is now partly one of coordination: allowing more products and trading hours while keeping responsibility legible. A tokenized market will be easier to evaluate when investors can identify who owes them what, who controls a transaction and which regulator oversees each service.
