#5146. Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

President Donald Trump has nominated four people to fill vacant seats at the two federal agencies writing the rules for crypto, in a bipartisan slate that could reshape the commissions that have increasingly taken the lead on digital-asset policy after Congress stalled.

The White House said Thursday it sent the nominations to the Senate: Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and Kristin Johnson and Steven Levine for the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Each requires Senate confirmation. Notably, the slate pairs a Republican and a Democrat at each agency, with Anonick and Levine the Republicans and Rowland and Johnson the Democrats, marking the first time the administration has put forward Democratic nominees for either commission.

The appointments matter because of how depleted both agencies have become. The CFTC in particular has been running on a skeleton crew, operating with Michael Selig as its lone Senate-confirmed member after a wave of departures, even as it has pursued one of the most aggressive crypto agendas in its history.

Filling those seats would give the commissions the quorum and staying power to turn proposals into durable rules.

Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which shares jurisdiction over crypto market structure and will vet their nominations. Anonick, a Republican, is legislative counsel to committee Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the panel’s portion of the Clarity Act, the crypto market-structure bill that collapsed in the Senate this fall.

Rowland, a Democrat, is a career CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and an earlier 2024 crypto bill. His enforcement-heavy background and party lean could introduce a dissenting voice to a commission that, under Selig, has leaned firmly pro-industry.

On the SEC side, which the Senate Banking Committee will review, the picks would replace two commissioners central to crypto policy in opposite ways. Levine, a Republican, is slated to fill the seat of Hester Peirce, the agency’s most prominent crypto advocate and the head of its Crypto Task Force.

Levine’s own views on digital assets are not well established publicly, making his future votes a key variable for whether the SEC’s crypto-friendly push holds.

Johnson, a Democrat and former CFTC commissioner, would take the seat of frequent crypto skeptic Caroline Crenshaw; at the CFTC she focused on digital-asset custody and DeFi and pressed for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules.

The timing underscores a shift following the collapse of the Clarity Act, the crypto industry’s marquee market structure bill that would have established more-favorable-than-not rules for most of crypto.

After the legislation failed to advance in the Senate, the SEC and CFTC moved to fill the vacuum with their own authority, leaving the industry to get its “clarity” from regulators rather than legislators. A fully staffed pair of commissions would cement that dynamic.

Those agency efforts have been sweeping: The CFTC has cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, floated bringing crypto exchanges under federal oversight, and moved to define event contracts as “swaps.” The SEC, meanwhile, rolled out an “innovation exemption” for tokenized stocks, proposed rules letting investment advisers custody crypto, and issued guidance suggesting most crypto assets aren’t securities.

The nominations are the first Trump has sent for these seats in roughly a year, a gap that reflected turbulence around crypto appointments. The administration previously pulled its CFTC chair nominee, Brian Quintenz, amid a clash involving the Winklevoss twins.

The confirmation window is now tight: with the Senate heading toward Democratic control in January, Republicans have only a short lame-duck stretch to move the slate before the calculus changes.

#5144. Harvard and Dartmouth Keep Bitcoin ETF Share Counts Steady as Q3 Values Rise

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Two university investment portfolios offer a quieter picture of institutional Bitcoin exposure than the usual buying-and-selling headlines. Harvard and Dartmouth reported the same numbers of shares in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF at the end of September as they had at the end of June. The positions became more valuable as the fund rose.

The distinction is useful: a larger dollar figure can describe a change in market prices without showing an increase in the number of shares held. These filings, submitted on November 13, also reveal other portfolio choices that put the Bitcoin positions into perspective.

Harvard Management Company’s September filing lists 3,044,612 shares of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, valued at $144.1 million. Dartmouth’s disclosure lists 201,531 shares worth approximately $9.5 million.

The corresponding June disclosures show identical share counts, valued at about $101.4 million and $6.7 million. That works out to an increase of roughly 42% in the reported value of each position. The calculation compares the two filing snapshots; it is not a measure of fresh cash invested during the quarter.

Matching endpoints do not establish that no transactions happened between them. A manager could trade during a quarter and finish with the same holding. The documents establish the reported balances on the two dates.

The difference is easier to see in Harvard’s SPDR Gold Shares position. Its latest filing reports 1,161,000 GLD shares, compared with 58,862 in the June information table. That is nearly twenty times the earlier share count. The September position was worth about $442.2 million.

Those figures support a statement that Harvard’s reported exposure through that gold fund expanded substantially. They do not, by themselves, explain why. Inflation protection, portfolio construction and other motives require evidence beyond a list of securities.

Nor does the gold increase prove that Bitcoin financed it. Establishing such a rotation would require information about cash movements and the wider portfolio. Here, the Bitcoin share count stayed level while the GLD count rose.

Dartmouth also reported 304,803 shares in the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF and 178,148 shares in the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF. Those share counts likewise match its June table. Their September values were approximately $4.9 million and $4.5 million respectively.

The fund names describe distinct underlying exposures. Combining their dollar values can show the size of the reported crypto-linked positions, but it does not turn them into one interchangeable investment. Bitcoin, Ether and Solana can respond differently to network developments, and a staking product introduces mechanics that a straightforward Bitcoin trust does not have.

NewsBTC’s recent report on JPMorgan’s crypto-linked securities holdings shows another reason to inspect the actual instrument before interpreting an institutional total.

The SEC’s Form 13F guidance explains the delayed quarterly reporting framework. These disclosures are a record of reportable securities holdings, not a complete picture of each university’s assets or a live trading feed.

That timing matters after November’s sustained Bitcoin ETF withdrawals. A September position can coexist with subsequent market selling, and the latest filings cannot show whether either university changed its exposure after quarter-end.

The evidence is specific but useful: both reported stable Bitcoin ETF share counts through September, while Harvard’s gold holding expanded sharply. The next comparable filing will show whether that pattern survived the market’s later reversal.

Shiba Inu fell to a rare low of $0.0000037 as cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend. This low marked the lowest seen in years, going back to 2021, as it fell below the $0.000004 level, which has served as support since the start of 2026.

Last week’s bruising selloff following a tougher interest-rate outlook and a risk-off mood deepened the gloom around the cryptocurrency.

Shiba Inu fell for four straight days in the past week, dropping to a low of $0.0000037 on November 14, 2026, coinciding with the first death cross on its daily chart in 2026.

At the time of writing, Shiba Inu was down 3.36% in the last 24 hours to $0.00000386 as the crypto market selloff intensified, with a total of $203.7 million liquidated. Mazrael, a long-time Shiba Inu community member and SHIB developer, reacted to the token's latest price weakness with a simple message: "1 SHIB is always 1 SHIB" in response to an X user who pointed out Shiba Inu's price drop.

The phrase, often used in the context of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies during price downturns, serves as a reminder to focus on the unit itself rather than short-term fiat volatility. While a single coin always counts as one unit of the network, the argument against this saying is that fiat value changes amid volatility.

#5139. Is The $30B XRP Burn Offer Acceptable For Ripple?

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Is The $30B XRP Burn Offer Acceptable For Ripple?

A courageous plan to burn more than half of the remaining XRP supply lands on Ripple’s table.

Lawyer and longtime XRP observer Bill Morgan reacted to a fresh call for Ripple to destroy its entire escrow by stating the obvious: “Imagine asking a company to destroy an asset valued at $30 billion, believe they would ever do it, and expect to be viewed as sane.”

The demand in question came from an open letter urging Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse to burn the full remaining escrow, currently about 31.1 billion XRP, by the first quarter of 2027. At recent prices near $0.95, that amount is worth roughly $30 billion.

Ripple locked 55 billion XRP into on-ledger escrow contracts in December, 2017 specifically to make supply more predictable.

Each month, up to 1 billion XRP becomes available; historically, the company has re-locked the majority into new smart contracts further down the line and retained a smaller net amount for operational use.

It would make more sense for XRPL validators to vote on any major supply change, because the XRP Ledger is decentralized. Ripple runs only a small share of the default Unique Node List (roughly 1 of ~35, or low single-digit percent).Protocol amendments require ~80% of trusted… https://t.co/Ib7cTsQHUx

The escrow balance has already declined from 55 billion to roughly 31.1 billion as a result of this process.

Destroying the remaining escrow would mean permanently removing an asset that sits on Ripple’s balance sheet and that the company has repeatedly said is intended for controlled distribution, partnerships, and ecosystem growth.

No public company has ever willingly incinerated tens of billions of dollars in assets simply because a segment of token holders asked for it.

Morgan has addressed similar proposals before. He has pointed out that large burns by other projects, including Stellar’s well-known reduction of its XLM supply, did not produce lasting price strength or prevent later declines.

The recurring demand to burn the XRP escrow, in his view, often functions more as a signal that the requester doubts the asset’s underlying value than as a coherent supply-side strategy.

Critics of the XRP escrow schedule frequently treat every monthly unlock as an automatic dump that suppresses price.

In practice, the majority of each release is returned to escrow, and XRP’s price has continued to move largely in line with broader crypto market conditions rather than in lockstep with the XRP escrow schedule.

The supply was never meant to last forever. At the current net release rate of roughly 300 million XRP per month, the locked supply continues to decline gradually.

Imagine asking a company to destroy an asset valued at $30 billion, believe they would ever do it, and expect to be viewed as sane https://t.co/sft8TRMV80

Morgan the lawyer has also noted in earlier posts that the escrow has already fallen from 55 billion in late 2017 to the low-to-mid 30s of billions today.

That full distribution under the original monthly cap would have emptied it years ago had Ripple not retained the flexibility to re-lock unused amounts.

The South Korean crypto exchange said potentially exposed information includes passwords, bank account numbers, national identification numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.

On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records. Coinone said it learned about the breach in the same day.

According to Coinone, the information potentially exposed names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, national identification numbers, home and wallet addresses and transaction IDs.

Coinone said its account, trading and wallet infrastructure operates separately from MetaM’s servers, with no evidence of direct compromise. The exchange said it has reported the incident to South Korean authorities.

The disclosure comes as South Korea moves to strengthen financial-sector cybersecurity. In October, the Financial Services Commission identified security deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial firms reviewed.

On Thursday, the regulator said it would allow crypto exchanges to suspend withdrawals when hacking is suspected, alongside calls for round-the-clock monitoring.

#5136. US and Canada Announce Massive Crypto Fraud Crackdown

Authorities in the United States and Canada have announced a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) announced on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," said Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

The initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

#5135. Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact

Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will convene a public forum Monday to examine whether artificial intelligence will bring down inflation, drive prices higher, or replace American workers.

The November 16 conference in San Francisco will bring together technology executives, economists, and employers to examine how AI is reshaping the economy.

The findings could influence how the Fed approaches interest rates, a major factor in Bitcoin's price movements as investors weigh whether to put money into risky assets or safer alternatives.

Warsh has argued that AI could help companies produce more goods and services at lower costs, easing inflation without requiring the Fed to keep borrowing expensive.

But some of his colleagues see a different problem: The AI boom is already making things more expensive, while the promised productivity benefits remain largely theoretical.

Building data centers requires enormous quantities of electricity, computer chips, construction materials, and skilled workers. When technology companies compete for those limited resources, prices rise.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned in September that AI investment was adding inflationary pressure and delaying the central bank's return to its 2% inflation target.

If AI eventually allows businesses to produce more without raising costs, inflation could cool, giving policymakers room to lower interest rates.

Lower rates generally make risky assets like Bitcoin or tech stocks more attractive because government bonds and savings accounts offer smaller returns, encouraging investors to seek higher gains elsewhere.

But if AI spending keeps inflation elevated, the Fed could maintain high interest rates or raise them further. That would make borrowing more expensive, strengthen the appeal of interest-bearing assets, and potentially drain money from speculative investments, including cryptocurrencies.

Bitcoin is already feeling that pressure. The cryptocurrency dropped below $69,000 Friday as stronger-than-expected inflation figures fueled concerns about another Fed rate hike.

AI also has a more direct connection to the Bitcoin industry than most may think of.

Both AI data centers and Bitcoin mining operations need access to large amounts of electricity. As AI companies compete for power and infrastructure, miners face pressure to secure affordable energy or consider more profitable alternatives.

Some are already abandoning Bitcoin mining altogether. Hyperscale Data shut down mining operations at its Michigan facility in September to accommodate an AI customer under a deal potentially worth more than $1.2 billion. The same has happened with other big names like Coreweave and other former Ethereum miners from its proof-of-work era.

Meanwhile, AI's potential impact on employment adds another complication.

Fed Governor Michael Barr warned Thursday of possible “serious short-term disruptions” as businesses increasingly replace human tasks with AI systems.

Widespread job losses could weaken consumer spending, slow economic growth, and eventually increase pressure on the Fed to cut rates. But a deteriorating economy could also push investors away from Bitcoin as they look to reduce risk.

Warsh himself acknowledged in August that AI represents “a new variable” for monetary policy.

The question now is whether AI's economic benefits will arrive quickly enough to outweigh the costs of building it.

Monday's conference will not determine the Fed's next interest-rate decision, scheduled for December 9. But it could offer clues about how policymakers view a technology boom that is increasingly influencing both Wall Street and the crypto market.

#5134. Hong Kong’s SWIFT Push Puts XRP Back In Focus

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Hong Kong’s SWIFT Push Puts XRP Back In Focus

Programmable blockchain payments are coming: Swift is plugging its ledger into Hong Kong’s Project Ensemble.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced on 16 November, 2026 a strengthened partnership with Swift to explore how tokenised deposits can improve the speed and end-to-end experience of cross-border transactions.

The work builds on collaboration that began in 2023 through the Project Ensemble Sandbox, where the two organisations tested interoperability between central bank digital currency systems.

The latest phase brings in major Hong Kong banks, including Bank of China (Hong Kong), Standard Chartered, and HSBC, to examine how the Swift ledger can connect with Project Ensemble’s settlement layer.

The goal is to develop mechanisms that use multi-currency tokenised deposits for cross-border payments, using Swift’s global network to link international and local systems more tightly.

HKMA Deputy Chief Executive Howard Lee described it as another step toward supporting real-time, always-on, and programmable cross-border transactions.

Swift is plugging its ledger into Hong Kong's Project Ensemble.The HKMA, Swift, HSBC, Standard Chartered and Bank of China (Hong Kong) will explore moving tokenized deposits across borders in multiple currencies. The goal is real-time, 24/7, programmable payments.It's still…

Swift’s Chief Business Officer Thierry Chilosi noted that as domestic systems evolve to handle new forms of digital value, the organisation is exploring how its ledger can connect these platforms across borders so institutions can settle more efficiently.

This is not Hong Kong’s first experiment with tokenised assets and digital money infrastructure. In 2023, Ripple and Fubon Bank participated in the HKMA’s inaugural e-HKD Pilot Programme.

Their use case combined a hypothetical e-HKD with tokenised real estate (property liens) and lending protocols to enable faster access to home equity.

The solution ran on a private ledger built with the same technology as the XRP Ledger, with Ripple’s CBDC platform handling the digital currency layer.

That earlier pilot focused on domestic retail and asset-tokenisation scenarios. The new HKMA x Swift x XRP work shifts the emphasis toward wholesale interbank settlement and multi-currency cross-border flows using tokenised deposits.

Both efforts share the same underlying requirement: different systems, whether CBDC platforms, tokenized deposit ledgers, or traditional messaging networks, must be able to interoperate without forcing every participant on one rail.

Public blockchains such as the XRP Ledger have long been positioned by their proponents as neutral settlement layers that can sit between otherwise incompatible systems.

HKMA + SWIFT + tokenized deposits is a peak "TradFi meets onchain" moment 🤝 honest q fam: would you hold tokenized bank deposits, or stick with stablecoins? 🤔

XRP itself is frequently discussed as a potential bridge asset for currency conversions in corridors where no single national digital currency is suitable as an intermediary.

Ripple’s earlier work with the HKMA already demonstrated that XRPL-derived technology could support tokenized asset and CBDC-related use cases inside a regulated pilot.

The current Project Ensemble-Swift collaboration does not name any public blockchain or bridge asset. The programme focuses on connecting existing institutional infrastructure with emerging tokenised-deposit systems.

#5131. Trezor patches crypto wallet spy chips but warns users a new device may not be enough

The firmware update blocks malicious implants, but customers whose recovery phrases may have been exposed must create fresh wallets and transfer their funds.

Hardware wallet maker Trezor has slashed its reseller network by about 80% after discovering malicious implants that can steal cryptocurrency recovery phrases from devices sold through a third-party distributor.

The company confirmed on Nov. 12 that three Trezor Safe 5 wallets purchased from Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained hidden electronic components designed to capture sensitive information and transmit it to attackers.

Trezor also released firmware version 2.13.1 on Nov. 11 to disable the identified implants, although it warned that customers whose recovery phrases may have been exposed must still transfer their assets to newly created wallets.

The findings follow an October supply-chain security incident involving CryptoBilis and Ledger hardware wallets, which investigators linked to cryptocurrency thefts exceeding $86 million.

Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery subsequently traced approximately $102 million in losses across 335 wallets on six blockchains. Ledger confirmed finding a malicious hardware implant in a customer's device, although investigators have not established that the implant caused every reported loss.

The incidents exposed vulnerabilities in hardware-wallet distribution, where attackers can modify genuine devices before customers receive them.

Trezor identified three compromised Safe 5 devices purchased between Aug. 20 and Sept. 23 through CryptoBilis's Tokopedia and Shopee storefronts and direct sales.

Its security team physically examined one device and identified the other two through photographs supplied by their owners.

The attackers installed an additional circuit board between the wallet's main board and display, allowing the implant to monitor information shown on the screen without modifying the firmware or Secure Element.

The component could capture recovery phrases during wallet setup or restoration, along with passphrases displayed on the device.

It then encrypted the information and transmitted it through a mobile network to an attacker-controlled server. When connectivity was unavailable, the implant stored the data and retried transmission.

The attack exploited a critical weakness in cryptocurrency self-custody. Anyone who obtains a wallet's recovery phrase can potentially restore control over its assets without possessing the original hardware.

Trezor said its latest firmware prevents the identified implants from collecting additional information, but it cannot invalidate recovery credentials attackers may already possess.

Consequently, the manufacturer has urged anyone who purchased a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to create a new wallet with a different recovery phrase and move their funds.

The company has offered eligible customers replacement devices or refunds.

Trezor said 48 CryptoBilis customers had contacted it during the investigation. None of the three confirmed implant owners reported losing funds, and investigators found no evidence of similar tampering in devices examined from other resellers.

Meanwhile, Trezor is tightening requirements governing how its remaining distributors source, store, and handle devices.

The company continues working with cryptocurrency security response group SEAL 911 to investigate the compromises.

The unresolved risk concerns recovery phrases captured before the firmware update. Customers whose credentials were exposed remain vulnerable until they move their cryptocurrency to wallets secured by entirely new recovery credentials.

#5130. Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Two Bitcoin addresses that had been dormant since 2010 suddenly moved $6.9 million worth of BTC on Friday, bringing two early mining rewards back into circulation after more than 16 years.

Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert flagged the first transfer at 4:08 a.m. UTC on November 13, when 50 BTC worth approximately $3.44 million moved from an address that had not spent its original mining reward since September 2010.

Just over two minutes later, another 50 BTC moved from a separate wallet with an equally long history.

Both transfers involved Bitcoin originally generated through mining, rather than coins purchased on an exchange. Their combined value today was approximately $6,885,068.

The coins came from two blocks mined on September 8 and September 19, 2010, respectively. Back then, Bitcoin traded for roughly six cents, meaning each 50 BTC reward was worth about three bucks.

At Friday's transaction prices of around $68,800 per Bitcoin, their combined value had increased approximately 1,147,511 times, equivalent to a 114,751,033% increase.

That percentage measures the appreciation in Bitcoin's market price (what’s known as unrealized gains), not money the holder has actually made by selling (which would be known as realized gains). In fact, it’s unknown whether this was a peer-to-peer transaction, an OTC sell, or simply a wallet switch for security reasons.

The $3 valuation is also an estimate. Bitcoin barely had a functioning market in September 2010, with historical prices showing a trading range of around five to seven cents. The Mt. Gox exchange had only opened that July, with its first recorded trade taking place at $0.04951 per coin.

The transfers are part of a broader trend of ancient Bitcoin wallets waking up in 2026. According to Galaxy Research data highlighted in August, Bitcoin that had remained untouched for at least a decade was moving at a pace rarely seen in previous years. In one 10-day stretch alone, six wallets dating back to 2011, 2012, and 2014 transferred a combined 553.59 BTC, worth more than $40 million at the time.

Some of those movements have been linked to security concerns, wallet upgrades, or transfers to professional custodians rather than outright selling. Friday's activity adds another 100 BTC to the growing list of early Bitcoin holdings changing hands—or at least changing addresses—after more than a decade of silence.

The blockchain provides a detailed record of where the money moved, but it doesn't reveal who controls the receiving wallets.

The first transaction split the 50 BTC into two new addresses, sending nearly 49.99 BTC to one and approximately 0.01 BTC to another, minus a tiny network fee.

The second transaction followed a similar pattern, transferring nearly 49 BTC to one address and approximately 1 BTC to another.

Both transactions cost just 1,110 satoshis each in network fees, equivalent to approximately $0.75. A satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest unit, worth one hundred-millionth of a BTC.

As of an on-chain check at approximately 14:00 UTC Friday, the 100 BTC had not moved again from their new destinations following the consolidation, and no sale has been identified.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Nvidia, IBM and Fermilab announced new tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

Nvidia released a new decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the company, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia said that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing."

Nvidia and IBM also announced plans for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform."

In 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a new output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

#5126. Bitcoin flashes false recovery warning as $64 billion futures frenzy masks weak demand

Derivatives accounted for 83% of tracked trading volume while ETF investors withdrew more than $1 billion ahead of the weekend selloff.

Bitcoin‘s recovery above $64,000 risks losing momentum as leveraged traders dominate market activity while institutional investors continue withdrawing capital.

The cryptocurrency staged a modest rebound after plunging toward $62,000 over the weekend, its lowest level since July. However, the recovery comes against a backdrop of weakening demand, with US spot Bitcoin ETFs recording substantial withdrawals and futures positions shrinking across major exchanges.

The clearest warning came from Wall Street before the weekend crash.

According to Farside Investors, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw more than $1 billion in net outflows over the five trading sessions ending Nov. 13. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for about $908 million of those withdrawals, highlighting a retreat from one of Bitcoin's largest institutional investment channels.

With ETF demand retreating, leveraged traders dominated the weekend's market activity.

A CryptoQuant analysis showed that Bitcoin futures generated $64.11 billion in trading volume on Nov. 14, dwarfing the $13.36 billion recorded across tracked spot exchanges.

That meant derivatives accounted for nearly 83% of combined trading activity, with futures turnover almost five times larger than spot volume.

The imbalance was particularly striking on Binance, where $24.46 billion in Bitcoin futures trading exceeded the combined spot volume of every exchange tracked by CryptoQuant by 83%.

The disparity raises a troubling possibility for Bitcoin's recovery. Prices may stabilize as leveraged traders unwind bearish positions, but that buying can disappear quickly if investors don't return to accumulate the underlying cryptocurrency.

The weekend's derivatives frenzy coincided with a significant retreat in open interest, suggesting traders were reducing exposure as Bitcoin absorbed its latest losses.

Binance data showed that open interest in its coin-margined Bitcoin futures market dropped 7.3%, from 16.25 million contracts on Nov. 13 to 15.06 million by Monday morning.

The perpetual futures segment contracted even faster, declining approximately 7.8% over the same period.

Meanwhile, funding rates revealed another significant shift in trading conditions.

Binance's BTCUSD perpetual funding rate turned negative at -0.006022% on Nov. 15 as bearish pressure intensified. By Monday morning, the rate had reversed to 0.003593%, indicating that the earlier imbalance favoring short positions had eased.

Together, falling open interest and the funding reversal suggest Bitcoin's derivatives market has undergone a substantial reset.

They also leave room for a short-covering rebound, in which traders who bet on further losses buy futures contracts to close their positions, potentially pushing prices higher without attracting fresh spot investment.

However, the danger is that such buying is temporary.

Once bearish traders finish closing their positions, that source of demand disappears. Unless new buyers step in, Bitcoin could lose the support behind its recovery and become vulnerable to another round of selling.

#5125. Enterprise blockchain is going to come back from the dead

Opinion by Paul Brody, founder and chief executive, Nightfall Networks

Do you remember Pets.com? It raised $110 million from Amazon and others to build a business where people ordered pet toys and dog food online.

The company crashed and burned, and everyone learned an important lesson: you can’t profitably ship a 50-pound bag of dog food to a customer’s door.

As online retail entrepreneur Ed Baum asked in a 2001 postmortem: “Did Pets.com’s business plan assume the invention of transporters to magically move bags of pet food without shipping costs?”

Please, whatever you do, don’t share this with the people at Chewy; they might not realize their business model doesn’t work. Chewy reported $12.6 billion in sales and $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year.

The real lesson of Pets.com wasn’t that shipping dog food was a bad idea. It’s that the idea arrived before the logistics, customer habits and unit economics required to make it work.

As it was with chew toys and dog food, so it may be with enterprise blockchains.

Collectively, the crypto industry probably incinerated just as much money trying that between 2017 and 2023 as Pets.com. Maybe more. But the dozens of companies that went after enterprise blockchain were not delusional; they were just too early.

It’s not hard to understand the appeal of enterprise blockchain solutions, at least superficially. Nearly all enterprise systems today tend to fail at the boundaries between companies. There are two failure modes: mode 1, the OG failure mode, where collaboration information is constantly out of sync.

In this world, enterprise IT systems are islands, communicating asynchronously with each other by digital text messages and emailed spreadsheets. It’s cheap and easy to set up, if you don’t mind always having slightly wrong information.

Failure mode two is the costly, real-time proprietary integration. Powerful industry leaders politely request their key suppliers and partners to join their closed but always-on networks.

Chewy reported $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year. Source: Chewy.

These are very costly, but they work well and leave everyone with a kind of business version of Stockholm syndrome, where you come to appreciate the thoroughness and efficiency of the digital choke-hold you are in.

Blockchains offered a better path forward: shared information and business logic across an open ecosystem. All the benefits of a proprietary system in terms of real-time visibility and efficiency, without the lock-in.

Sometime around 2017, this started to look like a very obvious good idea. Investment poured in, consortia launched, press releases were drafted and released, and then pretty much everything crashed and burned. TradeLens, We.Trade, Contour, B3i, ASX Chess, Everledger. All came and went in just a few years.

No company wants their competition to see what they’re doing in detail. Mostly, this meant building a private/permissioned chain and then doing lots of non-blockchain-like things to it and in it to try to keep information private. The results were uniformly slow and expensive and failed to gain traction.

It’s hard to understate the bloodbath of companies and startups that tried and failed to make enterprise blockchain work. A quick web and history search turned up 18 different ones, some of them well-known.

What few survivors of this are left have “de-chained” themselves — giving up the blockchain theater and reverting to a classic software-as-a-service (SaaS) model. Many companies that tried and tested these permissioned enterprise systems as users came away from their experience with a clear learning: we tried blockchain, it didn’t work.

That’s unfortunate because everything is different now.

Blockchains have scale. Ethereum in 2020 handled 1 million transactions a day and costs per transaction periodically spiked to $30-50 when demand was high. Today, most transactions get done under a penny and capacity is ramping toward billions of transactions a day. Nobody talks about the “trilemma” anymore. Ethereum is decentralized and it is scaled.

Related: Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade launches on Sepolia testnet

Finally, there’s the money. It’s all moving onchain. Regulators around the globe have blessed stablecoins and the result is a tsunami of liquidity, with transaction volume reaching almost $1.8 trillion in June.

If we combine the operational benefits of blockchains with the financial ones, we get something that enterprises have never really had before: a single ecosystem where you can not only buy, sell, and move assets, but get paid for them as well.

There was just under $1.8 trillion in adjusted stablecoin transaction volume in June. Source: Visa

The return on investment from every single component of this equation is big. Combined, they can yield colossal advantages. McKinsey partners even found that digital supply chain tools could make inventory reductions of 35-75% possible through better planning.

More conservatively, from my experience in the field, just switching away from the existing cascades of spreadsheets and electronic data interchange (EDI) messages can allow firms to run most supply chains with about 20% less inventory at the same service level. That’s worth billions in working capital in most industries.

It gets better from there. Smart contracts reduce the time required to handle many business contract rules from days to minutes and cut the costs of administration in half.

Microsoft began moving its Xbox video game network onto smart contracts for handling royalties and cut the time to access monthly royalty statements from 45 days to four minutes. All that while handling more than 2 million transactions a day.

And once you have inventories, contracts, purchase orders and invoices onchain, you can go after working capital directly as well.

When you can prove your purchase order originates from a top-quality buyer, you can access credit for less. And when you have full visibility into inventory and delivery status, you can factor receivables immediately and efficiently.

The possibilities and the returns are big. The use cases are obvious. It’s time to try again.

#5124. Harvard Refuses to Dump Bitcoin Holdings Despite Downturn

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

As per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

The Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) showed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

As per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

In its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

#5123. JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion

JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion

JPMorgan Chase, whose CEO has spent years deriding crypto, is now sitting on close to $1 billion worth of crypto-linked stocks and funds, a regulatory filing shows, after the bank deepened those positions in the third quarter.

Adding up the disclosures in JPMorgan’s quarterly 13F, the form large institutional managers must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission to report their holdings, the bank held roughly $981 million across spot Bitcoin ETFs, Michael Saylor’s Strategy, and crypto exchange Coinbase as of Sept. 30.

Counting its stakes in Robinhood and Bitcoin miners, the total likely tips past $1 billion.

The largest piece is BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, or IBIT, where JPMorgan reported 11,408,930 shares worth about $540 million, a 9.6% increase in shares from the prior quarter, when the holding was valued at roughly $356 million. It held smaller positions in Grayscale’s and Bitwise’s Bitcoin ETFs, bringing its total spot Bitcoin ETF exposure to around $549 million.

The bank also leaned further into Strategy, the Bitcoin treasury company, raising its stake 36% to 848,932 shares, up from 624,387 at the end of June. That position was valued at about $131.3 million, up from $57.9 million a quarter earlier, reflecting both the added shares and a rise in Strategy’s stock over the period.

A roughly $301 million stake in Coinbase rounds out the core holdings, alongside positions in Robinhood and miners including Core Scientific and Hut 8. JPMorgan also disclosed sizable options tied to both IBIT and Strategy.

The company’s 13F is a snapshot as of Sept. 30 and doesn’t capture moves since, nor does it necessarily reflect directional bets. Banks often hold such positions to hedge or to facilitate client trades rather than to wager on price, so the near-$1 billion figure is better read as the scale of JPMorgan’s crypto-market activity than as a conviction call.

That nuance matters given CEO Jamie Dimon, who has called Bitcoin worthless and likened crypto to a fraud, even as the bank he runs steadily builds out digital-asset services.

Those services have expanded quickly. JPMorgan recently issued its first price forecast for Bitcoin, rolled out a deposit token called JPM Coin tied to bank dollars on Ethereum, and explored tokenized stocks alongside BlackRock and the DTCC.

The disclosure also lands during a rough stretch for Bitcoin funds. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have bled more than $1.4 billion over a recent five-day span as investors cut risk, a reminder that the institutional appetite captured in JPMorgan’s September snapshot has cooled since.

Bitcoin, which traded near $155 per Strategy share levels at quarter-end, has since slid well off its highs, today trading below $69,000.

His intervention followed reports that Huang had discussed a possible return with close allies, some of whom were reportedly organizing a lobbying campaign to pressure Nvidia's board.

Meanwhile, an online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has attracted more than 178,000 signatures, including names of prominent technology executives such as Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

Institutional shareholders have also entered the debate. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker urged Nvidia's board to keep all options open, including Huang's potential return, rather than rush into appointing a permanent successor.

Balaji Srinivasan, a prominent technology investor and former Coinbase executive, argued that Huang could mobilize enough shareholder support to challenge directors opposed to his reinstatement.

He suggested that Huang's influence at Nvidia and across the broader AI industry could push the board to reconsider its decision, citing provisions that allow qualifying shareholders to demand a special meeting.

“If Jensen says he wants back in, all of Nvidia and indeed the global AI ecosystem is still wired around him. The coup has no legitimacy. The anti-Jensen board members will immediately step down or likely be legally forced out.”

Yet shareholder support does not automatically translate into reinstatement. Nvidia's board retains responsibility for appointing a chief executive, and its investigation could significantly influence whether Huang is considered for another leadership role.

The next immediate test comes Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports quarterly earnings and holds its first major investor briefing since Huang's departure.

Investors will be looking for clarity on the company's leadership transition, strategic direction, and whether the board intends to consider its former chief executive as a potential successor.

#5121. Ripple's Schwartz Reveals Why XRP Ledger Used Satoshi's Code

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet said that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating new ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," said Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a new cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz said it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

"It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz said.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.

#5119. XRP’s proposed upgrade could improve trading without boosting token demand

New pool-pricing curves could improve execution, but additional XRP holding demand would depend on adoption, routing and persistent funding.

The XRP Ledger’s proposed AMM V2 overhaul would let creators of automated trading pools choose how those pools price trades, potentially giving traders more usable liquidity for the same deposit. For XRP holders, the potential benefits are better execution and new ways to provide liquidity; additional demand to hold the token would depend on which assets and routes attract capital.

The distinction is visible in today’s pools. XRPSCAN responses retrieved at 13:15 UTC on Nov. 15 showed roughly 25,065 of Ripple’s dollar stablecoin RLUSD and 25,068 of Circle’s USDC in the RLUSD/USDC pool, about $50,133 if both stablecoins are valued at $1. The XRP/RLUSD pool held about 1.94 million XRP and 1.88 million RLUSD.

Those are reserve snapshots, not amounts a trader could exchange at an unchanged price. They also illustrate two different inventory needs: the first pair holds two stablecoins, while the second holds XRP.

CryptoSlate’s XRP page displayed $0.97 when retrieved at 13:15 UTC on Nov. 15, with market data marked as updated eight minutes earlier.

An automated market maker, or AMM, lets users trade against a pool whose prices follow a formula. XRPL’s current design uses a constant-product-style curve. Liquidity supports trading across a broad price range, even when the assets usually trade close to one another.

The AMM Swappable Curves draft proposes alternatives. StableSwap would concentrate effective depth near the expected relationship between correlated assets, such as two dollar stablecoins. Concentrated liquidity would let providers allocate capital within chosen price ranges. Binned liquidity would place assets at discrete fixed prices, with execution moving to another price when a funded bin is exhausted.

The economic aim is more executable depth per unit of capital. A stablecoin pool could serve trades near parity with less money spread across distant prices. A provider choosing a narrower range could make the same deposit more useful while that range remains active.

The size of any trading improvement would depend on funding, price ranges, fees, trade size and whether correlated assets remain close in value.

Routing matters as much as the curve. XRPL already combines AMMs and order books. The draft would compare curve offers at each routing step using their actual output after fees at the offer’s size, rather than choosing solely by the displayed marginal price. Any execution comparison must therefore include order-book liquidity and alternative routes, not just these two pools.

A more efficient direct RLUSD/USDC pool could improve stablecoin execution without holding XRP as either trading asset. Users still face XRP transaction costs and applicable account or trust-line reserve requirements. Those requirements are separate from funding XRP inventory in a trading pair; current AMM ledger entries themselves have reserve exemptions, which do not automatically extend to new position entries proposed for AMM V2.

An XRP pair creates a different opportunity because its inventory includes XRP. Even there, capital efficiency cuts both ways. Less XRP could support a given amount of executable depth, while a larger, more active market could attract enough providers to raise aggregate deposits.

Proposed curves can change how efficiently liquidity works. The assets in each pair determine whether XRP is trading inventory.

A direct stablecoin pair can provide execution liquidity without XRP as a trading asset.

An XRP pair includes XRP trading inventory. Larger pool balances alone do not establish additional market-wide holding demand.

Better execution can arrive without additional XRP holdings; adoption and persistent funding must be measured.

AMM V2 is proposed. No efficiency multiple, executable quote, adoption forecast or new XRP buying is established. XRP fees and applicable user reserves are separate from trading inventory.

Qualitative mechanism diagram from the draft specification and current AMM mechanics. Lines and circle sizes are schematic, not quoted prices, measured depth or proportional reserves. Pair choices show asset roles, not tested routes.

AMM V2 is proposed. No efficiency multiple, executable quote, adoption forecast or new XRP buying is established. XRP fees and applicable user reserves are separate from trading inventory.

Higher turnover alone would not distinguish those outcomes. The same inventory can support repeated trades. A stronger holding-demand case would require persistent additional XRP balances across relevant pools and routes, with deposits, withdrawals and swaps separated so reserve changes are not mistaken for fresh buying.

Fee income also belongs to liquidity providers rather than all XRP holders. XRPL’s documentation describes relative-price and arbitrage risks. Concentrated liquidity adds range management: Uniswap’s explanation shows how a position can become entirely one asset and stop earning fees outside its range. More efficient capital is not automatically more profitable capital.

AMM V2 remains proposed work. The discussion opened in May, and the Foundation’s feasibility page was updated Nov. 4. Its roadmap lists rebasing and reopening the implementation pull request, then review and audit, as next steps. Activation requires validator approval. The current specification gives binned pools a separate amendment gate from concentrated liquidity and StableSwap.

The Foundation’s Nov. 4 assessment said no issuer, wallet, exchange or DEX front end had publicly committed to using the pools.

For XRP holders, persistent inventory tied to additional funded use would strengthen the demand case, but larger pool balances alone could reflect capital moved from elsewhere. Better execution could arrive before any additional holding demand is demonstrated.

#5118. China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts

China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts

Chinese developers are planning and building billions of dollars worth of AI data centers around Nvidia processors restricted by Washington, according to a Reuters investigation published Friday.

After examining more than 150 procurement notices, investment plans and corporate records, the news agency identified projects worth over 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion). Many specify Nvidia's H100, H200, or H800 chips, which provide the computing power used to train and run advanced AI models.

But $3.2 billion is the total value of the projects, including buildings, electricity and other infrastructure. The documents do not establish that all the processors were obtained, or that any export laws were broken.

One proposed computing center in Fujian province is valued at 6.2 billion yuan ($873 million). Its official investment listing specifies H100 servers but is still seeking financing partners.

In Shaanxi, a state-owned engineering group won a contract linked to a 3 billion yuan center naming H100 and H200 chips. A 2.26 billion yuan project in Jilin proposes combining Nvidia hardware with Chinese processors.

Inner Mongolia has another proposed development specifying 625 H200 servers. Meanwhile, authorities in Wuxi reported that an H800 computing cluster began operating in March 2025. Operating facilities and proposed investments are not evidence of the same level of chip access.

Nvidia's processors can carry out thousands of calculations at once, making them valuable for AI training. Its widely used software also makes switching to rival systems more complicated and potentially expensive.

The United States began restricting advanced AI chip sales to China in 2022, citing national security concerns. In January 2026, the Commerce Department moved H200 export applications to case-by-case review, although sales still require licenses. H100 shipments remain more tightly restricted.

That leaves Chinese developers with a dilemma: design facilities around familiar Nvidia equipment they may struggle to acquire, or invest in alternative processors that can require software changes and additional engineering.

An IDC report cited by Reuters estimated Nvidia accounted for 34% of China's AI accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026, compared with 28% for Huawei. Those figures cover the broader chip market, not confirmed shipments of restricted models.

Chinese AI developer Z.AI has already released an image-generation model trained entirely on Huawei chips, demonstrating that competitive systems need not depend on American hardware.

Still, the new project records show how deeply Nvidia remains embedded in Chinese AI infrastructure plans. They also add pressure on U.S. officials facing congressional scrutiny over how advanced chip export rules are enforced.

#5117. US sellers drive Bitcoin crash, Jensen plots Nvidia comeback: Hodler’s Digest

Anchorage Digital data suggests the Bitcoin selloff is being driven by US investors. A “war room” has been set up by supporters to reinstate Nvidia boss Jensen Huang.

Bitcoin bottomed after the US midterm elections in 2018 and 2022 — and the great Bitcoin crash of November 2026 looks like history repeating. Bitcoin plunged more than $10,000 this week, and is currently trading at $65,116 for a 12.4% loss.

According to Anchorage Digital researcher David Lawant, the call is coming from inside the house. “BTC sell pressure continues to come primarily from the U.S,” he noted, positing a chart highlighting showing continued heavy net taker sell flow primarily on Coinbase compared with overseas exchanges.

The US spot Bitcoin ETFs have seen heavy outflows, losing $2.35 billion over the past two weeks, and influencer Axel Bitblaze noted that Bitcoin fell in the hour before the US open on all but two of the past fifteen days.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao rebuffed the idea that Binance is behind the crash. “No, Binance did not sell crypto. I bought crypto in the past few days,” he said. He attributed the crash to money shifting to the Anthropic IPO, the Bitcoin ETF outflows, security fears about crypto in general in the wake of the Binance hack, and hot inflation data raising expectations of interest rate hikes. Markets are now pricing in a quarter point Fed hike in December.

Bitcoin fell to a four month low near $62,000 on Sunday but has since rebounded above $65,000. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index fell to 10, which is Extreme Fear.

History provides some good news in that Bitcoin more then doubled in price within 12 months of the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections.

The Financial Times reports that Jensen Huang is plotting a comeback to the top job at Nvidia with allies, following a determined push in Silicon Valley to pressure the board to reinstate him.

Nvidia shares plunged after Huang resigned as CEO and from the board on Nov. 12, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress named as interim CEO. The resignation came shortly after news broke he’d had two other affairs, including one with a subordinate.

Multiple people confirmed Huang has been discussing the idea of returning with confidants, even though an independent probe by the board is examining allegations he was romantically involved with a Chinese spy who helped ferry chips to China.

The FT reported one ally saying that supporters have put together a “war room” to reinstate him. “Everybody that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the source said.

A petition to reinstate Huang has garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including 5,600 current Nvidia employees, along with SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

The turmoil at Nvidia has weighed heavily on AI stocks and risk assets like cryptocurrency and the story still has a long way to run, with Congressional moves to investigate the issue and three bills being advanced to tighten AI chip export restrictions to China. According to the New York Time, intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Trump about the allegations Alice Huang was a Chinese spy a year ago, but he did not take any action.

Ethereum research group Ethlabs is withdrawing its Quick Slots proposal from the forthcoming Hegotá upgrade, and has urged core developers to urgently prepare the network for quantum attacks by 2027.

On Wednesday, the group outlined “pqai27,” a proposed roadmap that aims to protect Ethereum against threats from quantum computing and artificial intelligence.

At Devcon, researcher Justin Drake said he hopes to complete the transition in 2028 while the published roadmap still targets December 2029.

Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses. Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist. The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30.

“Index inclusion meant ordinary passive investors, like someone holding a global index fund in their pension, were getting leveraged Bitcoin exposure they never chose. MSCI just fixed that,” Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, told Cointelegraph. Strategy fell 6.49% on Thursday and are down by more than one quarter over the past month.

US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $2.35 billion in net outflows over two consecutive weeks, as redemptions reached more than $1 billion each week.

According to Farside Investors data, spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $1.07 billion between from Monday to Friday, following $1.28 billion in outflows the previous week, the largest weekly redemptions since late June.

Friday marked the seventh consecutive trading session of net withdrawals, with about $1.71 billion redeemed since Nov. 5

At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 12.4% to trade at $65,116, Ethereum (ETH) is down 14.4% to trade at $1,822 and XRP (XRP) is down 13.3% to $0.96. The total market cap is at $2.2 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.

Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Kite (KITE) with a 35.5% gain, Pieverse (PIEVERSE) on 33.8%, and Midnight (CRV) on 28.7%.

The top three altcoin losers of the week are Zcash (ZEC) which was down 25.4%, Uniswap (UNI) down 23.2% and Aero (AERO) down 23.1%.

Microsoft said that the outage stemmed from a problem introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade that emerged after a recent network change. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents,” the company said.

The crypto market remains under pressure, with Bitcoin dropping to a four-month low around $62,000 on November 15. SHIB, SOL and XLM all printed new lows on November 14, yet selling volume stayed well below earlier spikes, and oversold RSI readings suggest a recovery could be near, even though fundamental catalysts are still missing.

Thankfully, Shiba Inu's bearish rally might be fading sooner rather than later. The price's most recent red candle wasn't followed by a surge in selling volume, which could hint at a potential reversal.

On November 14, a single daily candle took SHIB below the July bottom around $0.0000041, with the wick reaching $0.0000037. At press time, the asset is trading at $0.00000387, the lowest level on the chart since March. Selling volume that day stayed well below the late July and August spikes.

Usually, when the price hits the bottom like that, the point of previously growing demand might become a source of additional selling pressure. For SHIB, it's the July zone, where buyers stepped in last time.

If we dive inside the 4HR price chart, we can clearly see a price/volume divergence, which is a good sign for bulls. Moving averages are diverging, so a quick retrace isn't yet possible. There's also potential for a quicker recovery thanks to RSI, which is sitting in the oversold zone on the daily chart.

SHIB is trading below all of its moving averages, with the 200 EMA hanging at around $0.0000054. Bitcoin's drop to a four-month low around $62,000 on November 15 didn't help either.

Despite the death cross on the chart solidifying, there's a good chance it's not critical. The price is showing negative performance one way or another, but it's not going to add more fuel to the bearish furnace.

The cross formed near $96, where a shorter moving average dropped below the 200 EMA, and another moving average is about to follow. SOL is trading at $71.70 after a wick to around $67.50 on November 14. Since its late September peak near $125, Solana has lost over 40% of its value.

First of all, death crosses aren't as scary as they used to be. Second, the signal is inherently lagging, so it only reflects what was already priced in. It's more of a guideline for those who are looking for an entry.

The chart shows a negative dynamic indeed, but, in a similar fashion to Shiba Inu, the bearish rally printed the first descending volume bar in a long time. Though it's only a single candle, it might be the start of a recovery.

The price is already oversold, but the bottom might be closer to $62, which is also reinforced by RSI. Back in June, $62 was the point where SOL bottomed out before the summer recovery.

Stellar has reached a potential price bottom where it might finally find ground for a retrace. The volume is relatively low, but the main issue is the lack of foundational recovery fuel.

XLM is trading at $0.1384 after dropping to $0.13 on November 14. That's below the May low around $0.142, the zone from which XLM spiked toward $0.30 in June. The RSI dipped below 30 during the drop. Since the late September high near $0.235, XLM has lost around 40%, while selling volume stayed far below the June and July spikes.

Short-term moving averages are crossing longer-term moving averages, and the issue here is that it's a signal of short-term aggravation. All of them are now above the price, with the 200 EMA at around $0.184.

The XLM update coming on November 23 is most likely priced in and unlikely to change the price direction fundamentally. Protocol 30, codenamed Bell, goes to a mainnet validator vote that day.

It adds post-quantum signature checks and muxed addresses for Soroban smart contracts and prepares the network for faster ledger timing. The upgrade has already been live on testnet since early November.

The key here is the crypto market recovery in general.

Perpetual futures exchange Lighter suspended withdrawals on Nov. 16 after a security incident that resulted in an estimated loss of roughly $15.5 million.

It said the protocol and smart contracts were unaffected and that it was targeting a resumption of withdrawals by the end of Nov. 16.

#5114. Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

The chairman of the House Oversight Committee is raising the prospect of barring government officials from trading on prediction markets, citing concerns that insiders are using nonpublic information to profit on platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.

In a staff memorandum released Friday, the committee detailed an investigation into insider trading by government officials, military personnel and people holding security clearances who have placed bets using information not available to the public.

The probe gathered nearly 1,700 pages of documents and included five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market platforms about how they detect and report suspicious activity.

Chairman James Comer framed the issue around public trust. “Americans are rightly concerned about public corruption,” he said, arguing Congress “has a duty to ensure our laws adequately prevent insider trading” and prohibit officials “from profiting from nonpublic information.”

He said lawmakers must weigh “additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people’s trust in government.”

The memo’s central recommendation is that Congress consider new restrictions on federal personnel, ranging from an outright ban on trading prediction markets to narrower limits on specific contracts, such as those tied to government decisions.

Applying such rules across all branches, the committee argued, would reinforce that government employees shouldn’t financially benefit from access to nonpublic information, and would remove even the appearance of it.

The memo stressed that existing insider trading laws already apply to prediction markets. It cited the Commodity Exchange Act, as amended by the STOCK Act, which bars federal employees, members of Congress and others from trading commodity futures, options, or swaps on nonpublic information drawn from their positions.

The committee credited the platforms themselves for policing their markets, noting that most reported insider trading incidents were first detected and flagged to regulators by the platforms. It singled out Polymarket, which recently hired a former law enforcement expert and rolled out surveillance software called “PolyGraph” built with analytics firm Chainalysis, and Kalshi for strengthening their detection protocols.

The scrutiny follows a string of cases involving alleged insider trading by public officials and government employees.

A U.S. soldier was charged in April over alleged Polymarket trades tied to a military operation that resulted in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Then, in August, the CFTC fined a former White House teleprompter operator for betting on presidential speeches.

The push also lands amid broader pressure on the sector, with the CFTC moving to assert authority over prediction markets in its fight against several states, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren sets her sights on the industry as the incoming Senate Banking chair.

Google reports matching conformance-test output and a 20–30% speed edge on sample clips, without announcing production deployment.

Google says its Antigravity /teamwork AI system rewrote libgav1, its AV1 video decoder, in Rust and made it 20–30% faster than the original C++ and hand-optimized assembly code on sample video clips. The result, disclosed in a November 13 engineering update, followed a port that initially ran around four times slower than the C++ version.

The company reports around 170,000 lines of Rust and 100% bit-exact parity across a broad conformance test suite, meaning the rewritten decoder matched the original’s output in those tests.

The performance reversal came after /teamwork received profiling tools and a goal of maximizing speed on sample clips, Google says. It reports the advantage on both x86_64 and ARM.

The migration separates two engineering problems: keeping an established program's behavior and making the replacement fast enough to use. Google's account illustrates why a successful translation alone does not settle the performance question.

Google reports a Rust rewrite of libgav1. Explore the output comparison and the profiling loop behind its reported performance result.

Google reports complete bit-exact parity across a broad conformance test suite.

The Rust port began slower; profiling and optimization on sample clips led to a reported advantage over C++ and assembly.

Matching a test suite answers a different question from measuring speed on sample video clips.

Keeping those checks intact gives the agents a fixed target while they change the implementation. Profiling then provides a separate feedback loop for finding where the new version spends its time.

The decoder work also predates this month's update. November's comparison is against C++ and assembly instead. The different baselines prevent treating those figures as one measured progression.

CryptoSlate's recent AWS Emulator coverage concerned agent-written software and human-designed release checks. Google's decoder example adds the challenge of preserving an existing implementation's outputs while improving its speed.

The November report does not specify processor models, compiler settings, clip identities, thread counts or timing distributions. It also does not identify a reproduction package for the Rust benchmark or announce that the rewritten decoder has entered production.

That leaves a concrete next test for the disclosure: a specified Rust revision, comparison build and video corpus would let other developers examine whether the reported advantage holds under their own conditions.
