#5112. Supreme Court Ends Custodia Bank’s Fight for a Fed Master Account, Leaving the Fed Free to Deny Crypto Banks Access

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied Custodia Bank’s petition to review the Federal Reserve’s refusal to give the Wyoming bitcoin bank a master account, ending chief executive Caitlin Long’s years-long fight for direct access to the central bank’s payment rails.

The case, Custodia Bank, Inc. v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, No. 26-62, is listed under “certiorari denied” on the Court’s Monday order list. The denial leaves in place a Tenth Circuit ruling that regional Federal Reserve Banks have discretion to reject even eligible applicants, and it closes the last court path Custodia had to force the Fed’s hand.

A master account is a bank’s account at a Federal Reserve Bank, and the entry point to Fedwire and other payment services. Without one, a state-chartered bank has to rely on a correspondent institution to move money.

Custodia is a Wyoming special purpose depository institution, a charter that bars it from making loans and requires dollar deposits to be fully reserved in liquid assets. After receiving that charter, it applied for a master account at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City in October 2020. In January 2021, the Kansas City Fed confirmed the bank was legally eligible and told it there were “no showstoppers.” In August 2021, Custodia also applied for Federal Reserve membership.

While those requests sat pending, the Board of Governors in August 2022 published guidelines for evaluating master-account applications. The rules put firms that are neither federally insured nor supervised by a federal banking agency into “Tier 3,” the group that “generally receive[s] the strictest level of review.” Custodia fell into that bucket.

On January 27, 2023, the Kansas City Fed denied the master account, citing an “unprecedented” business model “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities” and concluding the risks were “highly likely” to be “inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The same day, the Board denied Custodia’s membership application, saying approval “would be inconsistent with the financial, managerial, and corporate powers factors.”

Custodia had already sued the Fed and the Kansas City Fed in June 2022 over the delay. On March 29, 2024, U.S. District Judge Scott W. Skavdahl in Wyoming ruled that the Federal Reserve Act gives Reserve Banks discretion to grant or deny master accounts, dismissed Custodia’s Administrative Procedure Act claim for lack of a final agency action, and granted the Kansas City Fed summary judgment.

The Tenth Circuit affirmed on October 31, 2025, in a 2-1 decision Bitcoin Magazine covered at the time. Judge David Ebel, joined by Judge Veronica Rossman, held that Section 342 of the Federal Reserve Act, which says a Reserve Bank “may receive” deposits, is discretionary, and that the Monetary Control Act of 1980’s instruction that Fed services “shall be available” to nonmember banks is a pricing rule, not a right to an account.

Tymkovich dissented. “We are bound by the ordinary language of the statute and, in my view, shall means shall,” he wrote. The 1980 law, he said, “mandates access to the Fed’s payment services for all nonmember depository institutions.” On March 13, 2026, the full Tenth Circuit denied rehearing, with Judges Hartz, Tymkovich and Eid voting to grant. Being denied a master account, Tymkovich wrote in that later dissent, is “akin to a death sentence.”

Custodia’s July petition, filed by Kannon Shanmugam, asked whether the Monetary Control Act “gives presidents of regional Federal Reserve Banks discretionary authority to deny master accounts” to legally eligible nonmember banks. The Board and the Kansas City Fed opposed review. The Court distributed the case for its Nov. 13 conference and turned it down today.

The practical effect is that a state charter, even one that makes a bank legally eligible, does not guarantee a door into the Fed’s payment system. Crypto-focused banks and other novel charters now have little judicial recourse, at least in the Tenth Circuit, if a Reserve Bank turns them away. Critics have long described that pattern of exclusion, and of banks cutting off crypto firms, as Operation Choke Point 2.0.

Neither Custodia nor Long had commented on the Supreme Court’s denial as of 10:07 a.m. ET Monday.

#5111. Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT

Silicon Valley executives are reportedly organizing a campaign to bring Huang back and are looking to gain White House support.

Jensen Huang is reportedly considering a return as Nvidia CEO just days after resigning from the company following reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to Nvidia, according to the Financial Times, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. One source told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for Nvidia’s chief’s return, and are looking to gain support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said.

Meanwhile, a public campaign called “Bring Jensen Back” has attracted more than 161,000 signatures, according to its organizers, who list Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its supporters. The campaign website also claims to have over 9,000 signatures from current and former Nvidia employees.

The push for his return goes against calls for new leadership at the AI chipmaker and coincides with an independent board investigation and scrutiny of its chip sales to China.

Related: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shake-up” of Nvidia’s leadership, urging the company to hire a CEO from outside the company, while US President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook take the job.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation following reports of alleged extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.

The controversy has also raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with US restrictions on AI chip sales, particularly involving customers in Asia with potential ties to China.

Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% on Thursday before recovering to close 4.3% lower, underscoring investor uncertainty over the AI chipmaker’s future leadership.

#5110. Strategy planned to slow STRC buybacks near $100 but spent another $1.4 billion instead

More than half of its $2.7 billion repurchase spending came at average prices above $99, leaving just $332 million as Bitcoin purchases slow.

Strategy has spent more repurchasing STRC near $100 than at deeper discounts, testing its stated strategy of slowing purchases as the preferred stock approaches face value.

A CryptoSlate analysis of the Michael Saylor-founded company's regulatory filings shows that it spent approximately $1.4 billion buying back STRC between Sept. 28 and Nov. 15, when weekly average purchase prices ranged from $99.06 to $99.93.

That represents 52% of the nearly $2.7 billion Strategy has spent under its preferred-stock repurchase program since July. By comparison, the company spent approximately $1.28 billion during the preceding 10 weeks, when its average purchase prices were below $99.

Averages are shown to two decimals by STRC.live, derived from issuer-reported share counts and buyback spending rounded to $0.1 million, so cents are approximate. The Nov. 9–15 average is calculated from Strategy’s $228.1 million and 2,282,510 shares. The $100 series is the security’s stated amount.

Source: STRC.live buyback tracker, July 20 to Nov. 8, 2026 · Strategy Form 8-K, Nov. 16, 2026 (latest week)

The spending has coincided with STRC's recovery toward its $100 stated value. The preferred stock briefly touched $100 on Nov. 4 for the first time since May before retreating below that threshold.

However, the continued buying contrasts with the approach Strategy CEO Phong Le outlined in July.

Le said the company intended to scale purchases according to price and liquidity, buying “more at deeper discounts and less as the STRC trading price approaches $100 per share.”

The company's weekly disclosures show that its STRC spending generally increased as the discount narrowed.

Strategy initially spent $25 million repurchasing 288,930 shares at an average price of $86.52 between July 20 and July 26.

By Sept. 28-Oct. 4, weekly spending had climbed to $176.3 million at an average price of $99.39, even though the discount to stated value had narrowed from nearly 13.5% to approximately 0.6%.

Meanwhile, Crypto Banter founder Ran Neuner highlighted the scale of the intervention, observing that Strategy had repurchased nearly 30% of the STRC it had issued.

The company nevertheless has an economic incentive to continue retiring shares near face value.

STRC currently carries a 12% annualized dividend, meaning repurchases reduce future dividend obligations at the prevailing rate.

However, Strategy's ability to maintain its current buying pace under the existing program is diminishing.

Its latest SEC filing showed just $332.2 million remaining under its $3 billion authorization, with nearly 89% already exhausted.

At the latest weekly pace, another $228.1 million in repurchases would leave approximately $104 million available.

Zaid suggested another expansion could arrive soon, given the spending pace. Strategy previously raised the authorization from $1 billion to $2 billion in September and to $3 billion in October.

Strategy has continued accumulating Bitcoin alongside its preferred-stock repurchases, although purchases have slowed considerably.

Between Sept. 28 and Nov. 15, the company acquired 3,183 BTC for approximately $253.1 million, compared with the $1.39 billion spent on STRC during the same period.

The gap was particularly pronounced last week, when Strategy spent $228.1 million to repurchase STRC, compared with just $33.4 million to acquire 485 BTC.

Those transactions increased its Bitcoin holdings to 850,849 BTC, acquired for approximately $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,452 per coin. The firm currently has unrealized losses of more than $10 billion.

Strategy funded $206.3 million of its latest STRC repurchases through MSTR common-stock sales, highlighting the trade-off between reducing preferred-dividend obligations and expanding its Bitcoin treasury.

That capital-allocation decision comes as the company faces another challenge.

Index provider MSCI has confirmed Strategy's removal from its global equity indexes, effective Dec. 1, under rules excluding companies classified as non-operating businesses.

The exclusion could create additional selling pressure from index-tracking funds, potentially weakening MSTR's share price and making equity-funded Bitcoin purchases less attractive.

With its STRC repurchase authorization nearly exhausted, Strategy must decide whether to expand the program again or reduce purchases near $100.

That decision will also help determine whether the company can return to the larger Bitcoin acquisitions seen earlier this year while its common stock adjusts to the loss of MSCI index membership.

#5109. Harvard Holds 3.04 Million Bitcoin ETF Shares Steady

Harvard Management Company left its stake in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust unchanged at 3,044,612 shares in the third quarter, a position valued at $144.1 million as of Sept. 30 and now worth about $110.6 million after bitcoin’s slide.

The university’s endowment manager disclosed the holding in a Form 13F filed Friday, covering the quarter ended Sept. 30. The share count is the same one Harvard reported on June 30 and on March 31. At 10:40 a.m. ET Monday, IBIT traded at $36.32, putting the stake at about $110.6 million, a paper decline of roughly $33.6 million, or 23%, from the value in the filing. The Sept. 30 close of $47.34 matches the price implied by the reported value.

The same 3,044,612 shares were worth $101.4 million on June 30 and $117.0 million on March 31, so the position rose in value during the third quarter as bitcoin recovered, then gave back a large share of that gain after the quarter ended. Even after the November slide, the stake is still worth more than it was at midyear.

IBIT was Harvard’s eighth-largest position among 18 holdings in a 13F portfolio valued at $3.95 billion, or about 3.6% of that publicly disclosed book of U.S. securities, which does not include the rest of the endowment. The largest holding was Space Exploration Technologies, reported at $1.29 billion. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing was second, at $616.5 million. That ranking is a sharp change from late 2025, when the bitcoin ETF was Harvard’s largest publicly disclosed position.

Harvard first reported an IBIT position in its filing for the quarter ended June 30, 2025: 1,906,000 shares worth $116.7 million. It had not listed the fund in earlier 13Fs, including the report for March 31, 2025. By Sept. 30, 2025, Harvard had tripled the stake to 6,813,612 shares, valued at $442.9 million, making IBIT its largest public holding.

The endowment trimmed that position by about 21% in the fourth quarter of 2025, to 5,353,612 shares worth $265.8 million, and opened a first stake in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust of 3,870,900 shares, valued at $86.8 million. It cut the bitcoin ETF again in the first quarter of 2026, by about 2.31 million shares, or 43%, to the 3,044,612 shares it still reported on Sept. 30, and sold the Ethereum fund entirely. The latest filing lists no other bitcoin or crypto ETFs. The remaining IBIT position is still larger, in share terms, than the 1.91 million shares Harvard first disclosed.

Harvard’s gold ETFs are now much larger than its bitcoin position. The same 13F lists 1,161,000 shares of SPDR Gold Shares worth $442.2 million, the portfolio’s third-largest holding, and 1,980,085 shares of the iShares Gold Trust worth $154.6 million. Combined, the two gold funds were valued at $596.8 million, more than four times the IBIT stake. The iShares Gold Trust share count was unchanged from June 30. The SPDR Gold Shares position jumped from 58,862 shares at midyear.

Bitcoin traded near $64,200 as of 10:40 a.m. ET Monday, down about 17% in November from an Oct. 31 close near $77,400, and down about 23% from about $83,550 at the end of September. Since the quarter closed, U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have been seeing heavy redemptions. IBIT bled about $2 billion over nine straight sessions through mid-November, and the funds as a group extended their outflow streak to seven sessions through Friday, losing about $1.91 billion since Nov. 5.

The 13F is a snapshot of holdings as of Sept. 30. It does not show whether Harvard bought or sold any IBIT shares in October or November.

#5108. Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, putting a former Nvidia executive in contention for one of technology's biggest jobs.

Haas is one of several people under consideration, people familiar with the matter told the FT. There is no guarantee he will receive an offer or accept one. The FT said he maintains strong ties to Huang and some Nvidia directors.

Nvidia's board told Reuters it was still selecting an executive search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” it said.

Huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading the company he co-founded, following reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a business executive suspected by U.S. officials of having Chinese intelligence ties. The company said it had no reason to believe its secrets were compromised.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones has become board chair. Analysts have also floated Nvidia data-center executive Ian Buck and AMD chief Lisa Su as possible successors, though those names are not confirmed appointments or offers.

An internal Nvidia suggestion-box post has attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supportive of Huang's reinstatement, according to Wired. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one anonymous employee wrote.

Other staff members have demanded transparency around his departure. The campaign shows Huang still has supporters inside Nvidia; it does not mean the board has opened talks to reinstate him.

Haas, 64, is a Silicon Valley-based semiconductor executive whose career spans engineering, product development and sales. He earned an electrical engineering degree from Clarkson University and worked at chip companies Tensilica and Scintera Networks before joining Nvidia in 2006.

He spent seven years at Nvidia as vice president and general manager of its computing products business, then moved to Arm in 2013. At Arm, he rose from strategic alliances to chief commercial officer in 2015 and head of its intellectual-property products group in 2017, before becoming CEO in February 2022.

That appointment came as Nvidia's proposed $40 billion takeover of Arm collapsed under pressure from regulators. Haas was suddenly running a business his former employer had tried, unsuccessfully, to buy.

He steered Arm back onto the Nasdaq in September 2023 at an initial valuation of about $54.5 billion, one of the year's largest stock-market debuts. The IPO also gave Japanese owner SoftBank a way to sell shares while retaining control.

Unlike Nvidia, which primarily sells graphics processors and related computing systems, Arm licenses chip designs and computing architecture to companies including Apple, Amazon and Qualcomm, earning fees and royalties when customers use its technology. Arm-based designs are now increasingly found in cloud servers as well as phones.

Arm reported $1.44 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, up 27% from a year earlier. Royalties from data-center chips doubled, while Arm said initial commercial deliveries of its new CPU remain on track for early 2027.

Haas also sits on SoftBank's board and, since April, has served as CEO of SoftBank Group International, helping oversee its semiconductor and AI interests. A move to Nvidia would require untangling those ties, particularly because the companies are partners whose interests increasingly overlap in data-center hardware.

For Nvidia, the next leader would inherit not just its lead in AI chips, but delicate relationships with governments and customers as Washington debates tighter export restrictions on China. Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on November 17, with Kress at the helm and its permanent CEO search still underway.

#5107. Luxor CEO warns of AI ‘dark forest’ following Bitcoin miner hijack

Attackers redirected customers’ Bitcoin mining power through Luxor’s Commander platform over the weekend, prompting its CEO to issue a warning to crypto businesses.

Bitcoin mining services provider Luxor has warned that AI-enabled cyberattacks are becoming increasingly difficult to defend against after attackers compromised its mining-management platform and redirected customers’ computing power to another mining pool over the weekend.

In an X post on Sunday, Luxor CEO Nick Hansen said the attack came through a “sophisticated AI-enabled vector,” without specifying how AI was used in the attack, warning that these types of attacks will only get more frequent over time.

“At this moment, anyone running any sort of substantial business, especially in crypto, is inundated with AI-enabled attacks,” Hansen said in an X post. “This does not seem to be slowing down; rather, it’s speeding up as models get better and more attackers enter the arena.”

The warning comes as security researchers have documented the spread of AI-assisted hacking tools, raising the prospect of faster attacks against businesses holding money or controlling valuable infrastructure.

“Abliterated models are running 24/7 against your entire surface, looking for a little crack, which they then use to (almost instantly) expand,” added Hansen.

Hansen said Luxor has had to put the majority of its feature work on hold in order to harden its cybersecurity. The company has also acquired its own GPUs to run unrestricted open-weight AI models aimed at improving its security posture.

“I urge anyone running a similar service to do the same.  It’s your only defense in this new AI-powered dark forest. ‘The only thing that stops a bad guy with a gun is a good guy with a gun.’”

Initial reports suggested that about 64,000 mining machines representing 13 exahashes per second were redirected to the OCEAN mining pool on Saturday.

Luxor has not confirmed either figure, saying the incident affected just over a dozen customer accounts using its Commander mining-management tool.

Luxor said it patched Commander within two hours of detecting the unauthorized changes and began restoring affected machines to their original pool settings. It pledged to compensate customers in full for the redirected mining power and publish a post-mortem.

Cointelegraph contacted Luxor for comment.

Related: Coinone warns of phishing, identity theft after customer data breach

“We have explored the issue extensively, and it was isolated to the Commander tool. None of Luxor’s other services (including Luxor Pool and LuxOS) were affected,” said Luxor.

Initial reports suggested the attackers received no mining rewards. However, a Bitcoin address identified by CoreX as associated with the incident subsequently received two OCEAN payouts totaling approximately 0.162 BTC, worth about $10,500.

Hansen’s warning follows a string of reported AI-assisted intrusions targeting crypto businesses.

Earlier this month, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that a group called Crafty Falcon was using AI-powered tools to attack financial companies, including cryptocurrency exchanges, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis disclosed in October that an attacker used what it called “offensive agentic techniques” to access its systems. The breach exposed password hashes, live tokens and other customer information.

Anthropic said in a September report that multiple groups had developed “automated exploit foundries” with AI, accelerating the pace of vulnerability research, testing, and exploit design.

#5105. Bitcoin Lightning developers patch bug that could make completed payments disappear

A software flaw could cause nodes to lose track of settled payment updates after restarting, threatening the integrity of Lightning channel records.

Bitcoin Lightning developers patched a software vulnerability that could cause nodes to lose track of settled payments after a restart, potentially disrupting the accounting records that secure payment channels.

The flaw affected LND, a widely used implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning Network, which enables users to send Bitcoin through payment channels without recording every transaction directly on the blockchain.

Developers released v0.21.8-beta and v0.20.8-beta on Nov. 11 to address the issue, which stemmed from an error in how the software saved and restored channel updates.

The vulnerability could cause a node to reconstruct incomplete payment records after restarting, even when the original information remained stored on its disk.

That failure threatened the consistency of Lightning channels, where participants rely on accurate records to determine which payments have settled and what each party is owed.

According to LND maintainer Olaoluwa Osuntokun, known as Roasbeef, the problem involved a counter that tracked acknowledged updates from a connected Lightning peer.

The software stored the number of entries using a 16-bit unsigned integer, which can represent values only up to 65,535.

Once the list reached 65,536 entries, the counter reset to zero, even though LND continued writing the updates to storage.

Upon restarting, the node could interpret that zero as an empty list and omit a previously settled hashed timelock contract (HTLC), a conditional payment mechanism that helps secure transactions across Lightning channels.

At 65,536 log entries, LND's old stored count could wrap to zero. The released patch adds write guards and checks older records on load.

Oversized lists are rejected before commitment progress or revocation, and before serialization writes record bytes.

The updated reader validates entries and count. It can recover qualifying complete lists; malformed trailing data is rejected.

The fix prevents new oversized logs and conditionally recovers complete older records.

Applies to this unsigned acknowledged update log and its overflow condition. Complete legacy data must pass entry/count checks; malformed data is rejected. No observed exploitation or financial loss is established by the reviewed sources.

Schematic of the maintainer-described count/content mismatch and the released write and legacy-load checks. Geometry shows control flow, not measured traffic or payment values. Selected states distinguish newly rejected oversized logs from conditional recovery of older records.

Applies to this unsigned acknowledged update log and its overflow condition. Complete legacy data must pass entry/count checks; malformed data is rejected. No observed exploitation or financial loss is established by the reviewed sources.

The vulnerability became more concerning after developers identified a potential way for connected peers to push the affected update list toward its limit.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

In the GitHub discussion, LND collaborator ziggie1984 explained that a peer could repeatedly send transaction fee updates and commitment signatures while withholding a required revocation message.

That behavior allowed the list of pending acknowledgments to grow without being cleared.

The developer reproduced the behavior in a unit test, generating 201 stored updates after 200 rounds of messages.

Crucially, the accumulated entries survived reconnects, suggesting that repeatedly disconnecting and reconnecting would not necessarily prevent the list from eventually reaching the overflow threshold.

The potential weakness matters because Lightning depends on both parties maintaining consistent payment-channel states. Losing track of a settled update could undermine the records used to reconcile channel obligations.

However, the project's disclosures do not identify any confirmed exploitation or financial losses associated with the flaw.

To address the problem, developers introduced checks that prevent oversized update lists from advancing the channel state or being written to storage.

They also modified how LND reads existing records, allowing nodes to recover complete update lists saved by older versions when the underlying data passes validation.

The fix was merged into LND's main development branch on Nov. 5 before being included in both November releases.

#5101. OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s dots complete purchases with tokenized card details, after users approve each transaction. The limited rollout targets U.S. ChatGPT Pro users; the wallet does not hold crypto or a cash balance. Coinbase and Circle offer a different route, using stablecoins to let agents pay for services with less human involvement.

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on Friday, giving its AI agents a way to purchase products using American Express, Mastercard, and Visa cards. The new system lets an agent finish online checkout without accessing the customer's actual card number, and it doesn't involve cryptocurrency.

The wallet works through dots, OpenAI's always-on AI assistants, which can browse websites and carry out tasks for users. A customer saves an eligible card, reviews the order and approves the payment using a security check such as a fingerprint or Face ID.

After approval, the card network creates a payment token containing substitute card details. The agent submits the token through the merchant’s existing checkout system, while the customer keeps applicable card rewards and dispute protections, according to OpenAI’s announcement.

“An agent making a purchase should strengthen, not bypass, the trust built into payments,” Sherri Haymond, Mastercard's global head of digital commercialization, said in the announcement.

OpenAI previously introduced Instant Checkout with Stripe in September 2025, allowing people to buy from participating merchants inside ChatGPT. Wallet takes a different approach: agents can navigate ordinary online stores and use existing checkout forms, without requiring each business to build a special integration.

OpenAI is also courting merchants. Just three days before the Wallet launch, it introduced business profiles that let companies update product information and connect with potential customers through ChatGPT.

Google is working on a competing approach. Its Universal Commerce Protocol, introduced in January, aims to connect shopping agents with retailers, payment providers and post-purchase services across Google products.

Coinbase launched Agentic Wallets in February, giving software the ability to spend USDC, trade tokens, and pay for online services within preset limits. Unlike ChatGPT Wallet, the Coinbase product is primarily developer infrastructure, not a consumer checkout feature.

“It's not an SDK, it's not a library—it's a purpose-built wallet to work with an agent as quickly as possible,” Coinbase engineering executive Erik Reppel told Decrypt at the launch.

Coinbase's x402 protocol lets software pay for data or computing services as part of a web request, often using the USDC stablecoin. That makes tiny transactions possible without requiring an agent to enter card details or obtain human approval each time.

Stablecoin issuer Circle is pushing in the same direction. Its Agent Stack, launched in May, includes stablecoin wallets and tools for payments as small as $0.000001.

“USDC is uniquely well-suited for the agentic economy because it is internet-native, programmable, and always available,” Circle product chief Nikhil Chandhok said in a company statement.

Actual agent-driven demand is harder to measure. In September, blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs estimated that agents accounted for only 0.6% to 7.5% of filtered x402 commerce by value, using models that cannot conclusively distinguish agents from scripts.

For consumers, ChatGPT Wallet offers familiar card payments rather than a digital asset balance. OpenAI's terms say merchants remain responsible for deliveries and returns, and users must generally contact their card issuers for billing disputes.

OpenAI plans to let users authorize future purchases within spending limits or specified categories, but has not announced when that feature will arrive. In the meantime, it warns that merchant websites may block shopping agents or flag otherwise legitimate Wallet purchases as fraud.

#5100. Aave’s revenue falls $10M in Q3, but one metric tells a new story

Aave's quarterly revenue fell 36.6% as liquidation fees plunged and borrow-interest income declined despite rising deposits.

Aave’s deposits grew during the third quarter of 2026, but the lending protocol’s quarterly borrow-interest revenue remained below the second-quarter levels, according to an Aave Labs report published Nov. 13.

The report puts supplied assets up about 40% between July 1 and Oct. 1, while its borrow-interest revenue line fell roughly 23% from the previous quarter.

Lower liquidation-related receipts explain about 39% of the overall revenue decline, but a smaller borrow-interest line also contributed substantially. Monthly revenue improved through the third quarter, and Aave’s separate official dashboard shows net income rising, so the figures do not establish a fall in profit.

The report lists total protocol revenue of roughly $27.3 million in the second quarter and $17.3 million in the third quarter, a decline of almost $10 million (36.6%). Its named borrow-interest line fell from $16.2 million to $12.5 million, a reduction of $3.7 million.

Combining ordinary liquidation fees with Smart Value Recapture (SVR) liquidation fees gives $4.3 million in the second quarter against about $402,429 in the third quarter. That $3.9 million reduction accounts for 39.1% of the total revenue decrease.

The borrow-interest line explains another 37.1% of the decrease. Other revenue lines, net of increases, account for the remaining 23.8%. Staking income fell from nearly $1.3 million to zero, special income from about $684,000 to zero, and the separate aToken interest line declined by roughly $708,000.

Labs reports monthly protocol revenue of $5.4 million in July, $5.7 million in August and $6.2 million in September. Its borrow-interest line also rose each month, from $3.9 million to $4.1 million, then to $4.4 million.

Meanwhile, the report’s all-version supplied balance rose from $24.1 billion on July 1 to $33.8 billion on Oct. 1. Borrowed assets increased from $10.2 billion to $13.3 billion.

Asset-price changes can affect dollar balances, so without a matching average lending balance, the tables cannot establish that Aave earned less per dollar lent. They show an endpoint balance rebound alongside a smaller quarterly revenue total.

TokenLogic's Aave Insights dashboard reports revenue for the second and third quarters of $23.4 million and $17.8 million, respectively, different from the Labs report.

It shows net income rising from $197,930 to $1.7 million as expenses fell from $23.2 million to $16.1 million. The sources provide no numerical reconciliation between the two revenue series.

DefiLlama’s monthly revenue figures total approximately $21.3 million for April through June and $13.4 million for July through September.

DefiLlama’s methodology separates borrower fees, revenue retained by the protocol, supplier income, and tokenholder revenue. These measures cannot be substituted for Aave Labs’ profit, DAO net income or returns to AAVE holders.

Labs describes its operational figures as unaudited and subject to revision, and says they are not financial statements of Aave Labs or the DAO. The breakdown above uses that report’s revenue series throughout.

A separate development is TokenLogic’s Nov. 12 reserve-factor proposal, which changes the reserve factor across 54 asset reserves in 12 Aave V3 markets and the older V2 Ethereum market, projecting about $3.5 million in additional annualized DAO revenue at Nov. 9 balances and rates.

The proposal would lift the blended reserve factor from 12.0% to 12.7%. Its Plasma USDT0 component remains conditional on finalized terms, and the forum post lists community feedback and escalation to an on-chain proposal as next steps.

The reserve factor allocates borrower interest between suppliers and the DAO, but retaining a larger share is a different mechanism from attracting more deposits.

#5098. German Bundestag Lets Customs Freeze Crypto Over €100,000 Without a Criminal Case as the Bill Goes to the Bundesrat

The German Bundestag on Thursday approved a government bill that would let customs freeze cryptocurrency and other assets worth more than €100,000 when their lawful origin appears implausible, without first opening a criminal case. Permanent confiscation would still take a finance-court judgment. The measure still needs the Bundesrat’s consent before a planned Jan. 1, 2027 start, and the timing of that upper-house vote remains unclear.

The Bundestag passed the Customs Financial Justice Act, a Finance Ministry overhaul to strengthen the customs administration and fight financial crime, on Nov. 12. The federal government introduced the bill on Sept. 30. The Finance Committee recommended passage on Nov. 11, with the Christian Democrats, Social Democrats and Alternative for Germany in favor, The Left opposed and the Greens abstaining.

Crypto is covered expressly, using the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets definition, but it is not singled out. The same administrative procedure applies to cash, cars, real estate and other property. It reaches only “significant” assets: generally those worth more than €100,000, or more than €50,000 if the asset must be entered in a public register, such as vehicles or land. Because crypto is not registered that way, the €100,000 threshold applies. Customs may estimate the value, and closely related items can be treated as one asset.

Customs offices — not Germany’s Financial Intelligence Unit, which the same bill strengthens separately — may freeze those assets for up to 30 days without a criminal case if there are factual indications the origin is not lawful, meaning lawful acquisition “does not appear plausible.” A finance court may extend that hold once by 150 days. That extension is decided by a single judge, without a hearing, in an order that cannot be appealed. Filing a confiscation application stops the clock until the court rules, so the often-cited 180-day period is not a hard cap.

Permanent confiscation still requires a finance-court panel to be convinced the origin is unlawful. The committee shifted that decision away from a single judge. Owners must be told they are not required to produce records, and anything they do provide may be used in tax and criminal cases. The official justification says mere silence, or a denial of knowledge, will as a rule not be enough to prevent confiscation.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said in August that if suspects cannot show assets were legally acquired, “the Porsche or the Rolex are gone for now.” In Thursday’s debate, Social Democrat Ingo Vogel told the Bundestag that criminally acquired assets do not enjoy constitutional property protection, and that the bill is “no automatic confiscation” and “no blanket reversal of the burden of proof.”

The Bundesrat, in an earlier comment, had asked for a true burden-of-proof reversal and for the court extension to run up to 12 months, citing, among other things, “crypto concealment structures.” The government refused the fuller reversal and did not adopt the longer hold in the bill the Bundestag approved.

Germany’s Federal Bar Association opposes the bill, warning that vague terms and missing paperwork, including for inherited assets, should not be treated as proof of illegality. The German Bar Association also rejected the government draft. The Blockchain Bundesverband, commenting on the ministry draft, said the law needed to distinguish custodial, self-custodied and decentralized arrangements, because with a self-custodied wallet control “regularly lies with the holder of the private key,” and state access then exists only through measures against the person, not through third parties. The bill itself is silent on how, or whether, customs could take self-custodied keys. A freeze of crypto would be carried out by attachment under the Tax Code.

The government expects about €308 million a year in extra revenue from 2028 from the procedure as a whole, not from crypto alone. The Greens argued that figure is a sliver of Germany’s estimated €100 billion annual money-laundering volume.

The new power is separate from an earlier criminal case. In 2024, Saxony’s prosecutors, with the Federal Criminal Police Office, sold about 49,858 bitcoin from the Movie2k case between June 19 and July 12, for €2.64 billion. That sale was an emergency liquidation in a criminal proceeding, not an exercise of the administrative tool the Bundestag has now approved.

#5096. Louisiana blocks prediction markets and threatens $370M in revenue from exchanges

Louisiana’s crackdown on prediction markets targets Robinhood and Coinbase intermediaries as the CFTC challenges state enforcement.

Louisiana's Nov. 12 order related to prediction markets reaches the brokers and clearing firms behind the apps, as well as the exchanges themselves.

Its scope, documented in the CFTC's federal complaint, exposes a shared legal risk for platforms earning income from different kinds of trading.

Robinhood and Coinbase each report prediction-market revenue alongside their crypto businesses. Louisiana's action reaches several layers of the trading chain, including the intermediary serving the customer.

According to the CFTC's complaint, Louisiana obtained an ex parte temporary restraining order on Nov. 12 against entities including registered exchanges, futures commission merchants and derivatives clearing organizations. Ex parte means the initial order was obtained without the other side being heard.

The complaint quotes restrictions on offering, clearing, settling, brokering and otherwise facilitating specified event contracts involving people located in Louisiana without the required state license and permit.

Its description includes sports, elections, and award events within the order's stated statutory scope.

The court-filed copy of the order names Robinhood Derivatives and Coinbase Financial Markets, along with multiple Kalshi entities, ForecastEx and Rothera.

Robinhood's product disclosure identifies Robinhood Derivatives as the intermediary and lists KalshiEX, ForecastEx, Rothera, and Crypto.com Derivatives North America as venues. Coinbase says it offers its contracts through Coinbase Financial Markets and has Kalshi operate them, which determines outcomes.

Robinhood already has several exchange routes. If the same restricted broker remains involved, moving a contract to another venue leaves the intermediary within the order's documented reach. That conditional legal-scope analysis leaves each company's implementation unconfirmed.

Robinhood reported $173 million in event-contract revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30, more than six times the year-earlier figure. Cryptocurrency revenue was $120 million, down 55%.

Coinbase's Oct. 29 announcement said prediction markets had surpassed $200 million in annualized revenue.

The US and CFTC sued Louisiana and state officials on Nov. 13, arguing that federal derivatives law preempts the state's enforcement. They seek declaratory and injunctive relief, including a bar on enforcing or extending the state order.

The government's motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction is listed for submission Nov. 17. In Louisiana's enforcement case, which moved to federal court, Robinhood seeks to vacate the state order, and Rothera seeks its dissolution or modification.

In a separate federal case, Kalshi's Nov. 13 oral request concerned withdrawal of its own temporary-restraint application, with its preliminary-injunction hearing scheduled for Nov. 23.

Louisiana-specific treatment of new orders, existing positions, settlement and withdrawals remains unconfirmed.

Prediction markets can add income beyond crypto trading while leaving competing platforms exposed to the same state restrictions. A different exchange partner alone offers no demonstrated protection where the order also reaches the broker.
